questions.t: Liam spent $2 less than 23 of his money on a book, then $2 more than 34 of what remained on lunch. He had $2 left. How much money did he start with?
questions.a: Work backwards. Let R be the money left after buying the book. Lunch cost 34R + 2, so 14R − 2 = 2, giving 14R = 4 and R = $16. If M is the starting amount, the book cost 23M − 2, so R = M − (23M − 2) = 13M + 2 = 16, giving 13M = 14 and M = $42. Check: book $28 − $2 = $26, leaving $16; lunch $12 + $2 = $14, leaving $2.

questions.t: A fraction gives a terminating decimal exactly when its denominator is a product of powers of 2 and powers of 5. List every fraction with numerator 1 whose denominator is greater than 1 and less than 40 that gives a terminating decimal.
questions.a: The denominators must be of the form 2a × 5b: 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 16, 20, 25 and 32. So the fractions are 12, 14, 15, 18, 110, 116, 120, 125 and 132 — nine in all. (40, 50 and 64 are all 40 or more, so they are excluded.)

questions.t: Explain why the length of the repeating cycle of the decimal for 1n is always less than n.
questions.a: When 1 is divided by <var>n</var> using the division algorithm, each step leaves a remainder that must be one of 0, 1, 2, …, <var>n</var> − 1. A remainder of 0 would make the decimal terminate, so for a recurring decimal there are only <var>n</var> − 1 possible remainders. After at most <var>n</var> − 1 steps some remainder must occur a second time, and once a remainder repeats the following digits repeat in exactly the same order. So the cycle length is at most <var>n</var> − 1, which is less than <var>n</var>.

questions.t: A rectangular block of land measures 10 m by 7 m. A rectangle 4 m by 3 m is cut off one corner, leaving an L-shaped block in which every angle is a right angle.

ap: The sides are 10, 4, 4, 3, 6, 7, giving a perimeter of 34 m.

The two cut sides (4 m across and 3 m down) replace exactly the 4 m and 3 m that were removed from the top and the right-hand side, so the horizontal sides still total 10 + 10 = 20 m and the vertical sides still total 7 + 7 = 14 m: perimeter = 2 × (10 + 7) = 34 m.

questions.t: Are there more milliseconds in an hour than there are seconds in a week? Show the calculations that decide the question.
questions.a: Milliseconds in an hour = 60 × 60 × 1000 = 3 600 000. Seconds in a week = 7 × 24 × 60 × 60 = 604 800. Since 3 600 000 > 604 800, there are more milliseconds in an hour — almost 6 times as many.

questions.t: A rectangular pen is to be built using exactly 84 m of fencing. Each side length is a whole number of metres.

Which whole-number rectangle has the smallest area, and what is that area?
ap: The perimeter is 2 × (length + width) = 84, so length + width = 42.
Testing pairs adding to 42: 1 × 41 = 41, 10 × 32 = 320, 20 × 22 = 440, 21 × 21 = 441. The largest area is the square 21 m × 21 m, area 441 m<sup>2</sup>.
The smallest is 1 m × 41 m, area 41 m<sup>2</sup>. (The nearer the rectangle is to a square, the larger the area for a fixed perimeter.)

questions.t: A rectangular lawn measures 12 m by 7 m. A concrete path 1.5 m wide is laid all the way around the outside of the lawn.
p: Find the area of the path.
Find the perimeter of the outer edge of the path.
ap: The path adds 1.5 m at each end, so the outer rectangle is (12 + 3) m by (7 + 3) m = 15 m by 10 m, with area 15 × 10 = 150 m<sup>2</sup>. The lawn has area 12 × 7 = 84 m<sup>2</sup>, so the path has area 150 − 84 = 66 m<sup>2</sup>.
Outer perimeter = 2 × (15 + 10) = 50 m.

questions.t: A staircase-shaped figure has only right angles. Starting at the top-left corner, its boundary runs: right, down, right, down, right, down, then down the right-hand side, then left all the way along the bottom, then up the left-hand side back to the start. The left-hand side is 9 m and the bottom is 14 m, but none of the step lengths are given. Find the perimeter of the figure and explain how you can do this without knowing the individual steps.
questions.a: All the short horizontal steps together move the same total distance to the right as the bottom side does to the left, so they add to 14 m. Likewise all the short downward steps together add to the same total as the left-hand side, 9 m. Perimeter = 14 + 9 + 14 + 9 = 2 × (14 + 9) = 46 m.

questions.t: Six workers can paint 240 m of fence in 5 days. Working at the same pace, how many workers are needed to paint 480 m of fence in 4 days?
questions.a: 6 workers × 5 days = 30 worker-days paint 240 m, so one worker paints 240 ÷ 30 = 8 m in a day. To paint 480 m in 4 days, 480 ÷ 4 = 120 m must be painted each day, needing 120 ÷ 8 = 15 workers.

questions.t: Ravi cycles 6 km up a hill at an average speed of 8 km/h, then rides back down the same 6 km road at an average speed of 24 km/h.
p: Find his average speed for the whole trip.
Explain why the answer is not 16 km/h, the average of 8 and 24.
ap: Time up = 6 ÷ 8 = ¾ hour; time down = 6 ÷ 24 = ¼ hour. Total time = 1 hour for a total distance of 12 km, so the average speed is 12 ÷ 1 = 12 km/h.

Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, not the average of the two speeds. He spends three-quarters of the hour at the slow speed and only a quarter at the fast speed, so the slow speed counts for much more and pulls the average down below 16 km/h.

From the first to the fourth marker there are 3 gaps, so each gap is 450 ÷ 3 = 150 m. From the first to the ninth there are 8 gaps: 8 × 150 = 1200 m.

questions.t: Two whole numbers are multiplied together and the product is odd. Decide whether each statement below is always true, sometimes true or never true, and give a reason or a counter-example.
p: Both of the numbers are odd.
Their sum is even.
Their difference is a multiple of 4.
Their quotient is a whole number.
ap: Always true — if either number were even, the product would have a factor of 2 and so would be even.
Always true — both numbers are odd, and odd + odd = even.
Sometimes true — 5 − 1 = 4 is a multiple of 4, but 5 − 3 = 2 is not.
Sometimes true — 9 ÷ 3 = 3 is a whole number, but 5 ÷ 3 is not.

questions.t: Last digits of powers.
p: Explain, without using a calculator, how you can tell that 4 728 653 is not a square number.
The second-last digit of an odd square number is always even. Check this for 15<sup>2</sup>, 17<sup>2</sup> and 19<sup>2</sup>.
Find the last digit of 7<sup>4</sup> and the last digit of 3<sup>5</sup>. What do you notice about the last digit of a fifth power?
ap: A square number can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. This number ends in 3, so it cannot be a square number.
15<sup>2</sup> = 225, 17<sup>2</sup> = 289 and 19<sup>2</sup> = 361; the second-last digits are 2, 8 and 6, and all three are even.

7<sup>4</sup> = 7<sup>2</sup> × 7<sup>2</sup> = 49 × 49 = 2401, so the last digit is 1; 3<sup>5</sup> = 243, so the last digit is 3. A fifth power always ends in the same digit as the number being raised to that power.

questions.t: Find the value of the pronumeral in each case.

questions.t: Explain each answer carefully.
p: Can a triangle have two right angles?
Can a triangle have two acute exterior angles?
What is the smallest number of acute angles a triangle can have?
ap: No. Two right angles already add to 180°, leaving 0° for the third angle, which is impossible.
No. An exterior angle is acute only when the interior angle beside it is obtuse (greater than 90°), and two obtuse interior angles would add to more than 180°.
Two. A triangle can have at most one angle that is 90° or more, so at least two of its angles are acute.

questions.t: In ΔABC the side <var>BC</var> is produced in both directions, to <var>D</var> beyond <var>B</var> and to <var>E</var> beyond <var>C</var>, so that <var>D</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var>, <var>E</var> lie on one straight line. Given that ∠ABD = 115° and ∠ACE = 130°, find all three interior angles of ΔABC. Give reasons.
questions.a: ∠ABC = 180° − 115° = 65° (straight angle at B); ∠ACB = 180° − 130° = 50° (straight angle at C); ∠BAC = 180° − (65° + 50°) = 65° (angle sum of ΔABC). Check: 65° + 50° + 65° = 180°.

questions.t: In ΔABC, <var>AB</var> = <var>AC</var> and ∠BAC = 40°. The side <var>BC</var> is produced to <var>D</var>.
p: Find ∠ACB.
Find ∠ACD.
The bisector of ∠ABC meets <var>AC</var> at <var>M</var>. Find ∠ABM.
ap: ∠ABC = ∠ACB (base angles of isosceles ΔABC) and 2∠ACB = 180° − 40° = 140°, so ∠ACB = 70°.
∠ACD = 180° − 70° = 110° (straight angle at C). (Or 40° + 70° = 110° by the exterior angle theorem.)

questions.t: In quadrilateral PQRS, ∠P = 2<var>α</var>, ∠Q = 3<var>α</var>, ∠R = 4<var>α</var> and ∠S = 6<var>α</var>.
p: Find the value of <var>α</var>.
Find the size of the largest angle of PQRS.
Is PQRS convex? Explain your answer.
ap: 2<var>α</var> + 3<var>α</var> + 4<var>α</var> + 6<var>α</var> = 360° (angle sum of a quadrilateral), so 15<var>α</var> = 360° and <var>α</var> = 24°.
The angles are 48°, 72°, 96° and 144°, so the largest is ∠S = 144°.
Yes. Every angle is less than 180°, so no angle is reflex and the quadrilateral is convex.

questions.t: PQRS is a quadrilateral in which <var>PQ</var> is parallel to <var>SR</var>. ∠SPQ = 105° and ∠PQR = 82°. Find ∠PSR and ∠QRS, giving a reason for each.
questions.a: ∠PSR = 180° − 105° = 75° (co-interior angles, PQ ∥ SR, transversal PS). ∠QRS = 180° − 82° = 98° (co-interior angles, PQ ∥ SR, transversal QR). Check: 105° + 82° + 98° + 75° = 360°.

questions.t: Describe, step by step, how to carry out each construction using only compasses, a straight edge and a sharp pencil.
p: A triangle ABC with <var>AB</var> = 8 cm, <var>AC</var> = 6 cm and <var>BC</var> = 5 cm.
An angle of 30° at the endpoint <var>A</var> of an interval <var>AB</var>.
ap: Draw the interval AB of length 8 cm. With centre A and radius 6 cm draw an arc above AB. With centre B and radius 5 cm draw a second arc crossing the first at C. Join AC and BC.

First construct 60°: with any radius and centre A draw an arc cutting AB at P; with the same radius and centre P draw an arc cutting the first arc at Q; then ∠QAB = 60° because APQ is equilateral. Now bisect ∠QAB: with centre P and centre Q draw two equal arcs meeting at R, and join AR. Then ∠RAB = 30°.

questions.t: <var>AOB</var> is a diameter of a circle with centre <var>O</var>, and <var>P</var> is any other point on the circle. The radius <var>OP</var> is drawn. Let ∠OAP = <var>x</var> and ∠OBP = <var>y</var>.
p: Explain why ∠APO = <var>x</var> and ∠BPO = <var>y</var>.
By using the angle sum of ΔAPB, show that <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 90°.
Hence state the size of ∠APB, and describe this result in words.
ap: OA = OP (radii), so ΔAOP is isosceles and ∠APO = ∠OAP = <var>x</var> (base angles). Similarly OB = OP, so ∠BPO = ∠OBP = <var>y</var>.

In ΔAPB the angles are ∠A = <var>x</var>, ∠B = <var>y</var> and ∠APB = <var>x</var> + <var>y</var>. Hence <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> + (<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = 180°, so 2(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = 180° and <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 90°.
∠APB = <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 90°. So the angle subtended at the circle by a diameter is always a right angle (the angle in a semicircle is 90°).

questions.t: <var>ABCD</var> is a quadrilateral with all four vertices on a circle of centre <var>O</var>, and <var>O</var> lies inside <var>ABCD</var>. The four radii <var>OA</var>, <var>OB</var>, <var>OC</var> and <var>OD</var> are drawn, forming four isosceles triangles. Let ∠OAB = <var>a</var>, ∠OBC = <var>b</var>, ∠OCD = <var>c</var> and ∠ODA = <var>d</var>.
p: Explain why ∠OBA = <var>a</var>, ∠OCB = <var>b</var>, ∠ODC = <var>c</var> and ∠OAD = <var>d</var>.
Show that <var>a</var> + <var>b</var> + <var>c</var> + <var>d</var> = 180°.
Hence show that ∠DAB + ∠BCD = 180°.
ap: In each triangle the two sides from O are radii, so the triangle is isosceles and its base angles are equal: in ΔOAB, OA = OB so ∠OBA = ∠OAB = <var>a</var>, and similarly for the other three triangles.

The four interior angles of ABCD are ∠DAB = <var>d</var> + <var>a</var>, ∠ABC = <var>a</var> + <var>b</var>, ∠BCD = <var>b</var> + <var>c</var> and ∠CDA = <var>c</var> + <var>d</var>. Their sum is 2(<var>a</var> + <var>b</var> + <var>c</var> + <var>d</var>) = 360°, so <var>a</var> + <var>b</var> + <var>c</var> + <var>d</var> = 180°.
∠DAB + ∠BCD = (<var>d</var> + <var>a</var>) + (<var>b</var> + <var>c</var>) = 180°. So opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle are supplementary.

questions.t: <var>A</var>, <var>B</var> and <var>X</var> lie on a straight line, with <var>B</var> between <var>A</var> and <var>X</var>. <var>T</var> is a point above the line, and <var>M</var> is a point on the interval <var>AT</var> chosen so that <var>AM</var> = <var>MB</var> = <var>BT</var>. Let ∠TAB = <var>α</var>.
p: Explain why ∠MBA = <var>α</var>.
Show that ∠BMT = 2<var>α</var>.
Hence prove that ∠TBX = 3<var>α</var>.
ap: AM = MB, so ΔAMB is isosceles and ∠MBA = ∠MAB = <var>α</var> (base angles).
∠BMT is an exterior angle of ΔAMB at M, so ∠BMT = ∠MAB + ∠MBA = <var>α</var> + <var>α</var> = 2<var>α</var>.

MB = BT, so ΔMBT is isosceles and ∠BTM = ∠BMT = 2<var>α</var>. Since M lies on AT, ∠ATB = 2<var>α</var>. Now ∠TBX is an exterior angle of ΔABT at B, so ∠TBX = ∠TAB + ∠ATB = <var>α</var> + 2<var>α</var> = 3<var>α</var>.

questions.t: This question proves the theorem: if two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal. In ΔXYZ, ∠Y = ∠Z = α. Suppose the sides were not equal — say XY is longer than XZ. Mark the point P on XY so that XP = XZ, and join PZ. Let ∠XPZ = β.
p: Using ∠XPZ as an exterior angle of ΔYPZ, show that <var>β</var> is greater than <var>α</var>.
Show that ∠XZP = <var>β</var> as well, and hence explain why <var>β</var> must be less than <var>α</var>.
Explain how the theorem follows from this contradiction.
ap: ∠XPZ is an exterior angle of ΔYPZ, so <var>β</var> = ∠PYZ + ∠PZY = <var>α</var> + ∠PZY. As ∠PZY is greater than 0°, <var>β</var> > <var>α</var>.
XP = XZ, so ΔXPZ is isosceles and ∠XZP = ∠XPZ = <var>β</var>. But P lies between X and Y, so the ray ZP lies inside ∠XZY, giving ∠XZP < ∠XZY = <var>α</var>. Hence <var>β</var> < <var>α</var>.

We cannot have both <var>β</var> > <var>α</var> and <var>β</var> < <var>α</var>, so the assumption that XY is longer than XZ is false. The same argument with the letters swapped shows XZ cannot be longer than XY. Therefore XY = XZ, so the sides opposite the equal angles are equal.

questions.t: You are given a circle with centre <var>O</var>. Using a straight edge and compasses only, explain how to construct a square <var>ABCD</var> with all four vertices on the circle, and explain why your figure really is a square.
questions.a: Draw any line through O, cutting the circle at A and C; then AC is a diameter. Construct the perpendicular bisector of AC with compasses (equal arcs from A and from C, above and below, joined by a straight line); it passes through O and is perpendicular to AC there. Let it cut the circle at B and D. Join AB, BC, CD and DA. The diagonals AC and BD are both diameters, so they are equal in length, they bisect each other at O, and they meet at right angles — a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other at right angles is a square. (Equivalently, the four triangles AOB, BOC, COD, DOA are congruent right-angled isosceles triangles with legs equal to the radius, so the four sides are equal and each vertex angle is 45° + 45° = 90°.)

questions.t: Angles in a quadrilateral.
p: Explain why a quadrilateral cannot have more than one reflex interior angle.
What is the greatest number of obtuse interior angles a quadrilateral can have? Justify your answer and give an example.
ap: A reflex angle is greater than 180°, so two reflex angles would add to more than 360° on their own. But the four interior angles of a quadrilateral add to exactly 360°, and the other two angles are each greater than 0°. So there can be at most one reflex angle.

Three. If all four angles were obtuse, each would be greater than 90° and the sum would be greater than 360°, which is impossible. Three obtuse angles can occur, for example 100°, 100°, 100° and 60°, which add to 360°.

questions.t: The sum of two numbers is −415 and their difference is 112. Find the two numbers.
questions.a: Adding the two facts gives twice the larger number: −415 + 112 = −4.2 + 1.5 = −2.7, so the larger number is −1.35 = −1720. Subtracting gives twice the smaller: −4.2 − 1.5 = −5.7, so the smaller number is −2.85 = −21720. Check: −1.35 + (−2.85) = −4.2 ✓ and −1.35 − (−2.85) = 1.5 ✓

questions.t: The average of five numbers is −225. A sixth number is included and the average of all six numbers is now −12. Find the sixth number.
questions.a: Sum of the first five = 5 × (−2.4) = −12. Sum of all six = 6 × (−0.5) = −3. So the sixth number is −3 − (−12) = −3 + 12 = 9.

questions.t: In a 3 × 3 magic square every row, every column and both diagonals add to the same total. Write (r, c) for the cell in row r and column c. You are told that (1, 1) = 1, (1, 2) = −212, (2, 2) = −12, (3, 1) = −1 and (3, 3) = −2.

ap: The diagonal (1,1) + (2,2) + (3,3) = 1 + (−12) + (−2) = −112, so every line adds to −112.
Row 1: 1 − 212 + (1,3) = −112, so (1, 3) = 0. Column 1: 1 + (2,1) − 1 = −112, so (2, 1) = −112. Column 3: 0 + (2,3) − 2 = −112, so (2, 3) = 12. Column 2: −212 − 12 + (3,2) = −112, so (3, 2) = 112.
(1,3) + (2,2) + (3,1) = 0 + (−12) + (−1) = −112 ✓ (Row 2: −112 − 12 + 12 = −112; Row 3: −1 + 112 − 2 = −112.)

questions.t: Dario gives 40% of his weekly wage to his parents, and then 25% of the remainder to his sister. He still has $270 left. How much does he earn in one week?
questions.a: After giving 40% away, 60% of the wage is left. Keeping 75% of that leaves 75% of 60% = 45% of the wage. So 45% of the wage = $270, and 1% = $6, giving a wage of $600. Check: 40% of 600 = $240, remainder $360, 25% of 360 = $90, and 360 − 90 = $270. ✓

questions.t: Harriet spent 25% of her savings on a skateboard, and then 20% of the remainder on a helmet. What percentage of her savings does she have left?

questions.t: Leo spent $36 of his pocket money on a computer game, and then 25% of the remainder on a book. He still has 35 of his pocket money left. How much did he have before he began spending?
questions.a: Let the pocket money be M. After the game he has M − 36, and he keeps 75% of that, so ¾(M − 36) = 35M. Then 0.75M − 27 = 0.6M, so 0.15M = 27 and M = $180. Check: 180 − 36 = 144, 25% of 144 = 36, and 144 − 36 = 108 = 35 of 180. ✓

questions.t: Nina's salary is $950 per week. She receives a pay increase of 20% in March, and then a pay decrease of 10% in September.

ap: The 10% decrease is taken from the larger amount $1140, not from $950, so it removes $114 rather than $95. Overall she gains 1026 − 950 = $76, and 76950 × 100% = 8%, so it is a single 8% increase.

questions.t: Sam makes a cordial drink so that 15% of the drink is cordial and the rest is water. He has 600 mL of the drink in a jug. How much extra cordial must he add so that 20% of the drink is cordial?
questions.a: The jug holds 15% of 600 = 90 mL of cordial and 510 mL of water. The water does not change, and it must become 80% of the new total, so the new total = 510 ÷ 0.8 = 637.5 mL. Extra cordial = 637.5 − 600 = 37.5 mL. Check: cordial = 90 + 37.5 = 127.5 mL, and 127.5637.5 = 0.2 = 20%. ✓

questions.t: Jug 1 contains juice and water in the ratio 3 : 5. Jug 2 has juice and water in the ratio 1 : 3.

ap: Take each jug as 8 equal parts. Jug 1 has 3 parts juice and 5 parts water; jug 2 has 2 parts juice and 6 parts water. Combined: juice : water = 5 : 11.
Jug 1 is 8 parts (3 juice, 5 water) and jug 2 is 16 parts (4 juice, 12 water). Combined: juice : water = 7 : 17.

questions.al: There are 11 tiles: M A T H E M A T I C S.
ap: two A's, so 211
two T's, so 211
vowels A, E, A, I, so 411
11 − 4 = 7 consonants, so 711

questions.t: Twenty counters numbered 1 to 20 are placed in a bag and one is drawn at random. Find the probability that the number is:
p: not 13
a multiple of 5
not a multiple of 5
ap: 120
1 − 120 = 1920
multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20, so 420 = 15
1 − 15 = 45

questions.t: A box contains four red marbles numbered 1 to 4, six green marbles numbered 5 to 10, and two blue marbles numbered 11 and 12. One marble is drawn at random. Find the probability that:
p: the marble is red
the marble is green
the number is odd
the number is greater than 8
the marble is green with an even number
questions.al: There are 12 marbles altogether.
ap: 412 = 13
612 = 12
odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, so 612 = 12
9, 10, 11, 12, so 412 = 13
green evens are 6, 8, 10, so 312 = 14

questions.t: A packet of lollies contains 8 strawberry, 12 lime, 6 orange and 4 blackcurrant lollies, all the same size and shape. One lolly is taken out at random. Find the probability that it is:
p: orange
lime or blackcurrant
not strawberry
mango
neither orange nor lime
ap: 630 = 15
1630 = 815
2230 = 1115
0 (impossible)
strawberry or blackcurrant = 8 + 4 = 12, so 1230 = 25

questions.t: Each number from 1 to 200 is written on a card and the cards are placed in a box. One card is withdrawn at random. What is the probability of obtaining a number that is:
p: divisible by 4?
less than 50?
a multiple of 25?
ap: 4, 8, ..., 200 gives 200 ÷ 4 = 50 cards, so 50200 = 14
the numbers 1 to 49, so 49200
25, 50, ..., 200 gives 8 cards, so 8200 = 125

questions.t: A tennis club has 240 members. Of the 105 junior members, 60 play doubles and the other 45 play singles only. Of the 135 senior members, 90 play doubles and 45 play singles only. Every member's name is written on a card, the cards are placed in a barrel and one card is drawn at random. Find the probability that the name drawn belongs to:
p: a junior member
a member who plays doubles
a member who plays singles only
a junior member who plays doubles
ap: 105240 = 716
60 + 90 = 150, so 150240 = 58
45 + 45 = 90, so 90240 = 38
60240 = 14

questions.t: In a survey, every student who rode a bicycle through the school gate one morning was recorded by year level: 12 were in Year 7, 18 in Year 8, 15 in Year 9, 9 in Year 10 and 6 in Year 11. One of these riders is chosen at random. What is the probability that the rider is:
p: in Year 8?
in Year 9 or above?
not in Year 7?
below Year 9?
ap: 1860 = 310
15 + 9 + 6 = 30, so 3060 = 12
60 − 12 = 48, so 4860 = 45
12 + 18 = 30, so 3060 = 12 (parts b and d are complementary, and 12 + 12 = 1)

questions.t: A bag contains only red and white counters. There are 45 counters altogether and the probability of drawing a red counter is 25. How many white counters are in the bag? Show your reasoning.
questions.a: Number of red counters = 25 of 45 = 18. So white counters = 45 − 18 = 27. (Check: P(white) = 2745 = 35, and 25 + 35 = 1.)

questions.t: In a raffle, 40 tickets numbered 1 to 40 are sold. They are placed in a hat and one is drawn at random to win the prize. Find the probability that the number on the winning ticket:
p: contains the digit 3
does not contain the digit 1
contains the digit 2 at least once
is an odd number greater than 25
ap: 3, 13, 23 and 30–39 gives 3 + 10 = 13 tickets, so 1340
tickets containing a 1 are 1, 10–19, 21, 31, that is 1 + 10 + 1 + 1 = 13, so 40 − 13 = 27 do not, giving 2740
2, 12, 20–29, 32 gives 1 + 1 + 10 + 1 = 13, so 1340
27, 29, 31, 33, 35, 37, 39 gives 7 tickets, so 740

questions.t: The 40 raffle tickets in the previous question are coloured: tickets 1 to 18 are green, tickets 19 to 30 are yellow, and the rest are blue. Find the probability that the winning ticket:
p: is blue
is not yellow
is green or yellow
is both green and blue
is an even-numbered yellow ticket
is a prime-numbered green ticket
questions.al: Green 1–18 (18 tickets), yellow 19–30 (12 tickets), blue 31–40 (10 tickets).
ap: 1040 = 14
40 − 12 = 28, so 2840 = 710
18 + 12 = 30, so 3040 = 34
no ticket can be two colours, so the probability is 0
20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30 gives 6 tickets, so 640 = 320
primes up to 18 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, that is 7 tickets, so 740

questions.t: Ahmed, Bella, Chen and Dina enter a draw in which there are two equal prizes. No person can win more than one prize.
p: List all the ways the two prizes can be allocated.
What is the probability that Bella wins a prize?
What is the probability that neither Bella nor Chen wins a prize?
ap: There are 6 ways: Ahmed and Bella, Ahmed and Chen, Ahmed and Dina, Bella and Chen, Bella and Dina, Chen and Dina.
Bella appears in 3 of the 6 equally likely allocations, so 36 = 12
only Ahmed and Dina avoids both, so 16

questions.t: A two-digit number is chosen at random. Find the probability that it is divisible by:
p: four
six
questions.al: The two-digit numbers are 10 to 99, so there are 90 outcomes.
ap: multiples of 4 run 12, 16, ..., 96, that is (96 − 12) ÷ 4 + 1 = 22 numbers, so 2290 = 1145
multiples of 6 run 12, 18, ..., 96, that is (96 − 12) ÷ 6 + 1 = 15 numbers, so 1590 = 16

questions.t: A jar initially contains 9 green beads and 16 yellow beads. Some of the yellow beads are removed. A bead is then drawn out at random, and the probability that it is green is 35. How many yellow beads were removed?
questions.a: The 9 green beads are untouched. If n beads remain in the jar, then 9n = 35, so 3n = 45 and n = 15. That leaves 15 − 9 = 6 yellow beads, so 10 yellow beads were removed. (Check: 915 = 35.)

questions.t: A cafe offers three dishes of the day and Priya cannot decide between them. All she has is a fair coin. Describe how she can use the coin to choose one of the three dishes so that each dish has probability 13, and explain why your method is fair.
questions.a: Toss the coin twice and record the pair of results. The four outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT are equally likely, each with probability 14. Assign HH to the first dish, HT to the second and TH to the third; if TT comes up, ignore that pair and toss twice again. The three useful outcomes are equally likely, so at whatever stage the choice is finally made each dish is equally likely, giving each a probability of 13. (Tossing once and using 'heads for dish 1, tails then decide' would not be fair, because dish 1 would get 12.)

questions.t: Write down the coordinates of the image of each point under a translation of 3 units right and 2 units down.
p: <var>A</var>(1, 4)

questions.t: A point and its image under a translation are given. Describe each translation in words.
p: <var>P</var>(2, 1) and <var>P</var>′(6, 4)
<var>Q</var>(−3, 5) and <var>Q</var>′(−3, −1)
<var>R</var>(0, −2) and <var>R</var>′(−4, 3)
ap: 4 units right and 3 units up.
6 units down (no sideways shift).
4 units left and 5 units up.

questions.t: Write down the coordinates of the image of each point under the reflection stated.
p: <var>A</var>(3, −2) in the <var>x</var>-axis
<var>B</var>(−5, 4) in the <var>x</var>-axis
<var>C</var>(6, 1) in the <var>y</var>-axis
<var>D</var>(−2, −7) in the <var>y</var>-axis

questions.t: The point <var>P</var>(4, 1) is rotated about the origin <var>O</var>. Write down the coordinates of the image under:
p: a rotation of 90° anticlockwise
a rotation of 90° clockwise
a rotation of 180°

questions.t: Answer these questions about the three transformations: translation, rotation and reflection.
p: Which one has no fixed points at all?
Which one has exactly one fixed point, and what is that point called?
Which one reverses the order in which the vertices of a triangle are labelled?
ap: A (non-identity) translation — every point moves.
A (non-identity) rotation; its one fixed point is the centre of rotation.

A reflection: if <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var> are clockwise then <var>A</var>′, <var>B</var>′, <var>C</var>′ are anticlockwise. (The only fixed points of a reflection are the points on the axis of reflection.)

questions.t: State the order of rotational symmetry of each figure.
p: a rectangle that is not a square
an equilateral triangle
a regular decagon
a kite that is not a rhombus
ap: It has no rotational symmetry (only the identity rotation of 360° carries it onto itself).

questions.t: How many axes of reflection symmetry does each figure have?
p: a square
a rhombus that is not a square
an isosceles triangle that is not equilateral
a regular hexagon
ap: 2 (the two diagonals)

questions.t: For each capital letter, written in the usual block form, state how many axes of symmetry it has and its order of rotational symmetry.
p: H
N
T
ap: H: 2 axes of symmetry (one horizontal, one vertical); rotational symmetry of order 2.
N: no axes of symmetry; rotational symmetry of order 2.
T: 1 axis of symmetry (vertical); no rotational symmetry.

questions.t: A figure is translated 5 units right and 2 units down. Its image is then translated 3 units left and 6 units up.
p: Describe the single translation that has the same effect.
The point <var>M</var>(−1, 3) is on the original figure. Write down the coordinates of its final image.
ap: Sideways: 5 right then 3 left is 2 units right. Vertically: 2 down then 6 up is 4 units up. So the single translation is 2 units right and 4 units up.

questions.t: In each part, two rotations about the same centre <var>O</var> are carried out one after the other. Describe the single rotation that has the same effect.
p: 40° anticlockwise, then 110° anticlockwise
70° anticlockwise, then 160° clockwise
135° clockwise, then a further 135° clockwise
ap: 40° + 110° = 150° anticlockwise about <var>O</var>.
160° − 70° = 90° clockwise about <var>O</var>.
135° + 135° = 270° clockwise about <var>O</var> (the same as 90° anticlockwise about <var>O</var>).

questions.t: Triangle <var>PQR</var> has vertices <var>P</var>(1, 2), <var>Q</var>(5, 2) and <var>R</var>(5, 5). It is translated 3 units down, and the image is then reflected in the <var>y</var>-axis to give triangle <var>P</var>″<var>Q</var>″<var>R</var>″.
p: Write down the coordinates of <var>P</var>′, <var>Q</var>′ and <var>R</var>′ after the translation.
Write down the coordinates of <var>P</var>″, <var>Q</var>″ and <var>R</var>″.
Find the area of triangle <var>P</var>″<var>Q</var>″<var>R</var>″ in square units, and explain your answer.
ap: Subtract 3 from each <var>y</var>-coordinate: <var>P</var>′(1, −1), <var>Q</var>′(5, −1), <var>R</var>′(5, 2).
Reflecting in the <var>y</var>-axis changes the sign of each <var>x</var>-coordinate: <var>P</var>″(−1, −1), <var>Q</var>″(−5, −1), <var>R</var>″(−5, 2).

In the original triangle <var>PQ</var> = 4 and <var>QR</var> = 3 with a right angle at <var>Q</var>, so the area is ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units. Translations and reflections do not change lengths or angles, so the image also has area 6 square units.

questions.t: The point <var>A</var>(3, −5) is reflected in the <var>x</var>-axis, and the image is then reflected in the <var>y</var>-axis.
p: Write down the coordinates of the final image.
Describe a single transformation that has the same effect for every point.
ap: (3, −5) → (3, 5) in the <var>x</var>-axis → (−3, 5) in the <var>y</var>-axis. Final image (−3, 5).
Both coordinates have changed sign, so the combination is a rotation of 180° about the origin.

questions.t: A regular polygon is drawn by marking equally spaced rays out from the centre of a circle, as in the pentagon construction.
p: What angle must the rays be apart to construct a regular 15-gon?
How many axes of symmetry does a regular 15-gon have, and what is its order of rotational symmetry?
A regular polygon is constructed with rays 18° apart. How many sides does it have?
ap: 15 axes of symmetry, and rotational symmetry of order 15.

questions.t: The lines <var>m</var> and <var>n</var> are the vertical lines <var>x</var> = 1 and <var>x</var> = 5. A figure is reflected in <var>m</var>, and the image is then reflected in <var>n</var>.
p: Find the coordinates of the final image of the point <var>P</var>(0, 2).
Describe the single transformation that has the same effect as the two reflections.
Two parallel lines are <var>a</var> units apart. Describe the single transformation produced by reflecting in the first and then in the second.
ap: Reflecting in <var>x</var> = 1 sends (0, 2) to (2, 2) since it is 1 unit left of the line and must finish 1 unit right of it. Reflecting (2, 2) in <var>x</var> = 5 sends it to (8, 2), because it is 3 units left of that line. Final image (8, 2).
Every point moves 8 units right, so the combination is a translation of 8 units to the right — twice the 4-unit gap between the lines.
A translation of 2<var>a</var> units, perpendicular to the lines, in the direction from the first line towards the second.

questions.t: Triangle <var>ABC</var> has vertices <var>A</var>(0, 0), <var>B</var>(3, 0) and <var>C</var>(3, 2). It is translated onto triangle <var>A</var>′<var>B</var>′<var>C</var>′ with vertices <var>A</var>′(10, 0), <var>B</var>′(13, 0) and <var>C</var>′(13, 2). This translation is to be produced by reflecting in one line and then reflecting the image in a second, parallel line.
p: In what direction must the two lines run, and how far apart must they be?
Write down one possible pair of lines.
Is there only one possible pair? Explain.
ap: The translation is 10 units to the right, so the lines must be vertical (perpendicular to the movement) and 10 ÷ 2 = 5 units apart, with the second line 5 units to the right of the first.
For example <var>m</var>: <var>x</var> = 0 and <var>n</var>: <var>x</var> = 5.

No. Any pair of vertical lines 5 units apart works, provided the second is the right-hand one — for example <var>x</var> = 2 and <var>x</var> = 7, or <var>x</var> = −4 and <var>x</var> = 1. The pair may be slid sideways as much as we like.

questions.t: Two lines <var>m</var> and <var>n</var> both pass through the point <var>O</var>, and the acute angle between them is 35°.
p: A figure is reflected in <var>m</var> and the image is then reflected in <var>n</var>. What single rotation has the same effect?
A rotation of 90° anticlockwise about <var>O</var> is to be produced by two reflections in lines through <var>O</var>. What must the angle between the lines be?
In part b, is there only one possible position for the pair of lines? Explain.
ap: A rotation about <var>O</var> through 2 × 35° = 70°, turning in the direction from <var>m</var> towards <var>n</var>.
The rotation is twice the angle between the lines, so the angle must be 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.

No. The whole pair can be turned about <var>O</var> to any starting position, as long as the angle stays 45° and <var>n</var> is 45° anticlockwise from <var>m</var>. There are infinitely many such pairs.

questions.t: Triangle <var>ABC</var> has vertices <var>A</var>(1, 1), <var>B</var>(4, 1) and <var>C</var>(4, 3), and <var>m</var> is the vertical line <var>x</var> = 5.
p: Reflect triangle <var>ABC</var> in <var>m</var>, then translate the image 6 units right. Give the coordinates of the final image.
Translate triangle <var>ABC</var> 6 units right, then reflect the image in <var>m</var>. Give the coordinates of the final image.
Explain why the two answers are different, and state exactly how the second final image is related to the first.
ap: Reflecting in <var>x</var> = 5 replaces each <var>x</var> by 10 − <var>x</var>: <var>A</var>′(9, 1), <var>B</var>′(6, 1), <var>C</var>′(6, 3). Adding 6 to each <var>x</var>: <var>A</var>″(15, 1), <var>B</var>″(12, 1), <var>C</var>″(12, 3).
Adding 6 first: <var>A</var>′(7, 1), <var>B</var>′(10, 1), <var>C</var>′(10, 3). Then <var>x</var> → 10 − <var>x</var>: <var>A</var>″(3, 1), <var>B</var>″(0, 1), <var>C</var>″(0, 3).

The final image depends on the order in which the transformations are applied, because the translation is perpendicular to the axis of reflection: reflecting last sends the 6-unit shift back the other way. The second image is the first image translated 12 units to the left (each <var>x</var>-coordinate is 12 less), and both have the same shape and size as <var>ABC</var>.

questions.t: Consider a regular 36-gon and a regular 37-gon.
p: State the order of rotational symmetry of each, and the smallest angle of rotation that carries each onto itself.
State how many axes of symmetry each has.
Every axis of symmetry of the 37-gon joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, but the axes of the 36-gon come in two different kinds. Explain why.
ap: The 36-gon has rotational symmetry of order 36, with smallest angle 360° ÷ 36 = 10°. The 37-gon has order 37, with smallest angle 360° ÷ 37 ≈ 9.7°.
A regular <var>n</var>-gon has <var>n</var> axes of symmetry, so 36 axes and 37 axes respectively.

An axis of symmetry must pass through the centre, so it meets the polygon at two opposite places. With 37 vertices (an odd number) there is no vertex directly opposite a vertex, so every axis runs from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. With 36 vertices (an even number) the vertices pair up opposite one another, so 18 axes join opposite vertices and the other 18 join the midpoints of opposite sides.

questions.t:
A school canteen recorded the drinks it sold one lunchtime:
water 48, juice 30, milk 22, soft drink 20.
p: How many drinks were sold altogether?
How many more waters than milks were sold?
What percentage of the drinks sold were juice?

30120 × 100% = 25%

questions.t: A survey of 200 students asked how they travel to school. Of the 100 boys, 34 walk, 26 ride and 40 catch the bus. Of the girls, 30 walk, 20 ride and 50 catch the bus.

How many of the 200 students catch the bus?
What percentage of all the students surveyed are girls who walk?
What percentage of the boys ride to school?

26100 × 100% = 26%

questions.t: In a pictogram of the books borrowed from a library each day, one symbol stands for 8 books. Monday has 4 symbols, Tuesday 2½, Wednesday 5, Thursday 3½ and Friday 6.
p: How many books were borrowed on Tuesday?
How many books were borrowed during the whole week?
What percentage of the week's books were borrowed on Friday? Give your answer to the nearest per cent.
ap: 2½ × 8 = 20 books
4 + 2½ + 5 + 3½ + 6 = 21 symbols, so 21 × 8 = 168 books
Friday = 6 × 8 = 48 books, so 48168 × 100% ≈ 28.6% ≈ 29%

questions.t:
A Year 7 class was asked to name a favourite fruit. The results were:
apple 8, banana 6, grapes 5, mango 4, orange 2.

Which fruit was the most popular?

apple (8 students)
525 × 100% = 20%
25 − 6 = 19, so 1925 × 100% = 76%

questions.t: A farmer's 40 hectares are used as follows: wheat 18 ha, canola 12 ha, barley 6 ha and fallow 4 ha. A divided bar chart 10 cm long is to be drawn.
p: Find the length of the segment for each of the four uses.
Find the percentage of the farm used for each of the four uses.
ap: wheat 1840 × 10 cm = 4.5 cm, canola 1240 × 10 cm = 3 cm, barley 1.5 cm, fallow 1 cm (total 10 cm)
wheat 45%, canola 30%, barley 15%, fallow 10% (total 100%)

questions.t: A shop sold 72 hats one weekend: 24 red, 20 blue, 16 green and 12 black. A pie chart is to be drawn to show these sales.
p: Calculate the angle of the sector for each colour, and check that your four angles add to 360°.
What percentage of the hats sold were green? Give your answer to the nearest per cent.
ap: red 2472 × 360° = 120°, blue 2072 × 360° = 100°, green 1672 × 360° = 80°, black 1272 × 360° = 60°; 120° + 100° + 80° + 60° = 360°
1672 × 100% ≈ 22.2%, so about 22%

questions.t: A pie chart shows how 288 students travel to school. The sector for train has an angle of 150° and the sector for bus has an angle of 75°. The remaining students walk.

How many students travel by bus?

ap: 150360 × 288 = 120 students
75360 × 288 = 60 students
360° − 150° − 75° = 135°, and 135360 × 288 = 108 students (120 + 60 + 108 = 288 checks)

questions.t:
Rohan's mass was recorded at the end of each month for six months:
month 0: 3.4 kg, month 1: 4.2 kg, month 2: 5.0 kg, month 3: 5.7 kg, month 4: 6.3 kg, month 5: 6.8 kg, month 6: 7.2 kg.

How much mass did he gain over the whole six months?
During which month was his gain the smallest?

questions.t: The birds in a wetland are counted on 1 January each year. The counts were 2018: 240, 2019: 300, 2020: 360, 2021: 180, 2022: 210, 2023: 270. A drought occurred during one of these years.
p: In which year was the count the highest?
Between which two counts was the largest fall, and how large was that fall?
During which year did the drought most likely occur? Give a reason.
The wetland can support 250 birds. How many of the counts were above 250?

during 2020, because the population had dropped sharply by the January 2021 count
3 counts are above 250 (300, 360 and 270)

questions.t: A conversion graph is drawn using the rate A$1 = €0.75.
p: Convert A$20 to euros.
Convert A$36 to euros.
Convert €45 to Australian dollars.
Name two points you would plot in order to draw this graph for amounts up to A$40.

questions.t: In a survey of 400 people, 220 were adults and the rest were children. Of the adults, 165 owned a bicycle. Altogether 300 of the people surveyed owned a bicycle.
p: How many children were surveyed?
How many of the children owned a bicycle?
How many adults did not own a bicycle?
What percentage of the children owned a bicycle?

300 − 165 = 135 children
135180 × 100% = 75%

questions.t: Mia rides her bike from home to a lookout. She rides 12 km in the first hour, rests for half an hour, then rides a further 9 km in the next 1½ hours to reach the lookout. She returns home along the same road without stopping, taking 1½ hours.
p: How far is the lookout from Mia's home?
How long did the whole trip take?
What was her average speed during the first hour?
What was her average speed on the return journey?
What total distance did she ride?
ap: 1 + ½ + 1½ + 1½ = 4½ hours

questions.t: Wholetown and Halftown are 60 km apart on the same road. At 9 a.m. Anya leaves Wholetown for Halftown at a steady 20 km/h, and at the same time Ben leaves Halftown for Wholetown at a steady 40 km/h.
p: At what time do Anya and Ben pass each other?
How far from Wholetown do they pass each other?
Who reaches their destination first, and by how long?
ap: The gap closes at 20 + 40 = 60 km/h, so the 60 km takes 1 hour: they pass at 10 a.m.
Anya has travelled 20 × 1 = 20 km, so they pass 20 km from Wholetown
Ben takes 60 ÷ 40 = 1½ hours, arriving at 10:30 a.m.; Anya takes 60 ÷ 20 = 3 hours, arriving at 12 noon. Ben arrives first, by 1½ hours.

questions.t: A bus leaves Kelby at 8 a.m. and reaches Marne, 90 km away, at 9:30 a.m. It waits at Marne for 45 minutes, then travels the further 30 km to Purnell in 30 minutes. It leaves Purnell straight away and returns non-stop to Kelby along the same road, arriving at 1 p.m.
p: Find the average speed of the bus from Kelby to Marne.
Find the average speed of the bus from Marne to Purnell.
How long does the return journey from Purnell to Kelby take, and what is the average speed for it?
Find the average speed for the whole journey, including the stop at Marne.
ap: The bus leaves Purnell at 10:45 a.m. (8:00 + 1 h 30 min + 45 min + 30 min), so the return takes 2 h 15 min = 214 hours. The distance back is 90 + 30 = 120 km, so the average speed is 120 ÷ 214 = 53⅓ km/h.
Total distance = 120 + 120 = 240 km in 5 hours, so 240 ÷ 5 = 48 km/h

questions.t: A council's spending is shown on a pie chart with four sectors: roads, parks, libraries and waste. The waste sector is 100° and the libraries sector is 80°. The roads sector is three times the size of the parks sector.
p: Find the angle of the roads sector and the angle of the parks sector.
The total budget is $7.2 million. How much is spent on parks?
What percentage of the budget is spent on roads?
ap: roads + parks = 360° − 100° − 80° = 180°. If parks is one part and roads is three parts, then 4 parts = 180°, so parks = 45° and roads = 135°.
45360 × $7 200 000 = $900 000
135360 × 100% = 37.5%

questions.t: Last year 800 students at a school chose a language, and 25% of them chose French. This year 1000 students chose a language, and 22% of them chose French. Ravi says, "Fewer students are choosing French, because 22% is less than 25%." Is Ravi right? Support your answer with calculations.
questions.a: Last year: 25% of 800 = 25100 × 800 = 200 students. This year: 22% of 1000 = 22100 × 1000 = 220 students. Ravi is wrong — 20 more students chose French this year. The percentage fell only because the total number of students choosing a language rose from 800 to 1000, so the same number of French students would be a smaller share.

questions.t: Pia, Quinn, Rani and Sol played a round-robin tennis tournament. Each pair played one match, and the first player to win 3 sets won the match. The results were: Pia beat Quinn 3−1, Rani beat Pia 3−2, Pia beat Sol 3−0, Rani beat Quinn 3−0, Sol beat Quinn 3−2, Rani beat Sol 3−1.
p: Make a summary table showing the matches won and matches lost by each player.
How many sets did Pia win in total, and how many did she lose?
What percentage of the sets she played did Pia win?
ap: Pia: 2 won, 1 lost; Quinn: 0 won, 3 lost; Rani: 3 won, 0 lost; Sol: 1 won, 2 lost (6 matches in all)
Pia won 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 sets and lost 1 + 3 + 0 = 4 sets
She played 8 + 4 = 12 sets, so 812 × 100% = 6623%

questions.t:

p: Find the mean salary.
Find the median salary.
Which of the two better describes a typical salary at this business? Give a reason.
ap: already in order, so median = 56 000 + 60 0002 = $58 000

the median. Five of the six people earn less than $67 000, so the single very large salary of $240 000 drags the mean above almost every actual salary, while the median sits among the values most staff really receive.

questions.t: Over five tests, each marked out of 20, Anh scored 14, 16, 15, 17, 13 and Bianca scored 19, 8, 20, 9, 19.

Whose performance was more consistent? Give a reason.
ap: Anh: 75 ÷ 5 = 15; Bianca: 75 ÷ 5 = 15 (both means are 15)
Anh. The means are equal, but Anh's range of 4 is much smaller than Bianca's range of 12, so Anh's scores are far less spread out.

questions.t: The mean of the five numbers 14, 19, 23, 26 and <var>k</var> is 21.

Find the median of the five numbers.
ap: the total must be 5 × 21 = 105, and 14 + 19 + 23 + 26 = 82, so <var>k</var> = 105 − 82 = 23
in order: 14, 19, 23, 23, 26, so the median is 23

questions.t: Five positive whole numbers have a mean of 6, a median of 7 and a single mode of 10. Find the five numbers, and explain why no other set of five numbers works.
questions.a:
The numbers are 1, 2, 7, 10, 10.
Reasoning: five numbers with mean 6 have total 5 × 6 = 30, and the median 7 is the 3rd number when they are in order. Since 10 is bigger than the median, every 10 must be one of the two largest numbers, and 10 must occur at least twice to be the mode, so the two largest are both 10. The two smallest therefore add to 30 − 7 − 20 = 3, so they are 1 and 2 (they cannot be equal, since 3 ÷ 2 is not a whole number, and equal values would give a second mode). Check: 1 + 2 + 7 + 10 + 10 = 30, mean 6, median 7, mode 10.

questions.t:
A set of eight values is listed in order from smallest to largest:
17, 25, 31, 38, 44, x, 58, y
The range of the data is 48 and the mean is 41. Find:
p: <var>y</var>
the median
<var>x</var>
ap: <var>y</var> is the largest value, so <var>y</var> = 17 + 48 = 65
with 8 values the median is the average of the 4th and 5th: 38 + 442 = 41
the total must be 8 × 41 = 328; the seven known values give 17 + 25 + 31 + 38 + 44 + 58 + 65 = 278, so <var>x</var> = 328 − 278 = 50 (which correctly lies between 44 and 58)

questions.t: In a class test the 12 girls had a mean mark of 17 and the 8 boys had a mean mark of 14.5.
p: Find the mean mark for the whole class of 20 students.
Explain why the answer to part a is not the average of 17 and 14.5.
ap: girls' total = 12 × 17 = 204 and boys' total = 8 × 14.5 = 116, so the class total = 320 and the class mean = 320 ÷ 20 = 16

the two groups are different sizes. Averaging 17 and 14.5 gives 15.75, which treats the two groups as equally large. Because there are more girls (12) than boys (8), the girls' mean counts for more and the class mean is pulled up towards 17, landing at 16.

questions.t: Remember that the total of a set of values equals the mean multiplied by the number of values.
p: The mean of nine numbers is 12. A tenth number is included and the mean becomes 13. Find the tenth number.
The mean of a different set of seven numbers is 20. One number is removed and the mean of the remaining six numbers is 21. Find the number that was removed.
ap: total of the nine = 9 × 12 = 108 and total of the ten = 10 × 13 = 130, so the tenth number is 130 − 108 = 22
total of the seven = 7 × 20 = 140 and total of the six = 6 × 21 = 126, so the number removed is 140 − 126 = 14

questions.t:
The number of goals a hockey team scored in each of its 20 matches is summarised below.
0 goals: 3 matches
1 goal: a matches
2 goals: 6 matches
3 goals: b matches
4 goals: 2 matches
The mean number of goals per match was 1.85.
p: Find <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>.
Hence find the mode and the median number of goals per match.
ap: matches: 3 + <var>a</var> + 6 + <var>b</var> + 2 = 20, so <var>a</var> + <var>b</var> = 9. Goals: (1 × <var>a</var>) + (2 × 6) + (3 × <var>b</var>) + (4 × 2) = <var>a</var> + 3<var>b</var> + 20, and the total must be 1.85 × 20 = 37, so <var>a</var> + 3<var>b</var> = 17. Subtracting the first equation gives 2<var>b</var> = 8, so <var>b</var> = 4 and <var>a</var> = 5.

the frequencies are 3, 5, 6, 4, 2, so the mode is 2 goals. With 20 matches the median is the average of the 10th and 11th values; the running totals are 3, 8, 14, so both are 2 and the median is 2 goals.

questions.t: Which of the following solids are polyhedra?
p: a triangular prism
a cylinder
a square pyramid
a cone
a step shape made from three unit cubes glued face to face
a hemisphere
questions.a: a), c) and e) are polyhedra - every face is a flat polygon. b), d) and f) are not: the cylinder, cone and hemisphere all have curved surfaces and circular faces, which are not polygons.

questions.t: Write down the number of faces (<var>F</var>), edges (<var>E</var>) and vertices (<var>V</var>) of each solid.
p: a hexagonal prism
a square pyramid
an octahedron

questions.t: For each solid, say whether it is a prism, a pyramid or neither. If it is a prism, name the shape of its uniform cross-section.
p: a solid with two identical parallel octagonal faces and eight rectangular faces
a solid with one hexagonal face and six triangular faces that all meet at a single point
a cylinder
ap: A prism (an octagonal prism); its cross-section is always an octagon identical to the two end faces.
A pyramid (a hexagonal pyramid).
Neither - it is not even a polyhedron, because its curved surface and circular ends are not polygons.

questions.t: A pentagonal prism is shown in the textbook.
p: Write down <var>F</var>, <var>E</var> and <var>V</var> for this prism.
Show that <var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = 2.
ap: <var>F</var> = 7 (2 pentagons + 5 rectangles), <var>E</var> = 15, <var>V</var> = 10.
<var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = 10 − 15 + 7 = 2, as Euler's formula predicts.

questions.t: A polyhedron has 20 faces and 30 edges.
p: Use Euler's formula to find the number of vertices.
Which of the five Platonic solids is it?
ap: <var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = 2, so <var>V</var> = 2 + <var>E</var> − <var>F</var> = 2 + 30 − 20 = 12 vertices.
20 triangular faces, 30 edges and 12 vertices - it is the icosahedron.

questions.t: A prism has a cross-section with <var>n</var> sides. Find, in terms of <var>n</var>:
p: the number of faces <var>F</var>
the number of edges <var>E</var>
the number of vertices <var>V</var>
Hence show that <var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = 2.
ap: <var>F</var> = <var>n</var> + 2 (the two end faces plus <var>n</var> side faces)
<var>E</var> = 3<var>n</var> (<var>n</var> edges on each end, plus <var>n</var> joining edges)
<var>V</var> = 2<var>n</var>
<var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = 2<var>n</var> − 3<var>n</var> + <var>n</var> + 2 = 2.

questions.t: A pyramid has a base with <var>n</var> sides. Find, in terms of <var>n</var>, the number of faces, edges and vertices, and check that Euler's formula holds.
questions.a: <var>F</var> = <var>n</var> + 1 (the base plus <var>n</var> triangles), <var>E</var> = 2<var>n</var> (<var>n</var> base edges plus <var>n</var> slant edges), <var>V</var> = <var>n</var> + 1 (<var>n</var> base corners plus the apex). Then <var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = (<var>n</var> + 1) − 2<var>n</var> + (<var>n</var> + 1) = 2.

questions.t: Three unit cubes are placed in a row on a table, side by side from left to right, and a fourth cube is placed on top of the left-hand cube. You stand in front of the row, so that the long side of the row faces you. Describe the front view, the right side view and the plan view, stating how many unit squares each one contains.
questions.a: Front view: an L shape of 4 squares - a row of 3 squares with one extra square sitting on top of the left-hand one. Right side view: 2 squares, one directly above the other (the solid is only one cube deep and two cubes high). Plan view: 3 squares in a single row, a 1 by 3 rectangle.

questions.t: Four unit cubes are placed on a table in a 2 by 2 square, two across the front and two directly behind them. A fifth cube is placed on top of the front-left cube. Describe the front view, the right side view and the plan view of this solid.
questions.a: Front view: 3 squares - a row of 2 squares with one extra square on top of the left-hand one. Right side view: 3 squares - a row of 2 squares (front and back) with one extra square on top of the front one. Plan view: a full 2 by 2 square of 4 squares, since every position on the table is occupied.

questions.t: Name a solid that has the given three views.
p: front view a square, side view a square and plan view a square, all the same size
front view a triangle, side view a triangle and plan view a square
front view a rectangle, side view a triangle and plan view a rectangle
ap: A cube.
A square pyramid standing on its base.
A triangular prism lying on one of its rectangular faces, with the triangular ends facing the sides.

questions.t: A square pyramid is glued onto the top face of a cube, so that the base of the pyramid exactly covers the top of the cube.
p: How many faces does the new solid have?
How many edges and how many vertices does it have?
Check that Euler's formula holds.
ap: The top face of the cube is no longer on the outside, so <var>F</var> = 6 − 1 + 4 = 9 faces (5 squares and 4 triangles).
<var>E</var> = 12 + 4 = 16 (the cube's 12 edges plus the 4 slant edges); <var>V</var> = 8 + 1 = 9 (the cube's 8 corners plus the apex).
<var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = 9 − 16 + 9 = 2. ✓

questions.t: For each pair of numbers below, first use Euler's formula to find the number of faces, then name a polyhedron that has exactly those numbers of edges, vertices and faces.
p: 15 edges and 10 vertices
14 edges and 8 vertices
24 edges and 16 vertices
questions.al: Rearranging Euler's formula gives <var>F</var> = 2 − <var>V</var> + <var>E</var>.
ap: <var>F</var> = 2 − 10 + 15 = 7 faces: a pentagonal prism.
<var>F</var> = 2 − 8 + 14 = 8 faces: a heptagonal pyramid (7 triangles plus the 7-sided base, 8 vertices).
<var>F</var> = 2 − 16 + 24 = 10 faces: an octagonal prism.

questions.t: An extended pyramid is made by gluing a pyramid onto one end face of a prism that has the same cross-section. For example, an extended triangular pyramid is a triangular prism with a tetrahedron glued to one triangular end; it has 7 faces, 12 edges and 7 vertices.
p: Find <var>F</var>, <var>E</var> and <var>V</var> for an extended pentagonal pyramid.
The cross-section of the prism has <var>n</var> sides. Find <var>F</var>, <var>E</var> and <var>V</var> in terms of <var>n</var>, and check Euler's formula.
Name two different polyhedra that each have 9 faces and 9 vertices.
ap: The pentagonal prism has 7 faces, 15 edges, 10 vertices. Gluing on the pyramid hides one pentagon and adds 5 triangles, 5 edges and 1 vertex: <var>F</var> = 7 − 1 + 5 = 11, <var>E</var> = 15 + 5 = 20, <var>V</var> = 10 + 1 = 11. (Check: 11 − 20 + 11 = 2.)

<var>F</var> = (<var>n</var> + 2) − 1 + <var>n</var> = 2<var>n</var> + 1, <var>E</var> = 3<var>n</var> + <var>n</var> = 4<var>n</var>, <var>V</var> = 2<var>n</var> + 1. Then <var>V</var> − <var>E</var> + <var>F</var> = (2<var>n</var> + 1) − 4<var>n</var> + (2<var>n</var> + 1) = 2. ✓

Put <var>n</var> = 4: an extended square pyramid has 9 faces, 16 edges and 9 vertices. An octagonal pyramid also has 9 faces (8 triangles + base), 16 edges and 9 vertices. So those two solids have the same counts but are different polyhedra.

questions.t: Two identical tetrahedra are glued together so that one triangular face of each is joined to the other.
p: Describe the solid formed, find <var>F</var>, <var>E</var> and <var>V</var>, and check Euler's formula.
Every face of this solid is an equilateral triangle. Explain why it is still not a regular polyhedron.
ap: The joined face disappears inside, leaving a solid with two apexes above and below a shared triangle - a triangular bipyramid (a double tetrahedron). <var>F</var> = 3 + 3 = 6, <var>E</var> = 3 (shared triangle) + 3 + 3 = 9, <var>V</var> = 3 + 2 = 5. Check: 5 − 9 + 6 = 2. ✓

A regular polyhedron needs the same number of edges meeting at every vertex. Here only 3 edges meet at each of the two apexes, but 4 edges meet at each of the 3 vertices of the shared triangle, so the solid is not regular.

questions.t: A regular dodecahedron has 12 faces, each a regular pentagon.
p: Each edge is shared by exactly two faces. Use this to find the number of edges.
Use Euler's formula to find the number of vertices.
How many edges meet at each vertex?
ap: The 12 pentagons have 12 × 5 = 60 sides altogether, and each edge is counted twice, so <var>E</var> = 60 ÷ 2 = 30.
<var>V</var> = 2 − <var>F</var> + <var>E</var> = 2 − 12 + 30 = 20 vertices.
Each of the 30 edges has 2 ends, giving 60 edge-ends shared equally among 20 vertices, so 60 ÷ 20 = 3 edges meet at each vertex.

questions.t: The centre point of a cube is joined by straight lines to each of its eight vertices.
p: Explain why this cuts the cube into six identical square pyramids.
The cube has edge length 18 cm. Find the volume of one of the pyramids.
How many faces, edges and vertices does one of these pyramids have?
ap: Each of the 6 faces of the cube, together with the centre point, forms a square pyramid whose base is that face and whose apex is the centre. The six pyramids fill the cube with no overlap, and they are identical because the six faces of a cube are identical and all are the same distance from the centre.
Volume of cube = 18 × 18 × 18 = 5832 cm<sup>3</sup>, so each pyramid has volume 5832 ÷ 6 = 972 cm<sup>3</sup>.
<var>F</var> = 5, <var>E</var> = 8, <var>V</var> = 5 (and 5 − 8 + 5 = 2 ✓).

questions.t: Three circles P, Q and R sit at the corners of a triangle. The integer written on each side of the triangle is the sum of the integers in the two circles at the ends of that side. Side PQ reads −5, side QR reads −9 and side RP reads −14. Find the integer in each circle.
questions.a: Adding the three side totals counts every circle twice, so 2(P + Q + R) = −5 − 9 − 14 = −28, giving P + Q + R = −14. Then R = −14 − (−5) = −9, P = −14 − (−9) = −5 and Q = −14 − (−14) = 0. Check: −5 + 0 = −5, 0 + (−9) = −9, −9 + (−5) = −14.

questions.t:
Put the three numbers 6, −3 and −8, one in each space, into
____ + ____ − ____ = ____

In a 3 × 3 magic square every row, every column and both diagonals add to the same total. Reading left to right, the top row is 5, −9, 7 and the bottom-right entry is −3. Find the common total, then find the five missing entries.
questions.a:
The top row gives the total: 5 + (−9) + 7 = 3.
The diagonal from top-left gives 5 + centre + (−3) = 3, so the centre is 1.
Right-hand column: 7 + (middle right) + (−3) = 3, so the middle-right entry is −1.
Middle row: (middle left) + 1 + (−1) = 3, so the middle-left entry is 3.
Left column: 5 + 3 + (bottom left) = 3, so the bottom-left entry is −5.
Middle column: −9 + 1 + (bottom middle) = 3, so the bottom-middle entry is 11.
The completed square, row by row, is 5, −9, 7 / 3, 1, −1 / −5, 11, −3. Check the other diagonal: 7 + 1 + (−5) = 3.

questions.t: The average of six numbers is −3. When the largest of the six numbers is deleted, the average of the five that remain is −5. What is the largest number? Explain your reasoning.
questions.a: The six numbers total 6 × (−3) = −18. The remaining five total 5 × (−5) = −25. The number deleted is therefore −18 − (−25) = −18 + 25 = 7.

questions.t: In triangle <var>ABC</var>, the side <var>AB</var> is produced beyond <var>B</var> to <var>P</var>, the side <var>BC</var> is produced beyond <var>C</var> to <var>Q</var>, and the side <var>CA</var> is produced beyond <var>A</var> to <var>R</var>. questions.a:
Each of the three angles is an exterior angle of the triangle:
α = 180° − ∠ABC (straight angle ∠ABP)
β = 180° − ∠BCA (straight angle ∠BCQ)
γ = 180° − ∠CAB (straight angle ∠CAR)
Adding, α + β + γ = 540° − (∠ABC + ∠BCA + ∠CAB) = 540° − 180° = 360°, because the angle sum of ΔABC is 180°.

questions.a:

AD = DE, so ∠DAE = ∠DEA = 42° (base angles of isosceles ΔADE); that is, ∠BAC = 42°.

questions.t: <var>ABCD</var> is a square, with its vertices labelled in order around the figure, and <var>ABE</var> is an equilateral triangle drawn on the side <var>AB</var>. Find the two possible sizes of ∠<var>DEC</var> — one when <var>E</var> is inside the square and one when <var>E</var> is outside it. Give reasons for each.
questions.a:
In both cases AE = AD and BE = BC (all sides of the square and of the equilateral triangle are equal), and every angle of ΔABE is 60° (equilateral).
E inside the square: ∠DAE = 90° − 60° = 30°, so ∠AED = (180° − 30°) ÷ 2 = 75° (base angles of isosceles ΔADE), and likewise ∠BEC = 75°. The angles ∠AED, ∠AEB, ∠BEC and ∠DEC make a revolution at E, so ∠DEC = 360° − 75° − 60° − 75° = 150°.
E outside the square: ∠DAE = 90° + 60° = 150°, so ∠AED = (180° − 150°) ÷ 2 = 15° (base angles of isosceles ΔADE), and likewise ∠BEC = 15°. Now ED and EC lie inside ∠AEB, so ∠DEC = 60° − 15° − 15° = 30°.

questions.t: A school is planning a fair with an 'all you can eat' barbecue. Food will cost about $4 for each adult and $2.50 for each child, and hall hire plus cleaning will cost $340. A child ticket costs $3 and an adult ticket $6.

How many of the commuters only listen to music?
How many of the commuters do none of these three things?
ap: 28% of 800 = 28100 × 800 = 224 commuters.
15% of 800 = 120 commuters.

questions.t: In an orchard, 45% of the trees are apple trees, and 20% of the apple trees are more than ten years old.
p: What percentage of all the trees are apple trees more than ten years old?
The orchard has 1200 trees. How many of them are apple trees more than ten years old?
ap: 20% of 45% = 20100 × 45% = 9%.
9% of 1200 = 9100 × 1200 = 108 trees.

questions.t: Work backwards to find the original amount.
p: A jacket is reduced by 20% in a sale. Its sale price is $164. What was the price before the sale?
The number of students at a school increased by 12% and there are now 1848 students. How many students were there before the increase?
ap: Sale price = (100 − 20)% = 80% of the original price, so 80% is 164, 1% is $2.05 and 100% is $205.
112% of the old number is 1848, so 1% is 1848 ÷ 112 = 16.5 and 100% is 1650 students.

questions.t: Tom earns $560 per week for a 35-hour week. His weekly pay is increased by 20% and the number of hours he works each week is decreased by 20%.
p: Calculate his new hourly rate of pay.
By what percentage has his hourly rate increased?
questions.al: Old rate = 560 ÷ 35 = $16 per hour. New pay = 560 + 20% of 560 = $672; new hours = 35 − 20% of 35 = 28.
ap: New rate = 672 ÷ 28 = $24 per hour.
Increase = 24 − 16 = $8, and 816 × 100% = 50% increase. (Note that a 20% rise and a 20% cut do not cancel.)

questions.t: The length of a rectangle is decreased by 20% and its width is increased by 30%. The area of the original rectangle is 250 cm<sup>2</sup>.
p: Find the area of the new rectangle.
State the percentage change in the area.
questions.al: New length is 80% of the old and new width is 130% of the old, so the new area is 80% of 130% of the old area = 80100 × 130100 = 104100 = 104% of it.
ap: The area increases by 4%.

questions.t: In a raffle, only 0.005% of the tickets sold won a prize. There were 3 prizes. How many tickets were sold?
questions.a: 0.005% of the number of tickets is 3, so 1% is 3 ÷ 0.005 = 600 and 100% is 60 000. There were 60 000 tickets sold.

questions.t: A virus is spreading through the town of Merrivale. On 1 March, 25% of the residents have the virus. By 1 April, 20% of those who had the virus on 1 March have recovered, but 30% of those who did not have it on 1 March now do. What percentage of the population has the virus on 1 April?
questions.a: Of the 25% who had it, 80% still have it: 80% of 25% = 80100 × 25% = 20%. Of the 75% who did not have it, 30% now do: 30% of 75% = 30100 × 75% = 22½%. Total = 20% + 22½% = 42½% of the population.

questions.t: A fruit drink is made so that 12% of the drink is concentrate and the rest is water. A jug holds 400 mL of the drink. The maker now decides the concentrate should make up only 8% of the drink. How much extra water must be added to the jug?
questions.a: Concentrate = 12% of 400 = 48 mL, and no concentrate is added or removed. We need 48 mL to be 8% of the new total, so 1% is 6 mL and 100% is 600 mL. Extra water = 600 − 400 = 200 mL.

questions.t: In a class, 25% of the students play a musical instrument. Six more students who play an instrument then join the class, and now 40% of the class play one. How many students were in the class before the six joined?
questions.a: Let n be the original number of students. Then 25% of n, plus 6, is 40% of (n + 6): 0.25n + 6 = 0.4n + 2.4, so 3.6 = 0.15n and n = 24. Check: 25% of 24 = 6 players; 6 + 6 = 12 out of 30, and 1230 = 40%. There were 24 students.

questions.t: A two-digit number increases by 20% when its digits are reversed. Find the number, and explain why it is the only one.
questions.a: Let the digits be <var>a</var> (tens) and <var>b</var> (units), so the number is 10<var>a</var> + <var>b</var> and the reversal is 10<var>b</var> + <var>a</var>. Then 10<var>b</var> + <var>a</var> = 1.2(10<var>a</var> + <var>b</var>). Multiplying by 5 gives 50<var>b</var> + 5<var>a</var> = 60<var>a</var> + 6<var>b</var>, so 44<var>b</var> = 55<var>a</var>, that is 4<var>b</var> = 5<var>a</var>. So <var>b</var> must be a multiple of 5; <var>b</var> = 0 forces <var>a</var> = 0, and <var>b</var> = 5 gives <var>a</var> = 4. The only number is 45, and indeed 54 = 1.2 × 45.

questions.t: Entry to a science fair costs $18 per adult and $7 per child, and each show inside the fair costs $4 per person. The Nguyen family (2 adults and 3 children) spent $117 altogether on entry and shows. If the whole family always went to a show together, how many shows did they see?
questions.a: Entry costs 2 × $18 + 3 × $7 = $36 + $21 = $57, leaving $117 − $57 = $60 for shows. Each show costs 5 × $4 = $20, so they saw $60 ÷ $20 = 3 shows.

questions.t: A space station orbits the Earth once every 11 hours, and it passes over Sydney at 6 a.m. on a Monday. Using modular arithmetic (do not calculate 11 × 40 and then count), find the day of the week and the time when it passes over Sydney for the 40th time after that.
questions.a: 40 orbits take 11 × 40 = 440 hours. 440 = 24 × 18 + 8, so 440 ≡ 8 (mod 24): the time is 6 a.m. + 8 hours = 2 p.m. The 18 whole days give 18 = 7 × 2 + 4, so 18 ≡ 4 (mod 7) and the day is 4 days after Monday, i.e. Friday. Answer: 2 p.m. on Friday.

questions.t: The divisibility test for 9:
p: Prove that every power of 10 is congruent to 1 modulo 9.
Hence prove that every whole number is congruent modulo 9 to the sum of its digits.
Use this to find the remainder when 7 428 561 is divided by 9.
ap: 10 − 1 = 9, so 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9); taking powers, 10<sup><var>n</var></sup> ≡ 1<sup><var>n</var></sup> = 1 (mod 9) for every whole number <var>n</var>.

A whole number is the sum of each digit multiplied by a power of 10. Since every power of 10 is ≡ 1 (mod 9), each term is congruent to just the digit itself, so the whole number is congruent to the sum of its digits modulo 9.
7 + 4 + 2 + 8 + 5 + 6 + 1 = 33, and 33 = 9 × 3 + 6, so the remainder is 6.

questions.t: The divisibility test for 11:
p: Show that 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11), and deduce that every even power of 10 is congruent to 1 and every odd power is congruent to −1 modulo 11.
Hence find the remainder when 528 934 is divided by 11, using the alternating sum of its digits (units digit taken as positive).
ap: 10 − (−1) = 11, a multiple of 11, so 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11). Hence 10<sup><var>n</var></sup> ≡ (−1)<sup><var>n</var></sup>, which is 1 when <var>n</var> is even and −1 when <var>n</var> is odd.
The alternating sum is 4 − 3 + 9 − 8 + 2 − 5 = −1, so 528 934 ≡ −1 ≡ 10 (mod 11). The remainder is 10 (check: 528 934 = 11 × 48 084 + 10).

questions.t: Write out the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... in arithmetic modulo 4, continuing until the whole pattern repeats itself. State how long the repeating block is, and how often a zero occurs.
questions.a: Reducing each term modulo 4 gives 1, 1, 2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 1, 0, ... . The repeating block is 6 terms long (1, 1, 2, 3, 1, 0), and a zero occurs once every 6 terms — at the 6th, 12th, 18th, ... terms.

×2 gives 7 : 10, so 7 : 10
×6 gives 4 : 5 : 6

questions.t: Water flows into a tank at a constant rate of 450 litres per hour.
p: How much water flows in during 2½ hours?
How long does it take for 3600 L to flow in?
How long, in hours and minutes, does it take for 1200 L to flow in?
ap: 450 × 2.5 = 1125 L
3600 ÷ 450 = 8 hours
1200 ÷ 450 = 83 = 2⅔ hours = 2 hours 40 minutes

questions.t: Find the missing quantity in each case.
p: A train covers 420 km in 5 hours. What is its average speed?
A cyclist rides for 1 hour 45 minutes at 16 km/h. How far does she ride?
A bus travels 315 km at an average speed of 70 km/h. How long does the journey take?
A jet flies 1960 km in 2 hours 20 minutes. What is its average speed?
ap: 420 ÷ 5 = 84 km/h
16 × 1¾ = 28 km
315 ÷ 70 = 4.5, so 4 hours 30 minutes
2 h 20 min = 73 h, so speed = 1960 ÷ 73 = 1960 × 37 = 840 km/h

questions.t: Write each of the following as a ratio in simplest form.
p: Two-sevenths of the members of a club are left-handed. Find left-handed : right-handed.
A dressing is made from ⅓ vinegar, ½ oil and ⅙ lemon juice by volume. Find vinegar : oil : lemon juice.
ap: Left-handed is 27, so right-handed is 57; ratio = 2 : 5
13 : 12 : 16, ×6 gives 2 : 3 : 1

questions.t: The ratio of the number of adults to the number of children at a concert is 3 : 7. There are 189 adults.
p: How many children are there?
How many people are there altogether?
questions.al: 3 parts = 189, so 1 part = 63.
ap: 7 parts = 441 children
10 parts = 630 people

questions.t: Convert each rate to the units asked for.
p: A worker earns $27 per hour. What is this in cents per minute?
A tap leaks 15 mL per second. Express this rate in litres per hour.
A car travels 360 km on 45 L of petrol. At what rate is it using petrol, in litres per 100 km?
ap: $27 = 2700 cents per hour; 2700 ÷ 60 = 45 cents per minute
15 × 60 = 900 mL per minute; ×60 = 54 000 mL per hour = 54 L/h
360 km uses 45 L, so 100 km uses 45 ÷ 3.6 = 12.5 L per 100 km

questions.t: Divide each quantity in the ratio given.
p: Divide $612 in the ratio 4 : 5.
Divide 840 kg in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7.
The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 4 : 5 : 9. Find the size of each angle.
ap: 9 parts = $612, 1 part = $68, so $272 and $340
12 parts = 840 kg, 1 part = 70 kg, so 140 kg, 210 kg and 490 kg
18 parts = 180°, 1 part = 10°, so 40°, 50° and 90°

questions.t: Answer the following questions about scales.
p: Write the scale 1 cm : 5 m as a ratio of two numbers.
On a map with scale 1 : 250 000, two towns are 6.4 cm apart. How far apart are the towns?
A house plan is drawn to a scale of 1 : 200. A room is 4.8 m long. How long is it on the plan?
ap: 1 cm : 500 cm = 1 : 500
1 cm represents 250 000 cm = 2.5 km, so 6.4 × 2.5 = 16 km
4.8 m = 480 cm; 480 ÷ 200 = 2.4 cm

questions.t: The ratio of the cost of a bag to the cost of a wallet is 7 : 4. The bag costs $54 more than the wallet. Find the cost of the bag and the cost of the wallet.
questions.a: The difference is 7 − 4 = 3 parts, so 3 parts = $54 and 1 part = $18. Bag = 7 × 18 = $126, wallet = 4 × 18 = $72 (check: 126 − 72 = 54 ✓)

questions.t: Ella can paint a fence in 3 days and Sam can paint the same fence in 6 days. Working at these rates, how long will it take the two of them to paint the fence together?
questions.a: Ella: 1 fence in 3 days, so 2 fences in 6 days. Sam: 1 fence in 6 days. Together: 3 fences in 6 days, so 1 fence in 6 ÷ 3 = 2 days

questions.t: A rectangular paddock appears on a plan drawn to a scale of 1 : 1500. On the plan the paddock measures 6 cm by 4 cm.
p: Find the actual side lengths of the paddock, in metres.
Find the actual area of the paddock in square metres, and then in hectares (1 ha = 10 000 m<sup>2</sup>).
ap: 6 × 1500 = 9000 cm = 90 m; 4 × 1500 = 6000 cm = 60 m
Area = 90 × 60 = 5400 m2 = 5400 ÷ 10 000 = 0.54 ha

questions.t: Priya jogged the 12 km from her home to the beach in 1½ hours, then walked the same 12 km home in 2½ hours.
p: Find her average speed for the whole trip.
Find her speed on each leg of the trip, and explain why the answer to part a is not the average of those two speeds.
ap: Total distance 24 km in a total time of 4 hours, so average speed = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 km/h

Out: 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8 km/h; back: 12 ÷ 2.5 = 4.8 km/h. Their average is (8 + 4.8) ÷ 2 = 6.4 km/h, which is not 6 km/h. Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, and she spent more time at the slower speed, so the slower speed counts for more.

questions.t: An L-shaped metal plate is made by cutting a 4 m by 3 m rectangle out of one corner of a 9 m by 6 m rectangle.
p: Find the area of the plate.
Paint costs $2.75 per square metre. Find the cost of painting one face of the plate.
This plate is a scale model, at a scale of 1 : 20, of a giant plate of the same shape. Find the area of the giant plate.
ap: 9 × 6 − 4 × 3 = 54 − 12 = 42 m2

Every length is 20 times as long, so the giant plate is 180 m by 120 m with an 80 m by 60 m corner removed: 21 600 − 4800 = 16 800 m2. (Note this is 42 × 202 = 42 × 400: areas are in the ratio 400 : 1.)

questions.t: Four points <var>P</var>, <var>Q</var>, <var>R</var> and <var>S</var> are marked in that order on a straight line. <var>PQ</var> : <var>PR</var> = 3 : 5 and <var>QS</var> : <var>RS</var> = 7 : 2. Given that <var>RS</var> = 8 cm, find the length of <var>PQ</var>.
questions.a: Let PQ = 3k and PR = 5k, so QR = 2k. Then QS = QR + RS = 2k + 8. From QS : RS = 7 : 2 we get 2k + 88 = 72, so 2(2k + 8) = 56, giving 2k + 8 = 28 and k = 10. Hence PQ = 3 × 10 = 30 cm. (Check: PR = 50, QR = 20, QS = 28 and 28 : 8 = 7 : 2 ✓)

questions.t: A 50 L drum is full of pure apple juice. 10 L is drained off and replaced with water. The drum is stirred thoroughly, then a further 10 L of the mixture is drained off and again replaced with water. Find the ratio of apple juice to water in the drum at the end, in simplest form.
questions.a: After the first step: 40 L juice and 10 L water, so 45 of the mixture is juice. The 10 L removed next therefore contains 8 L juice and 2 L water, leaving 32 L juice and 8 L water; adding 10 L of water gives 32 L juice and 18 L water. Ratio = 32 : 18 = 16 : 9

questions.t: One bottle holds 1.2 L of cordial in which concentrate : water = 1 : 5. A second bottle holds 0.8 L of cordial in which concentrate : water = 1 : 3. Both bottles are emptied into a jug. Find the ratio of concentrate to water in the jug.
questions.a: First bottle: 6 parts make 1.2 L, so 1 part = 0.2 L, giving 0.2 L concentrate and 1.0 L water. Second bottle: 4 parts make 0.8 L, so 1 part = 0.2 L, giving 0.2 L concentrate and 0.6 L water. In the jug: concentrate = 0.4 L, water = 1.6 L, so concentrate : water = 0.4 : 1.6 = 1 : 4

questions.t: Two tanks, <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>, each hold 600 L of water. At the same moment both begin to drain at a constant rate. Tank <var>A</var> empties in 3 hours and tank <var>B</var> empties in 5 hours. After how long does tank <var>B</var> hold exactly three times as much water as tank <var>A</var>?
questions.a: Tank A drains at 600 ÷ 3 = 200 L/h, so after t hours it holds 600 − 200t. Tank B drains at 600 ÷ 5 = 120 L/h, so it holds 600 − 120t. Setting 600 − 120t = 3(600 − 200t) gives 600 − 120t = 1800 − 600t, so 480t = 1200 and t = 2.5. This happens after 2 hours 30 minutes. (Check: A holds 100 L, B holds 300 L ✓)

6(2x5 + 1) − 3x5

−7<var>x</var> = 21

−5<var>x</var> = −20, so <var>x</var> = 4

7<var>x</var> − 2 = 3<var>x</var> + 14

4<var>x</var> = 16, so <var>x</var> = 4

ap: x3 = 7, so x = 21

p: m4 + m6 = 5
5x6 − x4 = 7
2x3 + 3x5 = 19
ap: × 12: 3<var>m</var> + 2<var>m</var> = 60, 5<var>m</var> = 60, so <var>m</var> = 12
