questions.t: At 9 a.m. two trains leave stations that are 1080 km apart and travel towards each other along the same line. The average speed of one train is 1½ times the average speed of the other. The trains pass each other at 1 p.m. Find the average speed of each train.
questions.a: Each train travels for 4 hours. Let v km/h be the slower speed, so the faster speed is 3v2 km/h. Together they cover 1080 km: 4v + 4 × 3v2 = 1080, so 4v + 6v = 1080, 10v = 1080 and v = 108. The speeds are 108 km/h and 162 km/h (4 × 108 = 432 km and 4 × 162 = 648 km, and 432 + 648 = 1080).

questions.t: When she was asked her age, a museum guide replied, 'One-quarter of my age five years ago, added to half my age two years ago, gives my age nine years ago.' How old is she now?
questions.a: Let a be her present age in years. Then a − 54 + a − 22 = a − 9. Multiply by 4: (a − 5) + 2(a − 2) = 4a − 36, so 3a − 9 = 4a − 36 and a = 27. She is 27. Check: ¼ × 22 = 5.5 and ½ × 25 = 12.5, and 5.5 + 12.5 = 18 = 27 − 9.

questions.t: $600 is divided between Dev, Elin and Fatima. Elin receives $40 less than Dev, and Fatima receives half as much as Dev and Elin receive together. How much does each person receive?
questions.a: Let Dev receive $<var>d</var>. Then Elin receives $(<var>d</var> − 40), and Dev and Elin together receive $(2<var>d</var> − 40), so Fatima receives $(<var>d</var> − 20). Total: <var>d</var> + (<var>d</var> − 40) + (<var>d</var> − 20) = 600, so 3<var>d</var> − 60 = 600, 3<var>d</var> = 660 and <var>d</var> = 220. Dev gets $220, Elin $180 and Fatima $200. Check: 220 + 180 = 400, half of which is 200, and 220 + 180 + 200 = 600.

questions.t: A river flows at 4 km/h. A rowing boat travels upstream at one-third of the speed at which it travels downstream. Find the speed of the boat in still water.
questions.a: Let b km/h be the speed in still water. Downstream the boat travels at (b + 4) km/h and upstream at (b − 4) km/h, so b − 4 = b + 43. Then 3b − 12 = b + 4, 2b = 16 and b = 8. The boat travels at 8 km/h in still water. Check: downstream 12 km/h, upstream 4 km/h, and 4 = ⅓ × 12.

questions.t: Thirty litres of juice from tank A, whose sugar content is unknown, is mixed with 20 litres of juice from tank B, which contains 4% sugar. The 50 litres of mixture contains 5.2% sugar. Find the percentage of sugar in tank A.
questions.a: Let tank A contain p% sugar. The sugar in the mixture comes from the two tanks: 30 × p100 + 20 × 4100 = 50 × 5.2100. Multiply by 100: 30p + 80 = 260, so 30p = 180 and p = 6. Tank A contains 6% sugar. Check: 1.8 L + 0.8 L = 2.6 L of sugar in 50 L, which is 5.2%.

questions.t: A courier drives from her depot to a client at an average speed of 45 km/h. On the return trip she takes a route that is 8 km longer and averages 60 km/h. Each of the two trips takes exactly the same time. Find the total distance she travelled.
questions.a: Let the outward distance be d km, so the return distance is (d + 8) km. Equal times gives d45 = d + 860. Multiply by 180: 4d = 3(d + 8), so 4d = 3d + 24 and d = 24. The outward trip is 24 km and the return trip is 32 km, a total of 56 km. Check: 2445 = 815 hour = 32 minutes, and 3260 = 815 hour as well.

questions.t: Find the value of the subject when the other pronumerals have the values given.
p: <var>A</var> = <var>ℓ</var><var>w</var>, where <var>ℓ</var> = 7 and <var>w</var> = 9
s = dt, where d = 144 and t = 9

questions.t: The circumference <var>C</var> of a circle of radius <var>r</var> is given by <var>C</var> = 2π<var>r</var>. Find the value of <var>C</var> when <var>r</var> = 15:
p: in terms of π (that is, exactly)
correct to 2 decimal places

questions.t: For the formula <var>t</var> = <var>a</var> + (<var>n</var> − 1)<var>d</var>, find:
p: <var>t</var> if <var>a</var> = 12, <var>n</var> = 9 and <var>d</var> = 5
<var>a</var> if <var>t</var> = 40, <var>n</var> = 7 and <var>d</var> = 3

questions.t: The simple interest $I earned when $P is invested at r% per year for t years is given by I = Prt100.
p: Find the interest earned when $2400 is invested at 4.5% per year for 3 years.
Find the number of years for which $3500 must be invested at 6% per year to earn $630 interest.
ap: I = 2400 × 4.5 × 3100 = 32400100 = 324, so the interest is $324.
630 = 3500 × 6 × t100 = 210t, so t = 3 years.

questions.t: Fahrenheit and Celsius temperatures are related by the formula F = 95C + 32.
p: Convert 35°C to degrees Fahrenheit.
Rearrange the formula to make <var>C</var> the subject.
Convert 5°F to degrees Celsius.
ap: F = 95 × 35 + 32 = 63 + 32 = 95°F
F − 32 = 95C, so C = 5(F − 32)9
C = 5(5 − 32)9 = 5 × (−27)9 = −15°C

questions.t: Rearrange each of these formulas to make the pronumeral in brackets the subject.
p: <var>y</var> = <var>m</var><var>x</var> + <var>c</var>  (<var>m</var>)
<var>A</var> = ½<var>b</var><var>h</var>  (<var>h</var>)
<var>V</var> = ⅓π<var>r</var><sup>2</sup><var>h</var>  (<var>h</var>)
<var>P</var> = <var>A</var> + 2<var>ℓ</var><var>h</var>  (<var>ℓ</var>)
ap: mx = y − c, so m = y − cx
2A = bh, so h = 2Ab
3V = πr2h, so h = 3Vπr2
2ℓh = P − A, so ℓ = P − A2h

questions.t: Construct a formula for each of the following.
p: <var>g</var>, the number of grams in <var>k</var> kilograms
<var>s</var>, the number of seconds in <var>h</var> hours and <var>m</var> minutes
<var>c</var>, the number of cents in $<var>d</var> and <var>e</var> cents
<var>C</var>, the cost in dollars of one pen, if 12 identical pens cost $<var>k</var>
ap: C = k12

questions.t: A taxi charges a fixed flag fall of $4.50 plus $1.80 for each kilometre travelled.
p: Write a formula for the total fare $<var>F</var> for a trip of <var>x</var> kilometres.
Make <var>x</var> the subject of your formula.
How many kilometres long was a trip for which the fare was $33.30?
ap: 1.8x = F − 4.5, so x = F − 4.51.8
x = 33.30 − 4.501.8 = 28.81.8 = 16, so the trip was 16 km.

questions.t: The sum <var>S</var> of the interior angles of a convex polygon with <var>n</var> sides is <var>S</var> = 180(<var>n</var> − 2), where <var>S</var> is measured in degrees.
p: Rearrange the formula to make <var>n</var> the subject.
How many sides has a convex polygon whose interior angles add to 1440°?
Find the sum of the interior angles of a convex polygon with 15 sides.
ap: S180 = n − 2, so n = S180 + 2 = S + 360180
n = 1440180 + 2 = 8 + 2 = 10 sides

questions.t: The area <var>A</var> cm<sup>2</sup> of a circle of radius <var>r</var> cm is given by <var>A</var> = π<var>r</var><sup>2</sup>. If <var>A</var> = 45, find the value of <var>r</var>:
p: exactly
correct to 2 decimal places
questions.al: 45 = πr2, so r2 = 45π.
ap: r = √(45/π) cm (r is positive)

questions.t: The kinetic energy <var>E</var> joules of an object of mass <var>m</var> kg moving at a speed of <var>v</var> m/s is given by <var>E</var> = ½<var>m</var><var>v</var><sup>2</sup>.
p: Make <var>m</var> the subject of the formula.
Find the mass of an object that has kinetic energy 90 joules when moving at 6 m/s.
Make <var>v</var> the subject of the formula, given that <var>v</var> is positive.
Find the speed of an object of mass 8 kg that has kinetic energy 36 joules.
ap: 2E = mv2, so m = 2Ev2
m = 2 × 9062 = 18036 = 5 kg
v2 = 2Em, so v = √(2E/m)

questions.t: The thin lens formula is 1f = 1u + 1v.
p: Find <var>f</var> when <var>u</var> = 3 and <var>v</var> = 6.
Find <var>u</var> when <var>f</var> = 4 and <var>v</var> = 12.
Make <var>v</var> the subject of the formula.
ap: 1f = 13 + 16 = 12, so f = 2
1u = 14 − 112 = 212 = 16, so u = 6
1v = 1f − 1u = u − ffu, so v = fuu − f

questions.t: The period T seconds of a pendulum of length ℓ metres is given by T = 2π√(ℓg), where g is the acceleration due to gravity.
p: Rearrange the formula to make <var>ℓ</var> the subject.
Find the value of <var>ℓ</var>, correct to 2 decimal places, when <var>T</var> = 3 and <var>g</var> = 9.8.
ap: T2π = √(ℓ/g); squaring both sides gives T24π2 = ℓg, so ℓ = T2g4π2
ℓ = 9 × 9.84π2 = 88.239.4784... = 2.2342... ≈ 2.23 m

questions.t: Rearrange each of these formulas to make the pronumeral in brackets the subject. All pronumerals represent positive numbers.
p: P = M + mM − m (M)
1S = 1R + 1T (R)
E = Ri + P (i)
T = t − hℓ (ℓ)
ap: P(M − m) = M + m, so PM − Pm = M + m, giving PM − M = m + Pm, M(P − 1) = m(P + 1) and M = m(P + 1)P − 1
1R = 1S − 1T = T − SST, so R = STT − S
E − P = Ri, so i = RE − P
hℓ = t − T, so ℓ = ht − T

questions.t: In the formula L = ℓ√(1 + v2c2) all the pronumerals represent positive numbers.
p: Make <var>v</var> the subject of the formula.
Use your answer to find <var>v</var> when <var>L</var> = 13, <var>ℓ</var> = 5 and <var>c</var> = 10.
ap: Lℓ = √(1 + v2/c2); squaring gives L2ℓ2 = 1 + v2c2, so v2c2 = L2 − ℓ2ℓ2 and v = cℓ√(L2 − ℓ2)
v = 105 × √(169 − 25) = 2√144 = 2 × 12 = 24. Check: 5√(1 + 576/100) = 5 × 2.6 = 13. ✓

questions.t: At a club meeting <var>n</var> people attend, and every person shakes hands exactly once with every other person.
p: Explain why the number of handshakes H is given by H = n(n − 1)2.
How many handshakes take place when 12 people attend?
At another meeting there were exactly 105 handshakes. How many people attended?
ap: Each of the n people shakes hands with the other n − 1 people, which counts n(n − 1) handshakes; but each handshake involves two people, so it has been counted twice. Hence H = n(n − 1)2.
H = 12 × 112 = 66
n(n − 1)2 = 105, so n(n − 1) = 210 = 15 × 14, giving n = 15 people.

questions.t: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four of its vertices on a circle. If its side lengths in centimetres are a, b, c and d, then its area A cm2 satisfies Brahmagupta's formula A2 = (s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d), where s = a + b + c + d2. Find the exact area of a cyclic quadrilateral whose sides are:
p: 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm and 8 cm
4 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm
ap: s = 262 = 13; A2 = 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 = 1680, so A = √1680 = 4√105 cm2
s = 262 = 13; A2 = 9 × 8 × 6 × 3 = 1296, so A = 36 cm2

questions.t: The population of a town decreases by 4% each year.
p: The population is <var>P</var> now and <var>Q</var> after <var>n</var> years. Write a formula for <var>Q</var> in terms of <var>P</var> and <var>n</var>.
Over the whole <var>n</var>-year period the population decreases by <var>a</var>% of its starting value. Write a formula for <var>a</var> in terms of <var>n</var>.
Use your formula to find the total percentage decrease over 3 years, correct to 1 decimal place.
ap: Each year the population is multiplied by 0.96, so Q = P × 0.96<sup>n</sup>
The decrease is P − P × 0.96<sup>n</sup> = P(1 − 0.96<sup>n</sup>), which is 100(1 − 0.96<sup>n</sup>)% of P, so a = 100(1 − 0.96<sup>n</sup>)

questions.t: Answer each of the following.
p: Classify 118° using the standard terms (acute, obtuse or reflex).
Classify 305° using the standard terms.
Write down the complement of 27°.
Write down the supplement of 118°.
ap: obtuse (it lies between 90° and 180°)
reflex (it lies between 180° and 360°)

questions.t: Find the value of each pronumeral, giving a reason.
p: The rays OP, OQ and OR are drawn on one side of the straight line SOT, so that in order around the point O the rays are OS, OP, OQ, OR, OT. Given that ∠SOP = 3<var>a</var>, ∠POQ = 2<var>a</var>, ∠QOR = <var>a</var> and ∠ROT = 60°, find <var>a</var>.
The straight lines AB and CD cross at the point M, and ∠AMC = 5<var>b</var> − 30° while ∠BMD = 3<var>b</var> + 10°. Find <var>b</var>, and then find the size of ∠AMD.
ap: 3<var>a</var> + 2<var>a</var> + <var>a</var> + 60° = 180° (angles on the straight line SOT), so 6<var>a</var> = 120° and <var>a</var> = 20°.

5<var>b</var> − 30 = 3<var>b</var> + 10 (vertically opposite angles at M), so 2<var>b</var> = 40 and <var>b</var> = 20. Then ∠AMC = 5 × 20 − 30 = 70°, so ∠AMD = 180° − 70° = 110° (angles on the straight line CD).

questions.t: AB and CD are parallel lines. A transversal crosses AB at X and crosses CD at Y, where X lies between A and B, Y lies between C and D, and A and C are on the same side of the transversal. Given that ∠AXY = 112°, find each angle below, giving a reason.
p: ∠XYD
∠XYC
ap: ∠XYD = 112° (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD).
∠XYC = 180° − 112° = 68° (∠AXY and ∠XYC are co-interior angles, AB ∥ CD). Check: ∠XYC + ∠XYD = 68° + 112° = 180°, as they are adjacent angles on the straight line CD.

questions.t: Find the value of each pronumeral, giving a reason.
p: In △DEF, ∠D = 4<var>x</var>, ∠E = 2<var>x</var> + 10° and ∠F = 3<var>x</var> − 10°. Find <var>x</var> and state the size of the largest angle of the triangle.
In the quadrilateral KLMN, ∠K = 2<var>y</var>, ∠L = 3<var>y</var>, ∠M = 90° and ∠N = <var>y</var> + 30°. Find <var>y</var>.
ap: 4<var>x</var> + (2<var>x</var> + 10) + (3<var>x</var> − 10) = 180 (angle sum of △DEF), so 9<var>x</var> = 180 and <var>x</var> = 20. The angles are ∠D = 80°, ∠E = 50°, ∠F = 50°, so the largest angle is ∠D = 80°.

2<var>y</var> + 3<var>y</var> + 90 + (<var>y</var> + 30) = 360 (angle sum of a quadrilateral), so 6<var>y</var> = 240 and <var>y</var> = 40. (The angles are 80°, 120°, 90° and 70°, which add to 360°.)

questions.t: Use the exterior angle of a triangle in each part.
p: In △ABC the side BC is produced to D. Given that ∠ACD = 130° and ∠BAC = 75°, find ∠ABC.
In △PQR the side QR is produced to S. Given that ∠QPR = 40° and that ∠PRS is three times ∠PQR, find ∠PQR.
ap: ∠ACD = ∠BAC + ∠ABC (exterior angle of △ABC equals the sum of the opposite interior angles), so 130° = 75° + ∠ABC and ∠ABC = 55°. (Check: ∠ACB = 50°, and 75° + 55° + 50° = 180°.)

Let ∠PQR = <var>q</var>. Then ∠PRS = 40° + <var>q</var> (exterior angle) and ∠PRS = 3<var>q</var>, so 3<var>q</var> = 40 + <var>q</var>, giving 2<var>q</var> = 40 and <var>q</var> = 20. So ∠PQR = 20° and ∠PRS = 60°.

questions.t: △ABC is isosceles with AB = AC, and ∠BAC = 40°.
p: Find ∠ABC, giving a reason.
The bisector of ∠ABC meets the side AC at D. Find ∠BDC, giving reasons.
ap: ∠ABC = ∠ACB (base angles of isosceles △ABC), and their sum is 180° − 40° = 140°, so ∠ABC = 70°.
∠DBC = ½ × 70° = 35° (BD bisects ∠ABC) and ∠BCD = ∠ACB = 70°, so ∠BDC = 180° − 35° − 70° = 75° (angle sum of △BDC).

questions.t: In each part, write a congruence statement with the vertices in matching order, and name the congruence test you used.
p: In △ABC and △PQR: AB = PQ = 7 cm, BC = QR = 5 cm and ∠ABC = ∠PQR = 62°.
In △DEF and △XYZ: ∠DEF = ∠XYZ = 90°, DF = XZ = 13 cm and EF = YZ = 5 cm.
In △KLM and △STU: ∠K = ∠S = 48°, ∠L = ∠T = 71° and KL = ST = 6 cm.
ap: △ABC ≡ △PQR (SAS — two sides and the included angle).
△DEF ≡ △XYZ (RHS — DF and XZ are the hypotenuses, since the right angles are at E and Y, and one other pair of sides is equal).
△KLM ≡ △STU (AAS — two angles and the matching side KL = ST, which joins the two given angles in each triangle).

questions.t: The intervals AB and CD intersect at the point M, and M is the midpoint of both AB and CD.
p: Prove that △AMC ≡ △BMD.
Hence prove that AC ∥ BD.
ap: In △AMC and △BMD: AM = BM (M is the midpoint of AB), CM = DM (M is the midpoint of CD), and ∠AMC = ∠BMD (vertically opposite angles at M). Hence △AMC ≡ △BMD (SAS).
So ∠MAC = ∠MBD (matching angles of congruent triangles). These are alternate angles for the lines AC and BD with transversal AB, and they are equal, so AC ∥ BD.

questions.t: In △ABC, AB = AC, and M is the midpoint of BC.
p: Prove that △ABM ≡ △ACM.
Hence prove that AM ⊥ BC.
ap: In △ABM and △ACM: AB = AC (given), BM = CM (M is the midpoint of BC), and AM = AM (common). Hence △ABM ≡ △ACM (SSS).
So ∠AMB = ∠AMC (matching angles of congruent triangles). But ∠AMB + ∠AMC = 180° (adjacent angles on the straight line BC), so each is 90°. Therefore AM ⊥ BC.

questions.t: Use the properties of a parallelogram in each part.
p: ABCD is a parallelogram in which ∠DAB = 2<var>x</var> + 20° and ∠ABC = 3<var>x</var> − 40°. Find <var>x</var>, and then find the size of ∠BCD.
The diagonals of the parallelogram PQRS meet at M, with PM = 3<var>y</var> − 2 cm and MR = <var>y</var> + 6 cm. Find <var>y</var>, and then find the length of the diagonal PR.
ap: ∠DAB + ∠ABC = 180° (co-interior angles, AD ∥ BC), so (2<var>x</var> + 20) + (3<var>x</var> − 40) = 180, giving 5<var>x</var> = 200 and <var>x</var> = 40. Then ∠DAB = 100° and ∠ABC = 80°, and ∠BCD = ∠DAB = 100° (opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal).
PM = MR (the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other), so 3<var>y</var> − 2 = <var>y</var> + 6, giving 2<var>y</var> = 8 and <var>y</var> = 4. Then PM = 10 cm, so PR = 2 × 10 = 20 cm.

questions.t: PQRS is a rhombus in which ∠PQR = 116°, and its diagonals PR and QS meet at M. Find each angle below, giving a reason.
p: ∠QRS
∠QPR
∠PMQ
ap: ∠QRS = 180° − 116° = 64° (co-interior angles, PQ ∥ SR, since a rhombus is a parallelogram).
∠SPQ = ∠QRS = 64° (opposite angles of a parallelogram), and the diagonal PR bisects ∠SPQ (a diagonal of a rhombus bisects the vertex angles it passes through), so ∠QPR = 32°.
∠PMQ = 90° (the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles). Check with △PQM: ∠PQM = 58° (QS bisects ∠PQR), and 32° + 58° + 90° = 180°.

questions.t: The diagonals WY and XZ of the quadrilateral WXYZ bisect each other at O. Name the most specific type of quadrilateral WXYZ must be in each case, and state the test you are using.
p: No further information is given.
In addition, WY = XZ.
Instead, in addition, WY ⊥ XZ.
Instead, in addition, WY = XZ and WY ⊥ XZ.
ap: A parallelogram (if the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram).
A rectangle (if the diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other, the quadrilateral is a rectangle).
A rhombus (if the diagonals bisect each other at right angles, the quadrilateral is a rhombus).
A square (it is both a rectangle and a rhombus, by parts b and c, and a square is a quadrilateral that is both).

questions.t: ABCD is a parallelogram. The point P lies on the side AB and the point Q lies on the side DC, and AP = CQ. Prove that APCQ is a parallelogram.
questions.a: AP lies along AB and CQ lies along DC, and AB ∥ DC (opposite sides of the parallelogram ABCD), so AP ∥ QC. Also AP = CQ (given). In the quadrilateral APCQ, AP and CQ are a pair of opposite sides that are equal and parallel, so APCQ is a parallelogram (if one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal and parallel, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram).

questions.t: The diagonals KM and LN of the convex quadrilateral KLMN meet at right angles at the point O.
p: Prove that KL<sup>2</sup> + MN<sup>2</sup> = LM<sup>2</sup> + NK<sup>2</sup>.
In such a quadrilateral, KL = 8 cm, LM = 4 cm and MN = 11 cm. Find the length of NK.
ap: Let OK = <var>p</var>, OL = <var>q</var>, OM = <var>r</var> and ON = <var>s</var>. Each of the four triangles at O is right-angled at O, so by Pythagoras' theorem KL<sup>2</sup> = <var>p</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>q</var><sup>2</sup>, LM<sup>2</sup> = <var>q</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>r</var><sup>2</sup>, MN<sup>2</sup> = <var>r</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>s</var><sup>2</sup> and NK<sup>2</sup> = <var>s</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>p</var><sup>2</sup>. Hence KL<sup>2</sup> + MN<sup>2</sup> = <var>p</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>q</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>r</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>s</var><sup>2</sup> = LM<sup>2</sup> + NK<sup>2</sup>.
NK<sup>2</sup> = KL<sup>2</sup> + MN<sup>2</sup> − LM<sup>2</sup> = 64 + 121 − 16 = 169, so NK = 13 cm.

questions.t: In △ABC, let P be the midpoint of BC and Q the midpoint of CA, and let the perpendicular bisector of BC meet the perpendicular bisector of CA at the point O.
p: Use congruent triangles to prove that OB = OC.
Prove similarly that OA = OC, and deduce that OA = OB.

Let R be the midpoint of AB. Prove that OR ⊥ AB, and explain why this means that all three perpendicular bisectors pass through O and that the circle with centre O and radius OA passes through A, B and C.
ap: In △OPB and △OPC: BP = CP (P is the midpoint of BC), ∠OPB = ∠OPC = 90° (OP is part of the perpendicular bisector of BC) and OP is common, so △OPB ≡ △OPC (SAS) and hence OB = OC.
In the same way, △OQC ≡ △OQA (SAS, using CQ = AQ, the right angles at Q and the common side OQ), so OA = OC. Since OB = OC and OA = OC, OA = OB.

In △ORA and △ORB: OA = OB (part b), AR = BR (R is the midpoint of AB) and OR is common, so △ORA ≡ △ORB (SSS). Hence ∠ORA = ∠ORB, and since they are adjacent angles on the straight line AB they add to 180°, so each is 90°. So OR ⊥ AB and OR bisects AB, i.e. the perpendicular bisector of AB is the line OR and passes through O. Thus all three perpendicular bisectors are concurrent at O, and since OA = OB = OC, the circle with centre O and radius OA passes through all three vertices (it is the circumcircle).

questions.t: This question is about exterior angles of convex polygons.
p: A hiker walks once around the outside of a convex hexagonal field, turning through the exterior angle at each of the six corners, and finishes at her starting point facing the direction she started in. Through how many degrees has she turned altogether, and how many revolutions is that?
Use this idea to explain why the sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon with <var>n</var> sides is 360°, no matter how large <var>n</var> is.
Hence find the size of each interior angle of a regular 15-sided polygon.
ap: 360°, which is exactly one revolution.

Walking once around a convex polygon, the walker turns through the exterior angle at each vertex, and every turn is in the same direction. Because she returns to her starting point facing her original direction, the total turning must be a whole number of revolutions, and for a convex polygon each individual turn is less than 180° and the walker never doubles back, so the total is exactly one revolution. Hence the exterior angles add to 360°, independently of <var>n</var>.
For a regular 15-gon each exterior angle is 360° ÷ 15 = 24°, so each interior angle is 180° − 24° = 156°. (Check: 15 × 156° = 2340° = (15 − 2) × 180°.)

questions.t: H is the midpoint of AB and K is the midpoint of AC in △ABC. The interval HK is produced to X so that KX = HK.
p: Prove that △AKH ≡ △CKX.
Hence prove that CX = BH and that CX ∥ BH.
Deduce that BHXC is a parallelogram, and hence prove that HK = ½ × BC and HK ∥ BC.
ap: In △AKH and △CKX: AK = CK (K is the midpoint of AC), HK = XK (given) and ∠AKH = ∠CKX (vertically opposite angles at K), so △AKH ≡ △CKX (SAS).

Hence AH = CX (matching sides), and AH = HB (H is the midpoint of AB), so CX = BH. Also ∠KAH = ∠KCX (matching angles of the congruent triangles); these are alternate angles for AB and CX with transversal AC, so AB ∥ CX, that is, BH ∥ CX.

In the quadrilateral BHXC the opposite sides BH and XC are equal and parallel, so BHXC is a parallelogram. Therefore its other pair of opposite sides are equal and parallel: HX = BC and HX ∥ BC. Since HK = ½ × HX (as KX = HK), it follows that HK = ½ × BC and HK ∥ BC.

questions.t: ABCD is a parallelogram whose diagonals meet at M. A line through M crosses the side AB at P and the side DC at Q.
p: Prove that △APM ≡ △CQM.
Hence prove that the line PQ divides the parallelogram into two regions APQD and PBCQ of equal area.
ap: In △APM and △CQM: AM = CM (the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other), ∠AMP = ∠CMQ (vertically opposite angles at M) and ∠PAM = ∠QCM (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC). Hence △APM ≡ △CQM (AAS).

Join M to each of A, B, C and D. Then region APQD = △APM + △AMD + △DMQ and region PBCQ = △CQM + △CMB + △BMP. Now △APM ≡ △CQM by part a; △AMD ≡ △CMB (SAS: AM = CM, DM = BM and ∠AMD = ∠CMB vertically opposite); and △DMQ ≡ △BMP (AAS: DM = BM, ∠DMQ = ∠BMP vertically opposite, ∠MDQ = ∠MBP alternate angles with DC ∥ AB). Congruent triangles have equal areas, so the three pieces of APQD have the same total area as the three pieces of PBCQ, and each region is half the parallelogram.

questions.t: A photocopier is set to enlarge, so that every length on the copy is 1.25 times the matching length on the sheet being copied. A rectangular photograph measuring 12 cm by 8 cm is copied, then that copy is copied, and so on.
p: Write down the length and the width of the picture after <var>n</var> enlargements, using a power of 1.25.
Hence write down the area of the picture after <var>n</var> enlargements, using a power of 1.25.

Use a calculator to find the smallest number of enlargements for which the area of the picture is more than 10 000 cm<sup>2</sup> (that is, more than 1 m<sup>2</sup>). Show the two calculations that justify your answer.
ap: Length = 12 × 1.25<sup><var>n</var></sup> cm and width = 8 × 1.25<sup><var>n</var></sup> cm.
Area = 12 × 1.25<sup><var>n</var></sup> × 8 × 1.25<sup><var>n</var></sup> = 96 × 1.25<sup>2<var>n</var></sup> cm<sup>2</sup> (equivalently 96 × 1.5625<sup><var>n</var></sup> cm<sup>2</sup>).

<var>n</var> = 11. For <var>n</var> = 10: 96 × 1.25<sup>20</sup> ≈ 96 × 86.74 ≈ 8327 cm<sup>2</sup>, which is less than 10 000. For <var>n</var> = 11: 96 × 1.25<sup>22</sup> ≈ 96 × 135.53 ≈ 13 010 cm<sup>2</sup>, which is more than 10 000.

questions.t: The index laws were first proved only for positive whole number indices. Using those laws together with the definitions a0 = 1 and a−n = 1an, explain why a−p × a−q = a−(p+q) for every non-zero number a and all positive whole numbers p and q. Set your reasoning out as a chain of equal steps, and name the law you use.
questions.a: By the definition of a negative index, a−p × a−q = 1ap × 1aq = 1ap × aq. Since p and q are positive whole numbers, index law 1 for positive whole number indices gives ap × aq = ap+q, so the product equals 1ap+q. Applying the definition of a negative index in reverse, 1ap+q = a−(p+q) = a−p+(−q). So index law 1 also holds when both indices are negative. (Accept any correct chain that uses only the positive-index laws and the two definitions; a marker should check that index law 1 for positive indices is applied to ap × aq and that the negative-index definition is used in both directions.)

Find the length of BC.
Given that ∠SPQ = 105°, write down the size of ∠DAB.
ap: AB/PQ = 7.5/3 = 2.5, so the similarity ratio is 2.5.
∠DAB = 105° (matching angles of similar figures are equal).

questions.t: In two triangles ABC and LMN, AB = 5 cm, LM = 15 cm, LN = 10 cm and MN = 20 cm. In each case state the similarity ratio of the enlargement that takes △ABC to the second triangle named. (The vertices are named in matching order.)
p: △ABC is similar to △LMN
△ABC is similar to △NML
△ABC is similar to △LNM
questions.al: In each case find the side matching AB and divide by 5.
ap: AB matches LM = 15, ratio = 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
AB matches NM = 20, ratio = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
AB matches LN = 10, ratio = 10 ÷ 5 = 2.

questions.t: At the same time of day, a vertical post 1.8 m high casts a shadow 60 cm long on level ground, and a vertical tower nearby casts a shadow 14 m long.
p: Explain why the triangle formed by the post and its shadow is similar to the triangle formed by the tower and its shadow.
Find the height of the tower.
ap: In each triangle the vertical object meets the level ground at 90°, so one pair of angles is equal. The sun's rays are parallel, so the angle of elevation of the sun is the same in both triangles. Hence the triangles are similar (AAA).
1.8 m and 60 cm = 0.6 m give a similarity ratio of 1.8 ÷ 0.6 = 3, so the tower's height = 3 × 14 = 42 m.

questions.t: In △ABC, the point X lies on AB and the point Y lies on AC, and XY is parallel to BC. Also AX = 4 cm, XB = 6 cm and XY = 5 cm.
p: Prove that △AXY is similar to △ABC, naming the similarity test used.
Find the length of BC.
ap: In △AXY and △ABC: ∠A = ∠A (common) and ∠AXY = ∠ABC (corresponding angles, XY ∥ BC), so △AXY is similar to △ABC (AAA).
AB = 4 + 6 = 10 cm, so the similarity ratio from △AXY to △ABC is AB/AX = 10/4 = 2.5. Hence BC = 2.5 × XY = 2.5 × 5 = 12.5 cm.

questions.t: In △ABC, the point P lies on AB with AP = 4 cm and PB = 6 cm, and the point Q lies on AC with AQ = 6 cm and QC = 9 cm.
p: Prove that △ABC is similar to △APQ, naming the similarity test used.
Hence prove that PQ is parallel to BC.
ap: AB = 4 + 6 = 10 cm and AC = 6 + 9 = 15 cm. In △ABC and △APQ: AB/AP = 10/4 = 2.5 and AC/AQ = 15/6 = 2.5, and ∠A = ∠A (common, and it is the angle included between these sides). So △ABC is similar to △APQ (SAS).
Hence ∠ABC = ∠APQ (matching angles of similar triangles), and these are corresponding angles for the lines PQ and BC cut by the transversal AB, so PQ ∥ BC.

questions.t: The intervals AC and BD meet at M, and AB is parallel to CD, with A and B on one side of M and C and D on the other. Also AM = 6 cm, MC = 9 cm, BM = 4 cm and AB = 5 cm.
p: Prove that △AMB is similar to △CMD.
Find the lengths of MD and CD.
ap: In △AMB and △CMD: ∠MAB = ∠MCD (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD, transversal AC) and ∠AMB = ∠CMD (vertically opposite at M), so △AMB is similar to △CMD (AAA).
The similarity ratio from △AMB to △CMD is MC/MA = 9/6 = 1.5. So MD = 1.5 × MB = 1.5 × 4 = 6 cm and CD = 1.5 × AB = 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 cm.

questions.t: In △ABM, ∠AMB = 90°, AB = 15 cm and BM = 9 cm. In △PQN, ∠PNQ = 90°, PQ = 10 cm and QN = 6 cm.
p: Explain why △ABM is similar to △PQN, naming the similarity test used.
Find the lengths of AM and PN.
ap: Both triangles are right-angled, with hypotenuses AB and PQ. AB/PQ = 15/10 = 1.5 and BM/QN = 9/6 = 1.5, so the hypotenuses and one other pair of sides are in the same ratio. Hence △ABM is similar to △PQN (RHS).
By Pythagoras' theorem, AM = √(15² − 9²) = √(225 − 81) = √144 = 12 cm and PN = √(10² − 6²) = √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8 cm. (Check: 12/8 = 1.5, as expected.)

questions.t: In △PQR, ∠PQR = 90°, and QS is the altitude from Q to the hypotenuse PR, so S lies on PR and ∠QSP = 90°. Also PS = 4 cm and SR = 9 cm.
p: Prove that △PSQ is similar to △QSR.
Hence find the length of QS.
Find the length of PQ, in simplest surd form.
ap: In △PSQ and △QSR: ∠PSQ = ∠QSR = 90°. Let ∠SPQ = α. In △PSQ, ∠PQS = 90° − α. Since ∠PQR = 90°, ∠SQR = 90° − ∠PQS = α = ∠SPQ. So △PSQ is similar to △QSR (AAA), with P matching Q, S matching S and Q matching R.
Hence PS/QS = QS/SR, so QS² = PS × SR = 4 × 9 = 36 and QS = 6 cm.
In right-angled △PSQ, PQ² = PS² + QS² = 16 + 36 = 52, so PQ = √52 = 2√13 cm (≈ 7.2 cm).

questions.t: In △ABC, D is the midpoint of AB and E is the midpoint of AC.
p: Prove that △ADE is similar to △ABC, and state the similarity ratio of the enlargement taking △ADE to △ABC.
Hence explain why DE is parallel to BC.
The perimeter of △ABC is 34 cm. Find the perimeter of △ADE.
ap: In △ADE and △ABC: AD/AB = ½ and AE/AC = ½ (D and E are midpoints), and ∠A = ∠A (common, included between these sides). So △ADE is similar to △ABC (SAS). The enlargement taking △ADE to △ABC has similarity ratio 2.
Hence ∠ADE = ∠ABC (matching angles of similar triangles); these are corresponding angles for DE and BC cut by AB, so DE ∥ BC.
All lengths in △ABC are twice those in △ADE, so the perimeter of △ADE = 34 ÷ 2 = 17 cm.

questions.t: ABCD is a trapezium with AB parallel to DC, where AB = 6 cm and DC = 15 cm. The diagonals AC and BD meet at M. Also AM = 6 cm and BD = 14 cm.
p: Prove that △ABM is similar to △CDM.
Find the length of MC.
Find the lengths of BM and MD.
ap: In △ABM and △CDM: ∠BAM = ∠DCM (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC, transversal AC) and ∠AMB = ∠CMD (vertically opposite), so △ABM is similar to △CDM (AAA).
The similarity ratio from △ABM to △CDM is DC/AB = 15/6 = 2.5, so MC = 2.5 × AM = 2.5 × 6 = 15 cm.
Also MD = 2.5 × BM. Since BM + MD = BD = 14, we get BM + 2.5BM = 14, so 3.5BM = 14, BM = 4 cm and MD = 10 cm.

questions.t: In △ABC, F is the midpoint of AB and E is the midpoint of AC. The medians BE and CF meet at G.
p: Prove that FE is parallel to BC and that BC = 2 × FE.
Prove that △GFE is similar to △GCB.
Hence prove that BG = 2 × GE.
ap: In △AFE and △ABC: AF/AB = ½, AE/AC = ½ and ∠A is common and included, so △AFE is similar to △ABC (SAS) with similarity ratio 2 from △AFE to △ABC. Hence ∠AFE = ∠ABC, which are corresponding angles for FE and BC cut by AB, so FE ∥ BC; and BC = 2 × FE.

In △GFE and △GCB: ∠FGE = ∠CGB (vertically opposite at G) and ∠GFE = ∠GCB (alternate angles, FE ∥ BC, transversal CF). So △GFE is similar to △GCB (AAA), with F matching C, E matching B and G matching G.
The similarity ratio is CB/FE = 2, so GB = 2 × GE (and likewise GC = 2 × GF). That is, BG = 2GE.

questions.t: ABC is an acute-angled triangle. BP is the altitude from B to AC, so P lies on AC and ∠BPC = 90°. CQ is the altitude from C to AB, so Q lies on AB and ∠CQB = 90°. Suppose BP = CQ.
p: Prove that △BPC is congruent to △CQB.
Hence prove that AB = AC.
ap: In △BPC and △CQB: ∠BPC = ∠CQB = 90°; the hypotenuses BC and CB are the same interval, so BC = CB; and BP = CQ (given). So △BPC ≡ △CQB (RHS).
Hence ∠PCB = ∠QBC (matching angles of congruent triangles), that is ∠ACB = ∠ABC. A triangle with two equal angles is isosceles, with the equal sides opposite the equal angles, so AB = AC.

questions.t: ABCD is a rectangle (vertices named in order, so AB is parallel to DC). K is the midpoint of AB and L is the midpoint of DC. The diagonal AC meets KL at M, and the interval DK meets AC at X.
p: Prove that M is the midpoint of KL.
Find the ratio AX : XC, giving a reason.
ap: In △AMK and △CML: ∠MAK = ∠MCL (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC, transversal AC) and ∠AMK = ∠CML (vertically opposite at M), so the triangles are similar (AAA). Also AK = ½AB and LC = ½DC, and AB = DC, so AK = LC. The similarity ratio is therefore 1 and the triangles are congruent, giving KM = ML. Hence M is the midpoint of KL.

In △AXK and △CXD: ∠XAK = ∠XCD (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC, transversal AC) and ∠AXK = ∠CXD (vertically opposite at X), so △AXK is similar to △CXD (AAA). The similarity ratio is AK/CD = ½, so AX/XC = ½, that is AX : XC = 1 : 2.

questions.t: ABCD is a quadrilateral. P, Q, R and S are the midpoints of the sides AB, BC, CD and DA respectively.
p: Prove that SP is parallel to BD with SP = ½BD, and that QR is parallel to BD with QR = ½BD.
Hence explain why PQRS is a parallelogram.
Given that BD = 12 cm and AC = 9 cm, find the perimeter of PQRS.
ap: In △ABD, S and P are the midpoints of AD and AB, so AP/AB = AS/AD = ½ with ∠A common and included; hence △APS is similar to △ABD (SAS) with ratio 2. So ∠APS = ∠ABD (corresponding angles), giving SP ∥ BD, and SP = ½BD. The same argument in △CBD (Q and R are the midpoints of CB and CD, ∠C common) gives QR ∥ BD and QR = ½BD.
SP and QR are both parallel to BD and both equal to ½BD, so one pair of opposite sides of PQRS is equal and parallel. Hence PQRS is a parallelogram.
By the same argument in △ABC and △ADC, PQ = RS = ½AC. So the perimeter = 2 × ½BD + 2 × ½AC = BD + AC = 12 + 9 = 21 cm.

questions.t: ABCD is a trapezium with AB parallel to DC, where AB = 6 cm and DC = 10 cm. The diagonals AC and BD meet at O. The line through O parallel to AB meets AD at P and BC at Q.
p: Prove that △AOB is similar to △COD, and hence find the ratio AO : OC.
Prove that PO = OQ, so that O is the midpoint of PQ.
Find the length of PQ.
ap: In △AOB and △COD: ∠OAB = ∠OCD (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC, transversal AC) and ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite), so △AOB is similar to △COD (AAA). The similarity ratio is DC/AB = 10/6 = 5/3, so OC = (5/3)AO and AO : OC = 3 : 5. (Likewise BO : OD = 3 : 5.)

In △ADC, P lies on AD, O lies on AC and PO ∥ DC, so △APO is similar to △ADC (AAA), giving PO/DC = AO/AC = 3/8 and PO = 3/8 × 10 = 3.75 cm. In △BDC, O lies on BD, Q lies on BC and OQ ∥ DC, so △BOQ is similar to △BDC (AAA), giving OQ/DC = BO/BD = 3/8 and OQ = 3.75 cm. Hence PO = OQ and O is the midpoint of PQ.

questions.t: A rectangular gate is 2.4 m wide and 1.8 m high. A straight brace is fitted along a diagonal of the gate, from one corner to the opposite corner.
p: Find the length of the brace.
A second gate is also 2.4 m wide, and its diagonal brace is 3.4 m long. Find the height of this second gate, correct to 1 decimal place.
ap: brace<sup>2</sup> = 2.4<sup>2</sup> + 1.8<sup>2</sup> = 5.76 + 3.24 = 9, so the brace is 3 m long.
height<sup>2</sup> = 3.4<sup>2</sup> − 2.4<sup>2</sup> = 11.56 − 5.76 = 5.8, so the height is √5.8 ≈ 2.4083, i.e. 2.4 m to 1 decimal place.

questions.t: Calculate each of the following.
p: Increase $840 by 15%.
A jacket is reduced by 20% in a sale, and the sale price is $148. Find the price of the jacket before the sale.
A bus fare rises from $60 to $69. Find the percentage increase.
ap: 0.8 × (original price) = 148, so the original price is 148 ÷ 0.8 = $185
the increase is $9, and 960 = 0.15, so the increase is 15%

questions.t: Nadia invests $4000 for 3 years.
p: How much interest does she earn if the account pays 6% p.a. simple interest?
What is the value of the investment if instead the account pays 4% p.a. compound interest? Give your answer to the nearest cent.
Which account earns her more interest over the 3 years, and by how much?
ap: the compound interest is 4499.46 − 4000 = $499.46, so the simple interest account earns more, by 720 − 499.46 = $220.54

questions.t: Solve each equation for <var>x</var>.
p: 5<var>x</var> − 7 = 3<var>x</var> + 11
2x3 − x4 = 5
x + 32 = 2x − 15
<var>ax</var> + <var>b</var> = 3<var>x</var> + <var>c</var>, where <var>a</var> ≠ 3
ap: 2<var>x</var> = 18, so <var>x</var> = 9
multiply by 12: 8<var>x</var> − 3<var>x</var> = 60, 5<var>x</var> = 60, <var>x</var> = 12
cross-multiplying, 5(<var>x</var> + 3) = 2(2<var>x</var> − 1), 5<var>x</var> + 15 = 4<var>x</var> − 2, <var>x</var> = −17 (check: both sides equal −7)
ax − 3x = c − b, x(a − 3) = c − b, so x = c − ba − 3

questions.t: Solve these inequalities.
p: 7 − 2<var>x</var> < 15
3x + 14 ≥ x − 23

multiply by 12: 3(3x + 1) ≥ 4(x − 2), 9x + 3 ≥ 4x − 8, 5x ≥ −11, so x ≥ −115

questions.t: The sum S of a list of n numbers that increase in equal steps, starting at a and finishing at ℓ, is given by S = n(a + ℓ)2.
p: Find <var>S</var> when <var>n</var> = 12, <var>a</var> = 5 and <var>ℓ</var> = 38.
Rearrange the formula to make <var>ℓ</var> the subject.
Hence find <var>ℓ</var> when <var>S</var> = 175, <var>n</var> = 10 and <var>a</var> = 4.
ap: S = 12 × (5 + 38)2 = 12 × 432 = 258
2S = n(a + ℓ), so a + ℓ = 2Sn and ℓ = 2Sn − a
ℓ = 35010 − 4 = 35 − 4 = 31

questions.t: In triangle <var>ABC</var>, the point <var>D</var> lies on the side <var>AB</var> and the point <var>E</var> lies on the side <var>AC</var>, and <var>DE</var> is parallel to <var>BC</var>. It is given that <var>AD</var> = 6 cm, <var>DB</var> = 4 cm and <var>DE</var> = 9 cm.
p: Explain why △<var>ADE</var> is similar to △<var>ABC</var>.
Find the length of <var>BC</var>.
Given also that <var>AE</var> = 7.5 cm, find the length of <var>EC</var>.
ap: ∠<var>DAE</var> = ∠<var>BAC</var> (it is the same angle) and ∠<var>ADE</var> = ∠<var>ABC</var> (corresponding angles, <var>DE</var> ∥ <var>BC</var>), so the triangles are similar by the AA test.
AB = 6 + 4 = 10 cm, so the enlargement factor from △ADE to △ABC is 106 = 53; hence BC = 9 × 53 = 15 cm.
AC = 7.5 × 53 = 12.5 cm, so EC = 12.5 − 7.5 = 5 cm.

questions.t: A rectangular vegetable bed is twice as long as it is wide, and its width is <var>x</var> m. The bed is surrounded on all four sides by a paved path of constant width 1.5 m.
p: Write down, in terms of <var>x</var>, the length of the bed, and also the length and the width of the large rectangle formed by the outer edge of the path.
Show that the area of the path alone is (9<var>x</var> + 9) m<sup>2</sup>.
The area of the path alone is 45 m<sup>2</sup>. Find the width and the length of the bed.
ap: The bed is 2<var>x</var> m long. The path adds 1.5 m at each end of each dimension, so the outer rectangle is (<var>x</var> + 3) m wide and (2<var>x</var> + 3) m long.

Outer area = (<var>x</var> + 3)(2<var>x</var> + 3) = 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3<var>x</var> + 6<var>x</var> + 9 = 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 9<var>x</var> + 9; the bed has area <var>x</var> × 2<var>x</var> = 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>. Path = (2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 9<var>x</var> + 9) − 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 9<var>x</var> + 9.
9<var>x</var> + 9 = 45, so 9<var>x</var> = 36 and <var>x</var> = 4. The bed is 4 m wide and 8 m long.

questions.t: Two cyclists ride along the same road from town <var>P</var> towards town <var>Q</var>. The first leaves <var>P</var> at 9:00 a.m. and averages 18 km/h. The second leaves <var>P</var> at 9:45 a.m. and averages 24 km/h.
p: How far has the first cyclist travelled by the time the second one sets out?
Let <var>t</var> be the number of hours after 9:45 a.m. Write an expression in terms of <var>t</var> for the distance from <var>P</var> of each cyclist.
At what time does the second cyclist draw level with the first, and how far from <var>P</var> are they at that moment?
ap: 45 minutes is ¾ hour, so the first cyclist has ridden 18 × ¾ = 13.5 km.
First cyclist: (13.5 + 18<var>t</var>) km. Second cyclist: 24<var>t</var> km.

24<var>t</var> = 13.5 + 18<var>t</var>, so 6<var>t</var> = 13.5 and <var>t</var> = 2.25 hours = 2 hours 15 minutes. This is 12:00 noon, and the distance from <var>P</var> is 24 × 2.25 = 54 km (check: 13.5 + 18 × 2.25 = 54).

questions.t: Petrol is sold at $<var>R</var> per litre. It costs $72.00 to fill a car's tank completely when petrol is $1.60 per litre.
p: How many litres does the tank hold?
After a price rise, filling the same tank completely costs $81.00. Find the new price per litre.

A driver always spends exactly $60 on petrol. Write a formula for the number <var>L</var> of litres bought in terms of <var>R</var>, and hence find how many fewer litres $60 buys at the new price than at $1.60 per litre. Give this answer correct to 2 decimal places.
ap: The tank still holds 45 litres, so the new price is 81 ÷ 45 = $1.80 per litre.
L = 60R. At $1.60, L = 60 ÷ 1.60 = 37.5 litres; at $1.80, L = 60 ÷ 1.80 = 33.333… litres. The difference is 4.1666… ≈ 4.17 litres.

questions.t: A club buys a number of identical trophies, each costing $<var>y</var>, and spends exactly $120 altogether.
p: How many trophies did the club buy? Give your answer in terms of <var>y</var>.
How many trophies could have been bought for $120 if each trophy had cost $2 more? Give your answer in terms of <var>y</var>.

At the price of $<var>y</var> each, the club got exactly 10 more trophies than it would have got at the dearer price. Write down an equation in <var>y</var> and show that it simplifies to <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>y</var> − 24 = 0.
Solve that equation, and state the cost of each trophy and the number of trophies bought.
ap: 120y
120y + 2
120y − 120y + 2 = 10. Multiplying every term by y(y + 2) gives 120(y + 2) − 120y = 10y(y + 2), so 240 = 10y2 + 20y; dividing by 10 gives 24 = y2 + 2y, that is y2 + 2y − 24 = 0.

(<var>y</var> + 6)(<var>y</var> − 4) = 0, so <var>y</var> = 4 or <var>y</var> = −6; a price must be positive, so <var>y</var> = 4. Each trophy cost $4 and 120 ÷ 4 = 30 trophies were bought. (Check: at $6 only 20 could be bought, and 30 − 20 = 10.)

questions.t: <var>ABCD</var> is a square of side length 15 cm, labelled so that <var>AB</var>, <var>BC</var>, <var>CD</var> and <var>DA</var> are its sides. Four points are marked, where 0 < <var>x</var> < 15: <var>M</var> on <var>AB</var> with <var>AM</var> = <var>x</var> cm, <var>N</var> on <var>BC</var> with <var>BN</var> = <var>x</var> cm, <var>P</var> on <var>CD</var> with <var>CP</var> = <var>x</var> cm, and <var>Q</var> on <var>DA</var> with <var>DQ</var> = <var>x</var> cm.
p: Explain why <var>MB</var> = <var>NC</var> = <var>PD</var> = <var>QA</var> = (15 − <var>x</var>) cm, and hence why the four triangles <var>AMQ</var>, <var>BNM</var>, <var>CPN</var> and <var>DQP</var> are congruent.
Show that the area of the quadrilateral <var>MNPQ</var> is (2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 30<var>x</var> + 225) cm<sup>2</sup>.
Find the two values of <var>x</var> for which the area of <var>MNPQ</var> is 125 cm<sup>2</sup>.
ap: Every side of the square is 15 cm, so <var>MB</var> = <var>AB</var> − <var>AM</var> = 15 − <var>x</var>, and in the same way <var>NC</var> = <var>PD</var> = <var>QA</var> = 15 − <var>x</var>. In △<var>AMQ</var> the two sides about the right angle at <var>A</var> are <var>AM</var> = <var>x</var> and <var>AQ</var> = 15 − <var>x</var>; the same is true of △<var>BNM</var> (<var>BN</var> = <var>x</var>, <var>BM</var> = 15 − <var>x</var>), △<var>CPN</var> and △<var>DQP</var>. So all four are congruent (SAS).

Each triangle has area ½ × <var>x</var> × (15 − <var>x</var>), so the four together have area 2<var>x</var>(15 − <var>x</var>) = 30<var>x</var> − 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>. The square has area 15<sup>2</sup> = 225, so area <var>MNPQ</var> = 225 − (30<var>x</var> − 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 30<var>x</var> + 225.

2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 30<var>x</var> + 225 = 125 gives 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 30<var>x</var> + 100 = 0, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 15<var>x</var> + 50 = 0 and (<var>x</var> − 5)(<var>x</var> − 10) = 0. Hence <var>x</var> = 5 or <var>x</var> = 10.

questions.t: Find the distance between each pair of points.
p: <var>P</var>(3, 5) and <var>Q</var>(9, 5)
<var>R</var>(−2, 4) and <var>S</var>(−2, −7)
ap: PQ is horizontal, so PQ = 9 − 3 = 6.
RS is vertical, so RS = 4 − (−7) = 11.

questions.t: Use the distance formula to find the exact distance <var>AB</var> for each pair of points.
