<var>A</var>(−3, 2) and <var>B</var>(1, −5)

questions.t: Midpoints of intervals.
p: Find the coordinates of the midpoint of the interval joining (4, 7) and (10, 1).
Find the coordinates of the midpoint of the interval joining (−5, 2) and (2, −7).
<var>M</var>(4, −1) is the midpoint of the interval <var>PQ</var> and <var>P</var> has coordinates (−2, 5). Find the coordinates of <var>Q</var>.
ap: (4 + 102, 7 + 12) = (7, 4).
(−5 + 22, 2 + (−7)2) = (−32, −52).
Let Q be (x, y). Then −2 + x2 = 4, so x = 10; and 5 + y2 = −1, so y = −7. Q is (10, −7).

questions.t: Find the gradient of the interval <var>AB</var>, or state that it has none.
ap: 14 − 25 − 1 = 124 = 3.
3 − 64 − (−2) = −36 = −12.
The run is 3 − 3 = 0, so AB is a vertical interval and has no gradient.

questions.t: Gradients and intercepts of straight lines.
p: Write down the equation of the line with gradient −3 and <var>y</var>-intercept 7.
Write down the gradient and the <var>y</var>-intercept of the line <var>y</var> = 5<var>x</var> − 2.
Rewrite 4<var>x</var> + 5<var>y</var> = 20 in the form <var>y</var> = <var>mx</var> + <var>c</var>, then state its gradient and its <var>y</var>-intercept.
ap: Gradient 5, y-intercept −2.
5y = 20 − 4x, so y = −45x + 4. The gradient is −45 and the y-intercept is 4.

questions.t: The line ℓ has equation <var>y</var> = 4<var>x</var> − 7.
p: Determine whether or not the point (3, 5) lies on ℓ.
Find the <var>y</var>-coordinate of the point on ℓ whose <var>x</var>-coordinate is −2.
Find the <var>x</var>-coordinate of the point on ℓ whose <var>y</var>-coordinate is 0.
ap: Substituting x = 3: RHS = 4 × 3 − 7 = 5 = LHS, so (3, 5) does lie on ℓ.
4x − 7 = 0, so 4x = 7 and x = 74.

questions.t: Find the coordinates of the <var>x</var>-intercept and of the <var>y</var>-intercept of each line.
p: 3<var>x</var> + 4<var>y</var> = 24
5<var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var> = 15
ap: y = 0 gives 3x = 24, x = 8, so the x-intercept is at (8, 0); x = 0 gives 4y = 24, y = 6, so the y-intercept is at (0, 6).
y = 0 gives 5x = 15, x = 3, so the x-intercept is at (3, 0); x = 0 gives −2y = 15, y = −152, so the y-intercept is at (0, −152).

questions.t: Find the equation of the line, in the form <var>y</var> = <var>mx</var> + <var>c</var>, that:
p: passes through (2, −5) and has gradient 3
passes through (−4, 1) and has gradient −12
ap: y − 1 = −12(x + 4), so y − 1 = −12x − 2 and y = −12x − 1.

questions.t: Find the equation of the line through each pair of points, giving your answer in the form <var>y</var> = <var>mx</var> + <var>c</var>.
p: <var>A</var>(1, 4) and <var>B</var>(5, 16)
<var>A</var>(−3, 7) and <var>B</var>(2, −3)
ap: m = 16 − 45 − 1 = 124 = 3; y − 4 = 3(x − 1), so y = 3x + 1. (Check: x = 5 gives y = 16.)
m = −3 − 72 − (−3) = −105 = −2; y − 7 = −2(x + 3), so y = −2x + 1. (Check: x = 2 gives y = −3.)

questions.t: The line ℓ has equation <var>y</var> = 4<var>x</var> − 9.
p: Find the equation of the line that is parallel to ℓ and passes through (−1, 3).
Find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to ℓ and passes through (−1, 3).
questions.al: ℓ has gradient 4.
ap: A parallel line also has gradient 4: y − 3 = 4(x + 1), so y = 4x + 7.
A perpendicular line has gradient −14: y − 3 = −14(x + 1), so y = −14x + 114 (equivalently x + 4y = 11).

questions.t: Circles with centre the origin <var>O</var>(0, 0).
p: Write down the equation of the circle with radius 2√5.
Find the equation of the circle that passes through the point (−3, 6).
Test whether the point (√7, 3) lies on the circle <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 16.
ap: r<sup>2</sup> = (2√5)<sup>2</sup> = 20, so the equation is x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = 20.
r<sup>2</sup> = (−3)<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup> = 9 + 36 = 45, so the equation is x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = 45.
(√7)<sup>2</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup> = 7 + 9 = 16, so the point does lie on the circle.

questions.t: The points <var>A</var>(1, 2), <var>B</var>(5, 4) and <var>C</var>(3, 8) are joined to form a triangle.
p: Calculate <var>AB</var><sup>2</sup>, <var>BC</var><sup>2</sup> and <var>CA</var><sup>2</sup>.
Hence state what type of triangle <var>ABC</var> is, giving a reason for each property you name.
ap: AB<sup>2</sup> = BC<sup>2</sup>, so AB = BC = 2√5 and the triangle is isosceles. Also AB<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup> = 20 + 20 = 40 = CA<sup>2</sup>, so by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem ∠ABC = 90°. Triangle ABC is a right-angled isosceles triangle, right-angled at B.

questions.t: The interval <var>AB</var> has endpoints <var>A</var>(−1, 2) and <var>B</var>(5, 6).
p: Find the gradient of <var>AB</var>.
Find the coordinates of <var>M</var>, the midpoint of <var>AB</var>.
Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of <var>AB</var>, that is, the line through <var>M</var> perpendicular to <var>AB</var>.
ap: Gradient of AB = 6 − 25 − (−1) = 46 = 23.
M = (−1 + 52, 2 + 62) = (2, 4).
The perpendicular gradient is −32, so y − 4 = −32(x − 2), giving y = −32x + 7, or 3x + 2y = 14. (Check: M(2, 4) gives 6 + 8 = 14.)

questions.t: <var>A</var> has coordinates (−2, 1) and <var>B</var> has coordinates (6, 5). Find the coordinates of the point <var>P</var> on the interval <var>AB</var> for which <var>AP</var> : <var>PB</var> equals:
p: 3 : 1 (so <var>P</var> is closer to <var>B</var>)
1 : 3 (so <var>P</var> is closer to <var>A</var>)
ap: P is the midpoint of AB: (−2 + 62, 1 + 52) = (2, 3).
AP : PB = 3 : 1 means P is 34 of the way from A to B, so P is the midpoint of (2, 3) and B(6, 5), which is (4, 4).
AP : PB = 1 : 3 means P is 14 of the way from A to B, so P is the midpoint of A(−2, 1) and (2, 3), which is (0, 2).

questions.t: Show that the points <var>P</var>(2, −2), <var>Q</var>(−2, 2) and <var>R</var>(2√3, 2√3) are the vertices of an equilateral triangle, and state the exact length of its side.
questions.a: PQ<sup>2</sup> = (−2 − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (2 − (−2))<sup>2</sup> = 16 + 16 = 32. PR<sup>2</sup> = (2√3 − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (2√3 + 2)<sup>2</sup> = (12 − 8√3 + 4) + (12 + 8√3 + 4) = 16 − 8√3 + 16 + 8√3 = 32. QR<sup>2</sup> = (2√3 + 2)<sup>2</sup> + (2√3 − 2)<sup>2</sup> = 32 as well. All three squared side lengths equal 32, so the three sides are equal and the triangle is equilateral, with side √32 = 4√2.

questions.t: The points <var>A</var>(1, −2), <var>B</var>(7, 2), <var>C</var>(5, 6) and <var>D</var>(−1, 2) are taken in this order around a quadrilateral <var>ABCD</var>.
p: By comparing gradients, show that <var>ABCD</var> is a parallelogram.
Find the exact lengths of the two diagonals <var>AC</var> and <var>BD</var>.
ap: Gradient AB = 2 − (−2)7 − 1 = 46 = 23 and gradient DC = 6 − 25 − (−1) = 46 = 23, so AB ∥ DC. Gradient AD = 2 − (−2)−1 − 1 = 4−2 = −2 and gradient BC = 6 − 25 − 7 = 4−2 = −2, so AD ∥ BC. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram.

questions.t: Find the equation of the line whose <var>x</var>-intercept and <var>y</var>-intercept are each three times the corresponding intercept of the line 3<var>x</var> − 4<var>y</var> = 12. Give your answer in the form <var>y</var> = <var>mx</var> + <var>c</var>.
questions.a: For 3x − 4y = 12: putting y = 0 gives 3x = 12, so the x-intercept is 4; putting x = 0 gives −4y = 12, so the y-intercept is −3. Trebling each intercept gives a new x-intercept of 12 and a new y-intercept of −9, so the new line passes through (12, 0) and (0, −9). Its gradient is 0 − (−9)12 − 0 = 912 = 34, and its y-intercept is −9, so the equation is y = 34x − 9. (Check: y = 0 gives 34x = 9, x = 12.)

questions.t: ABCD is a rhombus whose vertices are labelled in order, so that AB, BC, CD and DA are its four sides. A has coordinates (2, 2), B has coordinates (b, 4), and the gradient of AB is 12. The vertex C has coordinates (4, c), where c is an integer greater than 4.
p: Find the value of <var>b</var>.
Find the exact length of <var>AB</var>.
Find the value of <var>c</var>.
Find the gradient of <var>BC</var>, and hence write down the gradient of <var>AD</var>.
Find the coordinates of <var>D</var>.
ap: 4 − 2b − 2 = 12, so 2b − 2 = 12, giving b − 2 = 4 and b = 6. So B is (6, 4).

All sides of a rhombus are equal, so BC = AB and BC<sup>2</sup> = 20: (4 − 6)<sup>2</sup> + (c − 4)<sup>2</sup> = 20, so 4 + (c − 4)<sup>2</sup> = 20, (c − 4)<sup>2</sup> = 16 and c = 8 or c = 0. Since c > 4, c = 8. So C is (4, 8).
Gradient BC = 8 − 44 − 6 = 4−2 = −2. AD ∥ BC (opposite sides of a rhombus), so the gradient of AD is also −2.

The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other. The midpoint of AC is (2 + 42, 2 + 82) = (3, 5), and this is also the midpoint of BD, so D = (2 × 3 − 6, 2 × 5 − 4) = (0, 6). (Check: AD runs from (2, 2) to (0, 6), gradient 4−2 = −2 and length √(4 + 16) = 2√5.)

questions.t: A semicircle has centre the origin <var>O</var> and radius <var>a</var>, where <var>a</var> > 0. Its diameter runs from <var>A</var>(−<var>a</var>, 0) to <var>B</var>(<var>a</var>, 0), and <var>P</var>(<var>x</var>, <var>y</var>) is any point of the semicircle with <var>y</var> > 0.
p: Explain why <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = <var>a</var><sup>2</sup>.
Find the gradients of <var>PA</var> and <var>PB</var>, and hence show that <var>PA</var> is perpendicular to <var>PB</var>.
Show that <var>PA</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>PB</var><sup>2</sup> = 4<var>a</var><sup>2</sup>.
ap: P lies on the semicircle of radius a centred at O, so OP = a. By the distance formula OP<sup>2</sup> = (x − 0)<sup>2</sup> + (y − 0)<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup>, hence x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = a<sup>2</sup>.

Gradient PA = y − 0x − (−a) = yx + a and gradient PB = y − 0x − a = yx − a; both are defined because y > 0 forces x ≠ ±a. Their product is y2x2 − a2, and from part a) y2 = a2 − x2, so the product is a2 − x2x2 − a2 = −1. Since the product of the gradients is −1, PA ⊥ PB.

PA<sup>2</sup> = (x + a)<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> and PB<sup>2</sup> = (x − a)<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup>, so PA<sup>2</sup> + PB<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>2</sup> + 2ax + a<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> + x<sup>2</sup> − 2ax + a<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = 2(x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup>) + 2a<sup>2</sup> = 2a<sup>2</sup> + 2a<sup>2</sup> = 4a<sup>2</sup>.

questions.t: One letter is chosen at random from the word ‘PARALLEL’. Find the probability that the letter chosen is:
p: an L
an A
questions.al: ‘PARALLEL’ has 8 letters, so the sample space has 8 equally likely outcomes.
ap: L occurs 3 times, so P(L) = 38.
A occurs 2 times, so P(A) = 28 = 14.

questions.t: A whole number is chosen at random from the numbers 1 to 20 inclusive. Find the probability that the number chosen is:
p: a multiple of 4
a prime number
not a prime number
questions.al: There are 20 equally likely outcomes.
ap: The multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, so 5 outcomes are favourable and P = 520 = 14.
The primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, so 8 outcomes are favourable and P = 820 = 25.
Using the complement, P(not prime) = 1 − 25 = 35.

questions.t: A bag holds 12 red counters, 8 green counters and 5 blue counters. One counter is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is:
p: green
not blue
questions.al: The bag holds 12 + 8 + 5 = 25 counters.
ap: P(green) = 825.
P(blue) = 525 = 15, so P(not blue) = 1 − 15 = 45 (that is, 2025).

questions.t: In a group of 80 Year 9 students, 45 play netball, 32 play hockey and 12 play both sports. One student is chosen at random from the group. Find the probability that the student:
p: plays netball or hockey
plays netball but not hockey
plays neither sport
questions.al: Let <var>N</var> be ‘plays netball’ and <var>H</var> be ‘plays hockey’.
ap: By the addition rule the number playing netball or hockey is 45 + 32 − 12 = 65, so P(N or H) = 6580 = 1316.
Netball only: 45 − 12 = 33 students, so P = 3380.
Neither: 80 − 65 = 15 students, so P = 1580 = 316.

questions.t: In a survey of 240 people, each person was recorded as left-handed or right-handed, and as a child or an adult. Of the 90 children, 15 are left-handed. Of the 150 adults, 18 are left-handed. One of the 240 people is chosen at random. Find the probability that the person chosen is:
p: left-handed
an adult who is right-handed
a child or left-handed (or both)
not a left-handed child
questions.al: The four cells are: left-handed children 15, right-handed children 90 − 15 = 75, left-handed adults 18, right-handed adults 150 − 18 = 132.
ap: Left-handed altogether: 15 + 18 = 33, so P = 33240 = 1180.
P = 132240 = 1120.
All 90 children plus the 18 left-handed adults gives 108, so P = 108240 = 920.
P(left-handed child) = 15240 = 116, so the complement is 1 − 116 = 1516.

questions.t: A four-sided spinner has sides labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4, but it is not known to be fair. It is spun 400 times, giving a 1 on 76 spins, a 2 on 124 spins, a 3 on 88 spins and a 4 on 112 spins. Use these results to estimate the probability that the next spin gives:
p: a 2
an odd number
a number greater than 2
ap: Relative frequency of a 2 = 124400 = 31100.
Odd numbers (1 or 3) occurred 76 + 88 = 164 times, so the estimate is 164400 = 41100.
Numbers greater than 2 (3 or 4) occurred 88 + 112 = 200 times, so the estimate is 200400 = 12.

questions.t: A quality inspector tests 800 light globes and finds that 12 of them are faulty.
p: Use this data to estimate the probability that the next globe tested is faulty.
Estimate the probability that the next globe tested is not faulty.
How many faulty globes would you expect in a batch of 6000 globes?
ap: Relative frequency of a faulty globe = 12800 = 3200 (= 0.015).
P(not faulty) = 1 − 3200 = 197200 (= 0.985).
Expected number = 6000 × 3200 = 90 faulty globes.

questions.t: A 20-cent coin is tossed and an ordinary six-sided die is rolled. Draw an array of the 12 equally likely outcomes and use it to find the probability of obtaining:
p: a head and a 5
a tail and an even number
a head and a number greater than 4
questions.al: The array has 2 rows (H, T) and 6 columns (1 to 6), giving 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes.
ap: Only (H, 5) is favourable, so P = 112.
(T, 2), (T, 4), (T, 6) are favourable, so P = 312 = 14.
(H, 5) and (H, 6) are favourable, so P = 212 = 16.

questions.t: A coin is tossed three times and the result of each toss is recorded in order. Find the probability of obtaining:
p: exactly two heads
no heads
at least two tails
questions.al: The sample space has 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 equally likely outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.
ap: HHT, HTH, THH are favourable, so P = 38.
Only TTT, so P = 18.
HTT, THT, TTH, TTT have at least two tails, so P = 48 = 12.

questions.t: Two ordinary six-sided dice are rolled and the two uppermost numbers are noted. Using an array of the 36 equally likely outcomes, find the probability that:
p: both dice show the same number
the sum of the two numbers is 8
the sum of the two numbers is at least 10
the two numbers differ by 3
questions.al: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes.
ap: The 6 doubles (1,1) to (6,6) give P = 636 = 16.
Sum 8: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) — 5 outcomes, so P = 536.
Sum 10: 3 outcomes; sum 11: 2; sum 12: 1. Total 6, so P = 636 = 16.
Difference of 3: (1,4), (4,1), (2,5), (5,2), (3,6), (6,3) — 6 outcomes, so P = 636 = 16.

questions.t: A bag contains 4 red marbles and 3 yellow marbles. Two marbles are taken from the bag.
p: The first marble is replaced and the bag shaken before the second is drawn. Find the probability that both marbles are red.
With the same replacement as in part a, find the probability that one marble is red and the other is yellow, in either order.
This time the first marble is not replaced. Find the probability that both marbles are red.
With no replacement, find the probability that both marbles are yellow.
questions.al: There are 7 marbles in all. With replacement the array has 7 × 7 = 49 equally likely outcomes; without replacement it has 7 × 6 = 42.
ap: Both red: 4 × 4 = 16 outcomes, so P = 1649.
Red then yellow gives 4 × 3 = 12 and yellow then red gives 3 × 4 = 12, a total of 24, so P = 2449.
Both red: 4 × 3 = 12 outcomes out of 42, so P = 1242 = 27.
Both yellow: 3 × 2 = 6 outcomes out of 42, so P = 642 = 17.

questions.t: A two-digit number is made by choosing one of the digits 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 for the tens place and a different one of those digits for the units place. All such numbers are equally likely. Find the probability that the number formed is:
p: even
greater than 50
a multiple of 5
divisible by 3
questions.al: There are 5 × 4 = 20 equally likely numbers.
ap: Even means the units digit is 2 or 8; each choice leaves 4 possible tens digits, so 8 numbers are even and P = 820 = 25.
Greater than 50 means the tens digit is 5, 7 or 8, giving 3 × 4 = 12 numbers, so P = 1220 = 35.
A multiple of 5 must end in 5 (there is no 0), giving 4 numbers, so P = 420 = 15.
The digit sum must be divisible by 3. The pairs that work are {2, 7} (sum 9), {5, 7} (sum 12) and {7, 8} (sum 15), and each pair gives 2 numbers, so 6 numbers work and P = 620 = 310.

questions.t: In a group of 60 students, every student studies at least one of Chinese and Japanese. Altogether 38 study Chinese and 31 study Japanese.
p: How many students study both languages?
Find the probability that a student chosen at random studies Chinese only.
Find the probability that a student chosen at random studies exactly one of the two languages.
ap: Since nobody studies neither language, the addition rule gives 38 + 31 − (both) = 60, so both = 69 − 60 = 9 students.
Chinese only = 38 − 9 = 29 students, so P = 2960.
Japanese only = 31 − 9 = 22, so exactly one language is studied by 29 + 22 = 51 students and P = 5160 = 1720. (Check: 29 + 9 + 22 = 60.)

questions.t: A fair coin is tossed several times and the result of each toss is recorded in order.
p: The coin is tossed four times. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
The coin is tossed four times. Find the probability that at least one tail is obtained.
The coin is tossed <var>n</var> times. Write down an expression, in terms of <var>n</var>, for the probability that at least one tail is obtained.
ap: Each toss has 2 outcomes, so four tosses give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 outcomes.
The complement of ‘at least one tail’ is ‘no tails’, that is HHHH, which is 1 outcome. So P(at least one tail) = 1 − 116 = 1516.
With n tosses there are 2n outcomes and only one has no tails, so P(at least one tail) = 1 − 12n.

questions.t: Ordinary six-sided dice are rolled. Give each answer as a fraction in simplest form.
p: One die is rolled. Find the probability that the number obtained is not a 5.
Three dice are rolled. Find the probability that no 5 appears on any of them.
Three dice are rolled. Find the probability that at least one 5 appears.
ap: Five of the six faces are not a 5, so P = 56.
There are 63 = 216 equally likely outcomes for three dice, and 53 = 125 of them use only the five non-5 faces, so P(no 5) = 125216.
‘At least one 5’ is the complement of ‘no 5’, so P = 1 − 125216 = 91216.

questions.t: Ordinary six-sided dice are rolled, and this time we are interested in sixes.
p: Four dice are rolled. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
Four dice are rolled. Find the probability that at least one 6 appears.
<var>n</var> dice are rolled. Write down an expression, in terms of <var>n</var>, for the probability that at least one 6 appears.
ap: 6<sup>4</sup> = 1296 outcomes.
The number of outcomes with no 6 is 54 = 625, so P(no 6) = 6251296 and P(at least one 6) = 1 − 6251296 = 6711296.
For n dice, P(no 6) = 5n6n, so P(at least one 6) = 1 − (56)n.

questions.t: A city issues 10 000 parking permits, numbered 1, 2, 3, …, 10 000. One permit is chosen at random. Find the probability that its number contains no digit 7. (Hint: write every number with four digits by padding with zeros at the front, so that 58 becomes 0058, and treat 10 000 as 0000 — neither of these contains a 7, so the count is unaffected.)
questions.a: Written as four-digit strings, the 10 000 permits correspond exactly to the strings 0000 to 9999, so there are 10 000 equally likely outcomes. A string contains no 7 when each of its four positions is filled from the nine digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9. That gives 9 × 9 × 9 × 9 = 94 = 6561 strings. So P(no digit 7) = 656110000 = 0.6561.

questions.t: A bag contains 5 blue discs and 3 white discs. Two discs are taken out, one after the other.
p: The first disc is not replaced. Find the probability that both discs are blue.
The first disc is not replaced. Find the probability that the two discs are of different colours.

The experiment is now repeated with the first disc replaced before the second is drawn. Find the probability that the two discs are of different colours, and explain which of the two methods makes different colours more likely.
questions.al: There are 8 discs. Without replacement there are 8 × 7 = 56 equally likely ordered outcomes; with replacement there are 8 × 8 = 64.
ap: Both blue: 5 × 4 = 20 outcomes, so P = 2056 = 514.
Blue then white gives 5 × 3 = 15 and white then blue gives 3 × 5 = 15, a total of 30, so P = 3056 = 1528 ≈ 0.536.

With replacement, P(different colours) = 2 × 5 × 364 = 3064 = 1532 ≈ 0.469. Since 1528 > 1532, drawing without replacement makes different colours more likely. Any correct explanation is acceptable, for example: once the first disc is removed it cannot be drawn again, so the discs left in the bag are weighted more towards the other colour, which raises the chance that the second disc differs from the first.

questions.t: In △<var>PQR</var> the angle at <var>R</var> is a right angle, <var>PR</var> = 9 cm, <var>RQ</var> = 40 cm and <var>PQ</var> = 41 cm. Let θ = ∠<var>PQR</var>, the angle at <var>Q</var>. Write each ratio as a fraction in simplest form.
p: sin θ
cos θ
tan θ
questions.al: Relative to θ: opposite = <var>PR</var> = 9, adjacent = <var>RQ</var> = 40, hypotenuse = <var>PQ</var> = 41.
ap: sin θ = 941
cos θ = 4041
tan θ = 940

questions.t: Find each length, correct to 2 decimal places.
p: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 18 cm and one acute angle is 32°. Find the length of the side opposite the 32° angle.
In a right-angled triangle one acute angle is 47° and the side adjacent to that angle (not the hypotenuse) is 9.5 cm long. Find the length of the side opposite the 47° angle.
In a right-angled triangle one acute angle is 25° and the side opposite it is 11 cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse.
ap: opposite and hypotenuse, so use sine: <var>x</var> = 18 sin 32° = 9.54 cm.
opposite and adjacent, so use tangent: <var>x</var> = 9.5 tan 47° = 10.19 cm.
sin 25° = 11x, so x = 11sin 25° = 26.03 cm.

questions.t: Find θ, correct to the nearest degree, given that 0° < θ < 90°.
p: tan θ = 3.4

questions.t: Use complementary angles.
p: Complete: sin 24° = cos …
Complete: cos 68° = sin …
Find the value of θ, with 0° < θ < 90°, for which sin θ = cos θ.
ap: sin θ = cos (90° − θ), so θ = 90° − θ, giving θ = 45°.

questions.t: Find the size of each marked angle, correct to the nearest degree.
p: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 20 cm and the side opposite α is 13 cm. Find α.
In a right-angled triangle the side opposite β is 9.2 cm and the side adjacent to β is 6.5 cm. Find β.
In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 25 m and the side adjacent to γ is 18 m. Find γ.
ap: sin α = 1320 = 0.65, so α = sin⁻¹ 0.65 = 40.54…° ≈ 41°.
tan β = 9.26.5, so β = 54.76…° ≈ 55°.
cos γ = 1825 = 0.72, so γ = 43.95…° ≈ 44°.

questions.t: A triangle has sides of length 20 cm, 21 cm and 29 cm.
p: Show that the triangle is right-angled.
Find the sizes of the three angles of the triangle, correct to the nearest degree.
ap: 20<sup>2</sup> + 21<sup>2</sup> = 400 + 441 = 841 = 29<sup>2</sup>, so by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem the angle opposite the 29 cm side is 90°.

For the angle opposite the 20 cm side, tan θ = 2021, so θ = 43.60…° ≈ 44°. For the angle opposite the 21 cm side, tan θ = 2120, so θ = 46.39…° ≈ 46°. The angles are 44°, 46° and 90° (check: 44 + 46 + 90 = 180).

questions.t: A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse of 14 cm and one of its acute angles is 60°. Using the exact values for 60°, find:
p: the exact length of the side opposite the 60° angle
the exact length of the side adjacent to the 60° angle
ap: 14 sin 60° = 14 × √32 = 7√3 cm (≈ 12.12 cm).

questions.t: A ladder 7.2 m long leans against a vertical wall, making an angle of 63° with the horizontal ground.
p: How far up the wall does the top of the ladder reach, correct to the nearest centimetre?
How far is the foot of the ladder from the wall, correct to the nearest centimetre?
ap: Distance from wall = 7.2 cos 63° = 3.2687… m ≈ 3.27 m (327 cm).

questions.t: From a point <var>P</var> on level ground, 45 m from the base of a vertical tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 38°.
p: Find the height of the tower, correct to the nearest tenth of a metre.
Find the distance from <var>P</var> to the top of the tower (the length of the line of sight), correct to the nearest tenth of a metre.
ap: tan 38° = h45, so h = 45 tan 38° = 35.157… ≈ 35.2 m.
cos 38° = 45d, so d = 45cos 38° = 57.105… ≈ 57.1 m.

questions.t: From the top of a vertical cliff 84 m above sea level, the angle of depression of a yacht at sea is 21°. The base of the cliff is at sea level, directly below the observation point.
p: How far is the yacht from the base of the cliff, correct to the nearest metre?
Later the yacht is 150 m from the base of the cliff. Find the angle of depression of the yacht from the top of the cliff then, correct to the nearest degree.
ap: The angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the yacht, so tan 21° = 84x, giving x = 84tan 21° = 218.82… ≈ 219 m.
tan θ = 84150 = 0.56, so θ = 29.24…° ≈ 29°.

questions.t: An isosceles triangle has a base of length 16 cm, and the two equal sides are each 11 cm long.
p: Find the size of each base angle, correct to the nearest degree.
Find the size of the apex angle (the angle between the two equal sides), correct to the nearest degree.
questions.al: The perpendicular from the apex bisects the base, giving a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 11 cm and adjacent side 8 cm.
ap: cos θ = 811, so θ = 43.34…° ≈ 43°.

questions.t: Mia walks 640 m on a true bearing of 038°T from point <var>A</var> to point <var>B</var>.
p: How far north of <var>A</var> is <var>B</var>, correct to the nearest metre?
How far east of <var>A</var> is <var>B</var>, correct to the nearest metre?
questions.al: The 38° is measured from north, so north is the adjacent side and east the opposite side.

questions.t: Answer both parts about true bearings.
p: The true bearing of <var>B</var> from <var>A</var> is 118°T. Find the true bearing of <var>A</var> from <var>B</var>.
Kim is standing 300 m due east of a flagpole and Lee is standing 500 m due south of the same flagpole. Find the true bearing of Lee from Kim, correct to the nearest degree.
ap: The two bearings differ by 180°, so the bearing of <var>A</var> from <var>B</var> is 118° + 180° = 298°T.

From Kim, Lee is 300 m west and 500 m south. The angle between the south direction and the line to Lee is tan⁻¹ 300500 = 30.96…°, and this is measured west of south, so the bearing is 180° + 30.96…° = 210.96…° ≈ 211°T.

questions.t: Two points <var>A</var> and <var>B</var> are on level ground on the same side of a vertical tower and in line with its base. From <var>A</var> the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 26°; from <var>B</var>, which is 40 m closer to the tower than <var>A</var>, the angle of elevation is 41°.
p: Find the height of the tower, correct to the nearest tenth of a metre.
Find the distance from <var>A</var> to the base of the tower, correct to the nearest tenth of a metre.
questions.al: Let the height be h m and let the base be O. Then AO = htan 26° and BO = htan 41°, and AO − BO = 40.
ap: h(1tan 26° − 1tan 41°) = 40, so h × (2.0503… − 1.1504…) = 40, giving h = 400.8999… = 44.447… ≈ 44.4 m.
AO = 44.447…tan 26° = 91.13… ≈ 91.1 m (check: BO = 51.1 m and 91.1 − 51.1 = 40).

questions.t: At 1 p.m. ship <var>S</var> is 2 km due north of ship <var>T</var>. Ship <var>T</var> stays where it is, while <var>S</var> sails on a true bearing of 130°T.
p: When <var>S</var> has sailed 3 km from its 1 p.m. position, how far east and how far south of that position is it? Give each distance correct to the nearest metre.
Hence find how far <var>S</var> is from <var>T</var> at that moment, correct to the nearest metre.

Suppose instead that <var>S</var> sails <var>x</var> km from its 1 p.m. position on the same bearing. Show that the distance <var>d</var> km between the ships is given by <var>d</var> = √(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> cos 50° + 4).
questions.al: A bearing of 130°T is 50° east of due south.
ap: Take <var>T</var> as origin. <var>S</var> started 2 km north of <var>T</var>, so <var>S</var> is now 2.2981… km east and 2 − 1.9283… = 0.0716… km north of <var>T</var>. Hence <var>d</var> = √(2.2981…<sup>2</sup> + 0.0716…<sup>2</sup>) = 2.29924… km ≈ 2299 m.

After <var>x</var> km, <var>S</var> is <var>x</var> sin 50° east of <var>T</var> and (2 − <var>x</var> cos 50°) km north of <var>T</var>, so <var>d</var><sup>2</sup> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup>(sin 50°)<sup>2</sup> + 4 − 4<var>x</var> cos 50° + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup>(cos 50°)<sup>2</sup> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> cos 50° + 4, using (sin 50°)<sup>2</sup> + (cos 50°)<sup>2</sup> = 1. Taking the positive square root gives the result; with <var>x</var> = 3 it gives 2.29924…, agreeing with part b.

questions.t: A helicopter hovers at a constant height of 400 m directly above a straight, level road. A car is travelling along the road towards the point directly below the helicopter. At one instant the angle of depression of the car from the helicopter is 25°, and 8 seconds later it is 33°.
p: Find the horizontal distance from the helicopter to the car at each of the two instants, correct to the nearest tenth of a metre.
How far does the car travel during those 8 seconds? Give your answer correct to the nearest tenth of a metre.
Find the speed of the car in km/h, correct to 1 decimal place.
ap: tan 25° = 400d1, so d1 = 400tan 25° = 857.80… ≈ 857.8 m; d2 = 400tan 33° = 615.94… ≈ 615.9 m.
Speed = 241.856…8 = 30.232… m/s; × 3.6 gives 108.835… ≈ 108.8 km/h.

questions.t: In △<var>ABC</var> the angle at <var>C</var> is a right angle, ∠<var>BAC</var> = θ, <var>BC</var> = <var>a</var>, <var>AC</var> = <var>b</var> and <var>AB</var> = <var>c</var>.
p: Write down sin θ and cos θ in terms of <var>a</var>, <var>b</var> and <var>c</var>.
Hence show that (sin θ)<sup>2</sup> + (cos θ)<sup>2</sup> = 1.
θ is acute and sin θ = 513. Find the exact values of cos θ and tan θ.
ap: Relative to θ the opposite side is a, the adjacent side is b and the hypotenuse is c, so sin θ = ac and cos θ = bc.
(sin θ)2 + (cos θ)2 = a2 + b2c2 = c2c2 = 1, using Pythagoras' theorem a2 + b2 = c2.
(cos θ)2 = 1 − 25169 = 144169, and θ is acute so cos θ = 1213. Then tan θ = sin θcos θ = 513 ÷ 1213 = 512. (The triangle is a 5, 12, 13 triangle.)

questions.t: In △<var>ABC</var>, <var>AB</var> = 9 cm, <var>AC</var> = 14 cm and ∠<var>BAC</var> = 40°.
p: Find the perpendicular distance from <var>B</var> to the line <var>AC</var>, correct to 3 decimal places.
Hence find the area of △<var>ABC</var>, correct to 2 decimal places.
△<var>PQR</var> has ∠<var>QPR</var> = θ, where θ is acute, <var>PQ</var> = <var>c</var> and <var>PR</var> = <var>b</var>. Prove that the area of △<var>PQR</var> is ½<var>bc</var> sin θ.
ap: Let M be the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC. In right-angled △AMB, sin 40° = BM9, so BM = 9 sin 40° = 5.785088… ≈ 5.785 cm.
Drop the perpendicular QM from Q to the line PR. In right-angled △PMQ, sin θ = QMc, so QM = c sin θ. Taking PR = b as the base, area = ½ × b × c sin θ = ½bc sin θ.

questions.t: <var>O</var> and <var>A</var> are two points on level horizontal ground with <var>OA</var> = 10 m. <var>AB</var> is a vertical segment with <var>B</var> above <var>A</var>, so ∠<var>OAB</var> = 90°, and <var>B</var> is placed so that ∠<var>AOB</var> = 60°. <var>P</var> is the point on <var>AB</var> for which ∠<var>AOP</var> = 45°, so ∠<var>POB</var> = 15°.
p: Find the exact length of <var>OP</var>.
Find the exact lengths of <var>AP</var> and <var>AB</var>.
Show that <var>PB</var> = 10(√3 − 1).
Hence find <var>PB</var> correct to 2 decimal places.
ap: In right-angled △OAP, cos 45° = 10OP, so OP = 10cos 45° = 10√2 m.
<var>AP</var> = 10 tan 45° = 10 m and <var>AB</var> = 10 tan 60° = 10√3 m.
<var>P</var> lies between <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>, so <var>PB</var> = <var>AB</var> − <var>AP</var> = 10√3 − 10 = 10(√3 − 1).

questions.t: <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var> and <var>D</var> are four points in that order on a straight horizontal line, and <var>B</var> is the midpoint of <var>AC</var>. <var>E</var> is a point vertically above <var>D</var>, so ∠<var>EDA</var> = 90°.
p: Prove that <var>BD</var> = ½(<var>AD</var> + <var>CD</var>).
Hence prove that tan ∠<var>DEB</var> = ½ tan ∠<var>DEA</var> + ½ tan ∠<var>DEC</var>.
ap: Since the points are in the order <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var>, <var>D</var>, <var>BD</var> = <var>BC</var> + <var>CD</var>. As <var>B</var> is the midpoint of <var>AC</var>, <var>BC</var> = ½<var>AC</var> = ½(<var>AD</var> − <var>CD</var>). Hence <var>BD</var> = ½<var>AD</var> − ½<var>CD</var> + <var>CD</var> = ½(<var>AD</var> + <var>CD</var>).

△EDA, △EDB and △EDC are all right-angled at D with the same vertical side ED, so tan ∠DEA = ADED, tan ∠DEB = BDED and tan ∠DEC = CDED. Therefore tan ∠DEB = ½(AD + CD)ED = ½ × ADED + ½ × CDED = ½ tan ∠DEA + ½ tan ∠DEC.

questions.t: Determine by substitution whether the given point is a solution of the pair of simultaneous equations.
p: (2, 5), for <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 7 and <var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var> + 1
(−1, 4), for <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 3 and <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 6
ap: 2 + 5 = 7 ✓ and 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 ✓, so (2, 5) IS a solution.
−1 + 4 = 3 ✓ but <var>x</var> + 6 = −1 + 6 = 5 ≠ 4, so (−1, 4) is NOT a solution.

questions.t: Solve each pair of simultaneous equations for <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> using the substitution method.
p: <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 5 and <var>y</var> = 3<var>x</var> + 1
<var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var> − 3 and <var>y</var> = 5<var>x</var> + 9
ap: <var>x</var> + 5 = 3<var>x</var> + 1, so 4 = 2<var>x</var> and <var>x</var> = 2; then <var>y</var> = 7. Solution <var>x</var> = 2, <var>y</var> = 7.
2<var>x</var> − 3 = 5<var>x</var> + 9, so −12 = 3<var>x</var> and <var>x</var> = −4; then <var>y</var> = 2(−4) − 3 = −11. Solution <var>x</var> = −4, <var>y</var> = −11 (check: 5(−4) + 9 = −11 ✓).

questions.t: Solve each pair of simultaneous equations for <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> using the substitution method.
p: <var>y</var> = 3<var>x</var> − 1 and 2<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 9
<var>x</var> = 2<var>y</var> + 3 and 3<var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 4
ap: 2<var>x</var> + (3<var>x</var> − 1) = 9, so 5<var>x</var> = 10 and <var>x</var> = 2; then <var>y</var> = 3(2) − 1 = 5. Solution (2, 5).
3(2<var>y</var> + 3) − <var>y</var> = 4, so 6<var>y</var> + 9 − <var>y</var> = 4, 5<var>y</var> = −5 and <var>y</var> = −1; then <var>x</var> = 2(−1) + 3 = 1. Solution (1, −1).

questions.t: Solve each pair of simultaneous equations for <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> using the elimination method. In each case one pronumeral is eliminated by adding or subtracting the two equations as they stand.
p: 3<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 11 and 2<var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 4
2<var>x</var> + 5<var>y</var> = 23 and 2<var>x</var> − 3<var>y</var> = −1
ap: Adding: 5<var>x</var> = 15, so <var>x</var> = 3; then 9 + <var>y</var> = 11 gives <var>y</var> = 2. Solution (3, 2).
Subtracting: 8<var>y</var> = 24, so <var>y</var> = 3; then 2<var>x</var> = 23 − 15 = 8 gives <var>x</var> = 4. Solution (4, 3) (check: 2(4) − 3(3) = −1 ✓).

questions.t: Solve each pair of simultaneous equations for <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> using the elimination method. You will need to multiply one of the equations by a constant first.
p: <var>x</var> + 2<var>y</var> = 11 and 3<var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 12
5<var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var> = 16 and 3<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 14
ap: Multiply the first by 3: 3<var>x</var> + 6<var>y</var> = 33. Subtract the second: 7<var>y</var> = 21, so <var>y</var> = 3; then <var>x</var> = 11 − 6 = 5. Solution (5, 3).
Multiply the second by 2: 6<var>x</var> + 2<var>y</var> = 28. Add the first: 11<var>x</var> = 44, so <var>x</var> = 4; then <var>y</var> = 14 − 12 = 2. Solution (4, 2).

questions.t: Solve each pair of simultaneous equations using the elimination method. Here both equations must be multiplied by a constant.
p: 3<var>x</var> + 4<var>y</var> = 10 and 5<var>x</var> − 3<var>y</var> = 7
4<var>a</var> − 5<var>b</var> = 22 and 3<var>a</var> + 2<var>b</var> = 5
ap: (1) × 3: 9<var>x</var> + 12<var>y</var> = 30; (2) × 4: 20<var>x</var> − 12<var>y</var> = 28. Adding: 29<var>x</var> = 58, so <var>x</var> = 2; then 6 + 4<var>y</var> = 10 gives <var>y</var> = 1. Solution (2, 1).

(1) × 2: 8<var>a</var> − 10<var>b</var> = 44; (2) × 5: 15<var>a</var> + 10<var>b</var> = 25. Adding: 23<var>a</var> = 69, so <var>a</var> = 3; then 9 + 2<var>b</var> = 5 gives <var>b</var> = −2. Solution <var>a</var> = 3, <var>b</var> = −2.

questions.t: Ravi buys 3 muffins and 2 juices for $13.50. At the same shop Priya buys 5 muffins and 4 juices for $24.50. By introducing two pronumerals and forming two simultaneous equations, find the cost of one muffin and the cost of one juice.
questions.a: Let <var>m</var> be the cost of a muffin and <var>a</var> the cost of a juice, in dollars. 3<var>m</var> + 2<var>a</var> = 13.5 (1) and 5<var>m</var> + 4<var>a</var> = 24.5 (2). (1) × 2: 6<var>m</var> + 4<var>a</var> = 27. Subtracting (2): <var>m</var> = 2.5; then 7.5 + 2<var>a</var> = 13.5 gives <var>a</var> = 3. A muffin costs $2.50 and a juice costs $3.00 (check: 5(2.50) + 4(3.00) = $24.50 ✓).

questions.t: At present Dario is 26 years older than his son. In 6 years' time Dario will be three times his son's age. Find their present ages.
questions.a: Let <var>x</var> be Dario's present age and <var>y</var> his son's present age. <var>x</var> = <var>y</var> + 26 (1) and <var>x</var> + 6 = 3(<var>y</var> + 6) (2). Substituting (1) into (2): <var>y</var> + 32 = 3<var>y</var> + 18, so 14 = 2<var>y</var> and <var>y</var> = 7; then <var>x</var> = 33. Dario is 33 and his son is 7 (check: in 6 years, 39 = 3 × 13 ✓).

questions.t: For each pair of equations, state whether the simultaneous equations have no solution, exactly one solution, or infinitely many solutions, and give a reason based on the gradients and <var>y</var>-intercepts of the two lines.
p: 2<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 5 and 4<var>x</var> + 2<var>y</var> = 7
3<var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 4 and 6<var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var> = 8
<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 6 and <var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var> = 3
ap: No solution. Both lines have gradient −2 but the y-intercepts are 5 and 72, so the lines are parallel and distinct.
Infinitely many solutions. The second equation is exactly 2 × the first, so they are equivalent equations representing the same line.
Exactly one solution. The gradients are −1 and ½, which are different, so the lines meet at a single point; subtracting gives 3<var>y</var> = 3, <var>y</var> = 1 and <var>x</var> = 5, i.e. (5, 1).

questions.t: Show that the three lines <var>y</var> = 4<var>x</var> − 5, <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 1 and <var>y</var> = −2<var>x</var> + 7 are concurrent, and state the coordinates of their common point.
questions.a: Solve the first two: 4<var>x</var> − 5 = <var>x</var> + 1, so 3<var>x</var> = 6 and <var>x</var> = 2; then <var>y</var> = 2 + 1 = 3, giving (2, 3). Test (2, 3) in the third line: −2(2) + 7 = 3 ✓. Since (2, 3) satisfies all three equations, the lines are concurrent at (2, 3).

questions.t: The equations of two lines are <var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var> − 7 and <var>y</var> = <var>m</var><var>x</var> + 5.
p: For what value of <var>m</var> do the two lines NOT intersect? Explain why.
For what values of <var>m</var> do the two lines intersect?
Given that the two lines intersect at (−3, −13), find <var>m</var>.
ap: <var>m</var> = 2. The <var>y</var>-intercepts are −7 and 5, so the lines are different; two different lines fail to intersect only when they are parallel, i.e. when the gradients are equal.
All values of <var>m</var> with <var>m</var> ≠ 2.

Substituting <var>x</var> = −3, <var>y</var> = −13 into <var>y</var> = <var>m</var><var>x</var> + 5: −13 = −3<var>m</var> + 5, so −3<var>m</var> = −18 and <var>m</var> = 6. (Check: (−3, −13) does lie on <var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var> − 7, since 2(−3) − 7 = −13 ✓.)

questions.t: Find the area of the triangle formed by the line <var>x</var> + 2<var>y</var> = 8, the line <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> − 2 and the <var>y</var>-axis.
questions.a: The line <var>x</var> + 2<var>y</var> = 8 meets the <var>y</var>-axis at (0, 4) and <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> − 2 meets the <var>y</var>-axis at (0, −2). The two lines meet where <var>x</var> + 2(<var>x</var> − 2) = 8, so 3<var>x</var> = 12, <var>x</var> = 4 and <var>y</var> = 2, i.e. at (4, 2). Taking the side on the <var>y</var>-axis as the base, base = 4 − (−2) = 6 and the height is the <var>x</var>-coordinate of (4, 2), which is 4. Area = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 square units.

questions.t: A fraction becomes 23 when 2 is added to both its numerator and its denominator, and becomes 12 when 3 is subtracted from both its numerator and its denominator. Find the fraction.
questions.a: Let the fraction be xy. Then x + 2y + 2 = 23 gives 3(x + 2) = 2(y + 2), i.e. 3x − 2y = −2 (1), and x − 3y − 3 = 12 gives 2(x − 3) = y − 3, i.e. y = 2x − 3 (2). Substituting (2) into (1): 3x − 2(2x − 3) = −2, so −x + 6 = −2 and x = 8; then y = 13. The fraction is 813 (check: 1015 = 23 ✓ and 510 = 12 ✓).

questions.t: Throughout this question assume that <var>m</var> is positive.
p: Find, in terms of <var>m</var>, the coordinates of the point where the lines <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 6 and <var>y</var> = <var>m</var><var>x</var> + 2 intersect.
Find, in terms of <var>m</var>, the area of the triangle enclosed by the line <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 6, the line <var>y</var> = <var>m</var><var>x</var> + 2 and the <var>x</var>-axis.
Given that this area is 18 square units, find the value of <var>m</var>.
ap: From x + y = 6, y = 6 − x. Then 6 − x = mx + 2, so 4 = x(m + 1) and x = 4m + 1; y = 6 − 4m + 1 = 6m + 2m + 1. Point (4m + 1, 6m + 2m + 1).

x + y = 6 cuts the x-axis at (6, 0); y = mx + 2 cuts it where mx + 2 = 0, at (−2m, 0). Since m > 0 this is to the left of the origin, so the base on the x-axis has length 6 + 2m = 6m + 2m. The height is the y-coordinate of the apex, 6m + 2m + 1. Area = ½ × 6m + 2m × 6m + 2m + 1 = (6m + 2)22m(m + 1) square units.

(6<var>m</var> + 2)<sup>2</sup> = 36<var>m</var>(<var>m</var> + 1) gives 36<var>m</var><sup>2</sup> + 24<var>m</var> + 4 = 36<var>m</var><sup>2</sup> + 36<var>m</var>, so 12<var>m</var> = 4 and <var>m</var> = ⅓. (Check: the lines meet at (3, 3), the base runs from (−6, 0) to (6, 0) and ½ × 12 × 3 = 18 ✓.)

questions.t: In this question <var>a</var> and <var>b</var> are non-zero constants. Solve each pair of simultaneous equations for <var>x</var> and <var>y</var>, giving your answers in terms of <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>.
p: <var>a</var><var>x</var> + <var>b</var><var>y</var> = <var>a</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>b</var><sup>2</sup> and <var>b</var><var>x</var> − <var>a</var><var>y</var> = 0
xa + yb = 2 and xb + ya = 2, given also that a ≠ b and a + b ≠ 0
ap: From the second equation y = bxa. Substituting: ax + b2xa = a2 + b2, so x(a2 + b2) = a(a2 + b2). Since a2 + b2 ≠ 0, x = a and then y = b.

Multiplying both equations by ab: bx + ay = 2ab (1) and ax + by = 2ab (2). (1) − (2): (b − a)x − (b − a)y = 0, i.e. (b − a)(x − y) = 0. As a ≠ b, x = y. Substituting into (1): x(a + b) = 2ab, so x = y = 2aba + b.

questions.t:
Solve the simultaneous equations for x, y and z:
x + y + z = 9
2x − y + z = 5
x + 2y − z = 4
questions.a: Label them (1), (2), (3). (1) + (3): 2<var>x</var> + 3<var>y</var> = 13 (4). (2) + (3): 3<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 9 (5), so <var>y</var> = 9 − 3<var>x</var>. Substituting into (4): 2<var>x</var> + 27 − 9<var>x</var> = 13, so −7<var>x</var> = −14 and <var>x</var> = 2; then <var>y</var> = 3 and from (1) <var>z</var> = 9 − 2 − 3 = 4. Solution <var>x</var> = 2, <var>y</var> = 3, <var>z</var> = 4 (check in (2): 4 − 3 + 4 = 5 ✓ and in (3): 2 + 6 − 4 = 4 ✓).

questions.t:
Solve for x, y and z, where x, y and z are all non-zero:
1x + 1y = 5
1y + 1z = 7
1x + 1z = 6
questions.a: Let a = 1x, b = 1y and c = 1z. Then a + b = 5, b + c = 7 and a + c = 6. Adding all three: 2(a + b + c) = 18, so a + b + c = 9. Hence c = 9 − 5 = 4, a = 9 − 7 = 2 and b = 9 − 6 = 3. Therefore x = ½, y = ⅓ and z = 14 (check: 2 + 3 = 5 ✓, 3 + 4 = 7 ✓, 2 + 4 = 6 ✓).

questions.t: The three lines 2<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 8, <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 1 and <var>y</var> = −2 form a triangle <var>PQR</var>, where <var>P</var> is the point where 2<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 8 meets <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 1, <var>Q</var> is the point where 2<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 8 meets <var>y</var> = −2, and <var>R</var> is the point where <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 1 meets <var>y</var> = −2.
p: Find the coordinates of <var>P</var>, <var>Q</var> and <var>R</var>.
Find the area of △<var>PQR</var>, using <var>QR</var> as the base.

The area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2) and (x3, y3) is ½|x1(y2 − y3) + x2(y3 − y1) + x3(y1 − y2)|. Use this formula to check your answer to part b, then apply it to the points (1, 2), (4, 8) and (6, 12) and explain what the result tells you about those three points.
ap: <var>P</var>: adding 2<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 8 and <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 1 gives 3<var>x</var> = 9, <var>x</var> = 3, <var>y</var> = 2, so <var>P</var>(3, 2). <var>Q</var>: putting <var>y</var> = −2 in 2<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 8 gives 2<var>x</var> = 10, <var>x</var> = 5, so <var>Q</var>(5, −2). <var>R</var>: putting <var>y</var> = −2 in <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 1 gives <var>x</var> = −1, so <var>R</var>(−1, −2).

<var>QR</var> lies along <var>y</var> = −2, so its length is 5 − (−1) = 6, and the height is the vertical distance from <var>P</var> to <var>y</var> = −2, namely 2 − (−2) = 4. Area = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 square units.

Using <var>P</var>(3, 2), <var>Q</var>(5, −2), <var>R</var>(−1, −2): ½|3(−2 − (−2)) + 5(−2 − 2) + (−1)(2 − (−2))| = ½|0 − 20 − 4| = ½ × 24 = 12 ✓, agreeing with part b. For (1, 2), (4, 8), (6, 12): ½|1(8 − 12) + 4(12 − 2) + 6(2 − 8)| = ½|−4 + 40 − 36| = 0. A zero area means the three points do not form a triangle, i.e. they are collinear — indeed all three lie on <var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var>.

questions.t: Factorise by grouping in pairs.
p: 3<var>x</var>(<var>x</var> + 4) + 7(<var>x</var> + 4)
5<var>a</var>(2<var>a</var> − 3) − 4(2<var>a</var> − 3)
ap: (<var>x</var> + 4) is the common factor, so 3<var>x</var>(<var>x</var> + 4) + 7(<var>x</var> + 4) = (<var>x</var> + 4)(3<var>x</var> + 7).
(2<var>a</var> − 3) is the common factor, so 5<var>a</var>(2<var>a</var> − 3) − 4(2<var>a</var> − 3) = (2<var>a</var> − 3)(5<var>a</var> − 4).

questions.t: Factorise by grouping in pairs.
p: <var>mp</var> + 4<var>m</var> + 3<var>p</var> + 12
6<var>ab</var> − 15<var>a</var> + 2<var>b</var> − 5
10<var>xy</var> − 4<var>x</var> − 15<var>y</var> + 6
ap: <var>m</var>(<var>p</var> + 4) + 3(<var>p</var> + 4) = (<var>p</var> + 4)(<var>m</var> + 3).
3<var>a</var>(2<var>b</var> − 5) + 1(2<var>b</var> − 5) = (2<var>b</var> − 5)(3<var>a</var> + 1).
2<var>x</var>(5<var>y</var> − 2) − 3(5<var>y</var> − 2) = (5<var>y</var> − 2)(2<var>x</var> − 3).

questions.t: Factorise the quadratic expressions.
p: 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 11<var>x</var> + 12
3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 16<var>x</var> + 5
5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 7<var>x</var> − 6
ap: <var>ac</var> = 24 and the two numbers summing to 11 are 8 and 3: 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> + 3<var>x</var> + 12 = 2<var>x</var>(<var>x</var> + 4) + 3(<var>x</var> + 4) = (<var>x</var> + 4)(2<var>x</var> + 3).

<var>ac</var> = 15 and the numbers are −15 and −1: 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 15<var>x</var> − <var>x</var> + 5 = 3<var>x</var>(<var>x</var> − 5) − 1(<var>x</var> − 5) = (<var>x</var> − 5)(3<var>x</var> − 1).

<var>ac</var> = −30 and the numbers are 10 and −3: 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 10<var>x</var> − 3<var>x</var> − 6 = 5<var>x</var>(<var>x</var> + 2) − 3(<var>x</var> + 2) = (<var>x</var> + 2)(5<var>x</var> − 3).

questions.t: Factorise the quadratic expressions.
p: 6<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 17<var>x</var> + 12
10<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 11<var>x</var> − 6
12<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 7<var>x</var> − 12
ap: <var>ac</var> = 72, numbers −8 and −9: 6<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 8<var>x</var> − 9<var>x</var> + 12 = 2<var>x</var>(3<var>x</var> − 4) − 3(3<var>x</var> − 4) = (3<var>x</var> − 4)(2<var>x</var> − 3).

<var>ac</var> = −60, numbers 15 and −4: 10<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 15<var>x</var> − 4<var>x</var> − 6 = 5<var>x</var>(2<var>x</var> + 3) − 2(2<var>x</var> + 3) = (2<var>x</var> + 3)(5<var>x</var> − 2).

<var>ac</var> = −144, numbers 9 and −16: 12<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 9<var>x</var> − 16<var>x</var> − 12 = 3<var>x</var>(4<var>x</var> + 3) − 4(4<var>x</var> + 3) = (4<var>x</var> + 3)(3<var>x</var> − 4).

= (x + 2)(3x − 1)(x − 1)(x + 1) × (x + 1)2x(3x − 1) = (x + 2)(x + 1)x(x − 1).

questions.t: Express as a single fraction. Leave each denominator in factorised form.
p: 3x + 2 + 4x − 1
5x − 3 − 2x + 4
32a + 1 + 2a − 4
ap: 3(x − 1) + 4(x + 2)(x + 2)(x − 1) = 7x + 5(x + 2)(x − 1).
5(x + 4) − 2(x − 3)(x − 3)(x + 4) = 3x + 26(x − 3)(x + 4).

questions.t: Simplify. (In each part one denominator is the negative of the other.)

2xx − 5 + 105 − x
ap: 32 − b = −3b − 2, so the sum is 4 − 3b − 2 = 1b − 2.
105 − x = −10x − 5, so the sum is 2x − 10x − 5 = 2(x − 5)x − 5 = 2.

questions.t: Express as a single fraction, leaving the denominator in factorised form.
p: 2(x + 1)(x + 3) + 3(x + 3)(x − 2)
4x2 + 3x + 2 − 1x2 − 1
ap: The common denominator is (x + 1)(x + 3)(x − 2), giving 2(x − 2) + 3(x + 1)(x + 1)(x + 3)(x − 2) = 5x − 1(x + 1)(x + 3)(x − 2).

x2 + 3x + 2 = (x + 1)(x + 2) and x2 − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), so the common denominator is (x − 1)(x + 1)(x + 2): 4(x − 1) − (x + 2)(x − 1)(x + 1)(x + 2) = 3x − 6(x − 1)(x + 1)(x + 2) = 3(x − 2)(x − 1)(x + 1)(x + 2).

questions.t: Complete the square. That is, write each expression in the form (<var>x</var> + <var>h</var>)<sup>2</sup> + <var>k</var>.
p: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> + 3
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> + 11
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 1
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 3<var>x</var> + 5
ap: (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> + 16) − 16 + 3 = (<var>x</var> + 4)<sup>2</sup> − 13.
(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> + 9) − 9 + 11 = (<var>x</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup> + 2.
(x + 52)2 − 254 − 1 = (x + 52)2 − 294.
(x − 32)2 − 94 + 5 = (x − 32)2 + 114.

questions.t: Factorise each expression by first completing the square and then using the difference of two squares identity.
p: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6<var>x</var> + 8
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 8<var>x</var> + 5
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 3
ap: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6<var>x</var> + 8 = (<var>x</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> − 9 + 8 = (<var>x</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> − 1 = (<var>x</var> + 3 − 1)(<var>x</var> + 3 + 1) = (<var>x</var> + 2)(<var>x</var> + 4).
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 8<var>x</var> + 5 = (<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> − 16 + 5 = (<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> − 11 = (<var>x</var> − 4 − √11)(<var>x</var> − 4 + √11).
x2 + 5x − 3 = (x + 52)2 − 254 − 3 = (x + 52)2 − 374 = (x + 52 − √372)(x + 52 + √372).

questions.t: Simplify, giving each answer in simplest form.
p: 1m − n + 1n − m
aa − b + bb − a
p + qp − q + p − qp + q + 4pqq2 − p2
ap: 1n − m = −1m − n, so the sum is 0.
bb − a = −ba − b, so the sum is a − ba − b = 1.

Note q2 − p2 = −(p2 − q2), so over the common denominator p2 − q2 = (p − q)(p + q) the sum is (p + q)2 + (p − q)2 − 4pqp2 − q2 = 2p2 + 2q2 − 4pq(p − q)(p + q) = 2(p − q)2(p − q)(p + q) = 2(p − q)p + q.

questions.t: Use the method of completing the square to show that <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6<var>x</var> + 20 ≥ 11 for every value of <var>x</var>. State the value of <var>x</var> for which the two sides are equal.
questions.a: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6<var>x</var> + 20 = (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6<var>x</var> + 9) − 9 + 20 = (<var>x</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> + 11. A square is never negative, so (<var>x</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0 and therefore <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6<var>x</var> + 20 ≥ 11 for all <var>x</var>. Equality holds exactly when (<var>x</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> = 0, that is when <var>x</var> = −3 (and then both sides equal 11).

questions.t: A rectangle has perimeter 24 cm and its width is <var>w</var> cm.
p: Show that its area, <var>A</var> cm<sup>2</sup>, is given by <var>A</var> = <var>w</var>(12 − <var>w</var>).
By completing the square for 12<var>w</var> − <var>w</var><sup>2</sup>, show that <var>A</var> ≤ 36.
State the length and the width of the rectangle of perimeter 24 cm that has the largest possible area.
ap: If the length is <var>l</var> cm then 2(<var>l</var> + <var>w</var>) = 24, so <var>l</var> = 12 − <var>w</var> and <var>A</var> = <var>lw</var> = <var>w</var>(12 − <var>w</var>).

<var>A</var> = 12<var>w</var> − <var>w</var><sup>2</sup> = −(<var>w</var><sup>2</sup> − 12<var>w</var>) = −((<var>w</var> − 6)<sup>2</sup> − 36) = 36 − (<var>w</var> − 6)<sup>2</sup>. Since (<var>w</var> − 6)<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0, we get <var>A</var> ≤ 36.
Equality needs <var>w</var> = 6, and then <var>l</var> = 12 − 6 = 6. So the largest area is 36 cm<sup>2</sup>, given by the square of side 6 cm (length 6 cm, width 6 cm).

questions.t: By considering (√t − 3√t)2, prove that t + 9t ≥ 6 for every positive number t. State the value of t for which the two sides are equal.
questions.a: For t > 0, (√t − 3√t)2 = t − 2 × √t × 3√t + 9t = t − 6 + 9t. A square is never negative, so t − 6 + 9t ≥ 0, that is t + 9t ≥ 6. Equality holds when √t = 3√t, i.e. t = 3 (check: 3 + 3 = 6).

questions.t: Find all integer solutions of the equation xy + 3x + 2y = 4, by first writing the left-hand side in the form (x + a)(y + b) − c.
questions.a: xy + 3x + 2y = y(x + 2) + 3(x + 2) − 6 = (x + 2)(y + 3) − 6, so the equation becomes (x + 2)(y + 3) = 10. Test: every factorisation of 10 into two integers gives a solution, so with x + 2 = d and y + 3 = 10d for each divisor d of 10 (positive and negative), the eight solutions (x, y) are (−1, 7), (0, 2), (3, −1), (8, −2), (−3, −13), (−4, −8), (−7, −5) and (−12, −4). Check (0, 2): 0 + 0 + 4 = 4 ✓; check (−12, −4): 48 − 36 − 8 = 4 ✓.

questions.t: The real numbers <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> satisfy <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 41 and <var>xy</var> = 20.
p: Find the possible values of <var>x</var> + <var>y</var>.
Find the possible values of <var>x</var> − <var>y</var>.
List every pair (<var>x</var>, <var>y</var>) satisfying both equations.
ap: (<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>)<sup>2</sup> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>xy</var> = 41 + 40 = 81, so <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 9 or <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = −9.
(<var>x</var> − <var>y</var>)<sup>2</sup> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>xy</var> = 41 − 40 = 1, so <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 1 or <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = −1.
Solving each of the four sign combinations gives (5, 4), (4, 5), (−5, −4) and (−4, −5). Check (5, 4): 25 + 16 = 41 and 5 × 4 = 20 ✓.

questions.t: Convert each measurement into the unit shown in brackets.
p: 3.4 cm (mm)

2600 mm<sup>3</sup> (cm<sup>3</sup>)
7.2 L (cm<sup>3</sup>)
3.5 ha (m<sup>2</sup>)
ap: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 3.4 cm = 34 mm.
1 m<sup>2</sup> = 100<sup>2</sup> cm<sup>2</sup> = 10 000 cm<sup>2</sup>, so 0.45 m<sup>2</sup> = 4500 cm<sup>2</sup>.
1 cm<sup>3</sup> = 10<sup>3</sup> mm<sup>3</sup> = 1000 mm<sup>3</sup>, so 2600 mm<sup>3</sup> = 2.6 cm<sup>3</sup>.
1 L = 1000 cm<sup>3</sup>, so 7.2 L = 7200 cm<sup>3</sup>.
1 ha = 10<sup>4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, so 3.5 ha = 35 000 m<sup>2</sup>.
