p: Show that 2<sup>6</sup> + 2<sup>9</sup> + 2<sup><var>n</var></sup> = 2<sup>6</sup>(9 + 2<sup><var>n</var> − 6</sup>).

Find the only value of <var>n</var> for which 2<sup>6</sup> + 2<sup>9</sup> + 2<sup><var>n</var></sup> is a perfect square. State the number and its square root, and explain why no other value of <var>n</var> works.
ap: Take out the factor 2<sup>6</sup>: 2<sup>6</sup> + 2<sup>9</sup> + 2<sup><var>n</var></sup> = 2<sup>6</sup>(2<sup>0</sup> + 2<sup>9 − 6</sup> + 2<sup><var>n</var> − 6</sup>) = 2<sup>6</sup>(1 + 8 + 2<sup><var>n</var> − 6</sup>) = 2<sup>6</sup>(9 + 2<sup><var>n</var> − 6</sup>).

Write k = n − 6, so k > 3. Now 26 = (23)2 is a perfect square, and since k ≥ 1 the factor 9 + 2k is odd, so it has no factor 2 in common with 26. Hence 26(9 + 2k) is a perfect square exactly when 9 + 2k is a perfect square.
Put 9 + 2k = m2 with m > 0. Then m2 − 9 = 2k, so (m − 3)(m + 3) = 2k. Each factor divides 2k, so each factor is itself a power of 2, and the two powers differ by 6. The only two powers of 2 differing by 6 are 2 and 8 (1 and 7, 4 and 10, 8 and 14, 16 and 22, … all fail because the larger number is not a power of 2). So m − 3 = 2 and m + 3 = 8, giving m = 5 and 2k = 16, so k = 4.
Therefore n = k + 6 = 10, and 26 + 29 + 210 = 64 + 512 + 1024 = 1600 = 402. Since k = 4 is the only solution, n = 10 is the only value that works.

(x − 7)(x + 4) = 0, so x = 7 or x = −4.
(2x − 3)(3x + 5) = 0, so x = 32 or x = −53.
Completing the square: (x − 3)2 − 9 + 2 = 0, so (x − 3)2 = 7 and x = 3 ± √7.

questions.t: Consider the parabola <var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 8<var>x</var> + 5.
p: Express the equation in the form <var>y</var> = <var>a</var>(<var>x</var> − <var>h</var>)<sup>2</sup> + <var>k</var>, and write the coordinates of the vertex.
Write the <var>y</var>-intercept.
Find the <var>x</var>-intercepts as exact values.
Solve 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 8<var>x</var> + 5 < 0 for <var>x</var>.
ap: 2(x2 − 4x) + 5 = 2((x − 2)2 − 4) + 5 = 2(x − 2)2 − 3; vertex (2, −3).
At x = 0, y = 5.
2(x − 2)2 = 3, so (x − 2)2 = 32 and x = 2 ± √62, i.e. x = 4 − √62 or x = 4 + √62 (≈ 0.775 and ≈ 3.225).
The parabola opens upwards, so it is below the x-axis between the intercepts: 4 − √62 < x < 4 + √62.

questions.t: Find the equation of each parabola.
p: A parabola has <var>x</var>-intercepts −2 and 5, and <var>y</var>-intercept 20.
A parabola has vertex (−1, 4) and passes through the point (1, −8).
ap: y = a(x + 2)(x − 5). At x = 0: a × 2 × (−5) = 20, so −10a = 20 and a = −2. Hence y = −2(x + 2)(x − 5) = −2x2 + 6x + 20.
y = a(x + 1)2 + 4. At (1, −8): 4a + 4 = −8, so a = −3. Hence y = −3(x + 1)2 + 4 = −3x2 − 6x + 1.

questions.t: Surface area and volume. Use π on your calculator where a decimal answer is asked for.
p: A closed cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 15 cm. Calculate its volume, correct to the nearest cm<sup>3</sup>.
A cone has base radius 9 cm and slant height 15 cm. Calculate its total surface area, including the base, in terms of π.
Calculate the volume of the cone in part b, correct to the nearest cm<sup>3</sup>.
A sphere has radius 6 cm. Calculate its volume and its surface area, both in terms of π.
ap: V = π × 72 × 15 = 735π ≈ 2309 cm3.
πr2 + πrl = 81π + 135π = 216π cm2.
Perpendicular height = √(152 − 92) = √144 = 12 cm, so V = ⅓ × π × 81 × 12 = 324π ≈ 1018 cm3.
V = 43π × 63 = 288π cm3; surface area = 4π × 62 = 144π cm2.

questions.t: Two solid cones are similar. The smaller cone has height 8 cm and the larger cone has height 20 cm.
p: Write the length scale factor from the smaller cone to the larger cone.
The curved surface area of the smaller cone is 60 cm<sup>2</sup>. Calculate the curved surface area of the larger cone.
The volume of the larger cone is 500 cm<sup>3</sup>. Calculate the volume of the smaller cone.
ap: 208 = 52 (= 2.5).
Area scale factor = 2.52 = 6.25, so area = 60 × 6.25 = 375 cm2.
Volume scale factor = 2.53 = 15.625, so the smaller volume = 500 ÷ 15.625 = 32 cm3. (Check: 32 × 15.625 = 500. ✓)

questions.t: Indices, exponentials and logarithms.
p: Simplify (2a3b−1)24a−1b3, writing your answer with positive indices.
Evaluate 16<sup>3/4</sup>.
Evaluate 27<sup>−2/3</sup>.
Solve 5<sup>2<var>x</var> − 1</sup> = 125<sup><var>x</var> − 2</sup> for <var>x</var>.
Evaluate log<sub>4</sub>32.
ap: Numerator = 4a6b−2, so the quotient is 4a6b−24a−1b3 = a7b−5 = a7b5.
(161/4)3 = 23 = 8.
1272/3 = 132 = 19.
125x − 2 = 53x − 6, so 2x − 1 = 3x − 6, giving x = 5. Check: 59 = 1253. ✓
4y = 32 means 22y = 25, so 2y = 5 and log432 = 52.

questions.t: A colony of bacteria numbers 8000 and increases by 6% each hour.
p: Write an expression for the number of bacteria present after <var>t</var> hours.
Calculate the number of bacteria present after 5 hours, correct to the nearest whole bacterium.
Find the least whole number of hours after which the colony first exceeds 20 000.
ap: 8000 × 1.06t.
We need 1.06t > 2.5. At t = 15: 8000 × 1.0615 ≈ 19 172, which is below 20 000. At t = 16: 8000 × 1.0616 ≈ 20 323, which is above 20 000. So the answer is 16 hours.

questions.t: In △<var>ABC</var>, the point <var>P</var> lies on the side <var>AB</var> with <var>AP</var> = 4 cm and <var>PB</var> = 6 cm, and the point <var>Q</var> lies on the side <var>AC</var>. <var>PQ</var> ∥ <var>BC</var>, <var>AQ</var> = 5 cm and <var>BC</var> = 15 cm.
p: Explain why △<var>APQ</var> is similar to △<var>ABC</var>, naming the equal angles and giving the abbreviated reason.
Find the length of <var>QC</var>.
Find the length of <var>PQ</var>.
ap: ∠PAQ = ∠BAC (the same angle, common to both triangles) and ∠APQ = ∠ABC (corresponding angles, PQ ∥ BC). Two pairs of equal angles, so △APQ ⦀ △ABC (AA).
AB = 4 + 6 = 10 cm, so the ratio of matching sides is AP : AB = 4 : 10 = 2 : 5. Hence AQ : AC = 2 : 5, so AC = 5 × 52 = 12.5 cm and QC = 12.5 − 5 = 7.5 cm.
PQ : BC = 2 : 5, so PQ = 25 × 15 = 6 cm.

questions.t: A line <var>l</var><sub>1</sub> has gradient 3 and passes through the point (<var>k</var>, 2). A second line <var>l</var><sub>2</sub> is perpendicular to <var>l</var><sub>1</sub> and passes through the point (1, <var>k</var>). The two lines meet at the point (<var>p</var>, <var>q</var>). Find <var>p</var> and <var>q</var> in terms of <var>k</var>.
questions.a:
l1: y − 2 = 3(x − k), so y = 3x − 3k + 2.
l2 has gradient −13, so y − k = −13(x − 1), giving y = −13x + 13 + k.
Setting the two right-hand sides equal and multiplying by 3: 9x − 9k + 6 = −x + 1 + 3k, so 10x = 12k − 5 and p = 12k − 510.
Then q = 3p − 3k + 2 = 36k − 15 − 30k + 2010 = q = 6k + 510.
Check with k = 0: the lines are y = 3x + 2 and y = −13x + 13, meeting at (−0.5, 0.5), and the formulas give p = −510 = −0.5, q = 510 = 0.5. ✓

questions.t: Find every ordered pair of integers (<var>x</var>, <var>y</var>) for which <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 84, and explain why your list is complete.
questions.a:
x2 − y2 = (x − y)(x + y) = 84. The sum of the two factors is (x − y) + (x + y) = 2x, which is even, so the two factors have the same parity. They cannot both be odd, because then their product would be odd, whereas 84 is even. So both factors are even: put x − y = 2m and x + y = 2n, giving 4mn = 84, so mn = 21, and x = m + n, y = n − m.
The integer factorisations of 21 are (m, n) = (1, 21), (3, 7), (7, 3), (21, 1) and the four with both signs reversed. These give exactly eight ordered pairs: (10, 4), (10, −4), (−10, 4), (−10, −4), (22, 20), (22, −20), (−22, 20), (−22, −20).
Check: 102 − 42 = 100 − 16 = 84 and 222 − 202 = 484 − 400 = 84. ✓ Because every factorisation of 84 into two even factors has been used, the list is complete.

questions.t: Sum and product conditions.
p: The two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle have lengths adding to 23 cm, and the area of the triangle is 60 cm<sup>2</sup>. Find the length of the hypotenuse.
A rectangle has area 30 cm<sup>2</sup> and perimeter 26 cm. Find the exact length of its diagonal.
ap: Let the shorter sides be a cm and b cm. Then a + b = 23 and 12ab = 60, so ab = 120. Hence a2 + b2 = (a + b)2 − 2ab = 529 − 240 = 289, so the hypotenuse is √289 = 17 cm. (The sides are 8 cm and 15 cm, since t2 − 23t + 120 = 0 gives t = 8 or 15.)
Let the sides be l cm and w cm. Then l + w = 13 and lw = 30, so l2 + w2 = 169 − 60 = 109 and the diagonal is √109 cm (≈ 10.44 cm). (The sides are 3 cm and 10 cm.)

questions.t: Each figure below is rotated one full turn about the stated line. Find the exact volume of the solid produced in each case.
p: The rectangle <var>PQRS</var>, with <var>PQ</var> = 6 cm and <var>QR</var> = 3 cm, rotated about the line <var>PQ</var>.
△<var>ABC</var>, right-angled at <var>A</var>, with <var>AB</var> = 6 cm and <var>AC</var> = 3 cm, rotated about the line <var>AB</var>.
The regular hexagon <var>ABCDEF</var> of side length 4 cm, rotated about the diagonal <var>AD</var> that joins the opposite vertices <var>A</var> and <var>D</var>.
ap: Every point of the rectangle stays at most 3 cm from the line PQ, so the solid is a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm: V = π × 32 × 6 = 54π cm3.
The solid is a cone with base radius AC = 3 cm and height AB = 6 cm: V = ⅓ × π × 32 × 6 = 18π cm3.

Put A at the origin with AD along the axis. Then AD = 8 cm and the vertices above the axis are B and C, at perpendicular distance equal to the apothem, 4 × √32 = 2√3 cm, with B 2 cm along from A and C 2 cm back from D. So the solid is a cylinder of radius 2√3 cm and length 4 cm, with a cone of radius 2√3 cm and height 2 cm on each end.
V = π(2√3)2 × 4 + 2 × ⅓ × π(2√3)2 × 2 = 48π + 16π = 64π cm3. (In general, side s gives volume πs3.)

questions.t: A solid sphere of radius 6 cm and a solid cone of height 12 cm with base radius 6 cm both stand on a horizontal floor; the cone stands on its circular base with its apex vertically above the centre of that base. A horizontal plane at height <var>h</var> cm above the floor, where 0 < <var>h</var> < 12, cuts the sphere in a circle and cuts the cone in a circle. Find the value of <var>h</var> for which these two circles have equal area.
questions.a:
The centre of the sphere is 6 cm above the floor. If the sphere's cross-section has radius r1 cm, then by Pythagoras' theorem r12 = 62 − (h − 6)2 = 12h − h2.
For the cone, the radius falls linearly from 6 cm at height 0 to 0 at height 12, so r2 = 6(12 − h)12 = 12 − h2 and r22 = (12 − h)24.
Equal areas means r12 = r22, so 4(12h − h2) = (12 − h)2, giving 48h − 4h2 = 144 − 24h + h2 and 5h2 − 72h + 144 = 0.
Then h = 72 ± √(5184 − 2880)10 = 72 ± 4810, so h = 12 or h = 2.4. The root h = 12 gives both radii 0 (no circles), so h = 2.4 cm.
Check: sphere radius = √(36 − 3.62) = √23.04 = 4.8 cm; cone radius = 12 − 2.42 = 4.8 cm. ✓

questions.t: <var>ABCD</var> is a rectangle, so that <var>AC</var> and <var>BD</var> are its diagonals, and <var>P</var> is any point in the plane of the rectangle. Using coordinates, prove that (<var>PA</var>)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>PC</var>)<sup>2</sup> = (<var>PB</var>)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>PD</var>)<sup>2</sup>.
questions.a:
Choose axes along two sides of the rectangle, so that A = (0, 0), B = (a, 0), C = (a, b) and D = (0, b), where a > 0 and b > 0. Let P = (x, y) be any point of the plane.
Then (PA)2 = x2 + y2 and (PC)2 = (x − a)2 + (y − b)2, so
(PA)2 + (PC)2 = x2 + y2 + (x − a)2 + (y − b)2.
Also (PB)2 = (x − a)2 + y2 and (PD)2 = x2 + (y − b)2, so
(PB)2 + (PD)2 = (x − a)2 + y2 + x2 + (y − b)2.
The two totals contain exactly the same four terms, x2, y2, (x − a)2 and (y − b)2, so they are equal. ∴ (PA)2 + (PC)2 = (PB)2 + (PD)2 for every point P.

questions.t: Write down the centre and the radius of each circle.
p: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 49
(<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> = 36
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − 5)<sup>2</sup> = 12
ap: centre (0, 0), radius 7 (since 49 = 7<sup>2</sup>)
centre (4, −3), radius 6
centre (0, 5), radius √12 = 2√3 (about 3.46)

questions.t: Write down the equation of each circle in the standard form (<var>x</var> − <var>h</var>)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − <var>k</var>)<sup>2</sup> = <var>r</var><sup>2</sup>.
p: centre (0, 0), radius 6
centre (−3, 5), radius 2
centre (7, 0), radius √10
ap: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 36
(<var>x</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − 5)<sup>2</sup> = 4
(<var>x</var> − 7)<sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 10

questions.t: The rectangular hyperbola y = 6x + 2 is graphed.
p: Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote.
Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote.
Find the coordinates of the point where the graph crosses the <var>y</var>-axis.
Find the value of <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> = 4.
Explain why the graph has no <var>x</var>-intercept.
questions.al: The graph is y = 6x translated 2 units to the left.
ap: <var>x</var> = −2
<var>y</var> = 0
put x = 0: y = 62 = 3, so the point is (0, 3)
y = 66 = 1
An x-intercept needs 6x + 2 = 0, which would require the numerator 6 to be 0. Since 6 ≠ 0, y is never 0 and there is no x-intercept.

questions.t: Complete the square in <var>x</var> and in <var>y</var> to find the centre and the radius of each circle.
p: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> + 10<var>y</var> + 9 = 0
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var> − 19 = 0
ap: (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var>) + (<var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 10<var>y</var>) = −9, so (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> + 9) + (<var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 10<var>y</var> + 25) = −9 + 9 + 25, giving (<var>x</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> + 5)<sup>2</sup> = 25 = 5<sup>2</sup>. Centre (3, −5), radius 5.

(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> + 16) + (<var>y</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>y</var> + 1) = 19 + 16 + 1, giving (<var>x</var> + 4)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − 1)<sup>2</sup> = 36 = 6<sup>2</sup>. Centre (−4, 1), radius 6.  (Check b by expanding: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> + 16 + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>y</var> + 1 = 36 gives <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var> − 19 = 0 ✓)

questions.t: The circle (<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> = 25 is drawn on the coordinate plane.
p: Find the coordinates of both points where this circle meets the <var>x</var>-axis.
Find the coordinates of both points where this circle meets the <var>y</var>-axis.
ap: Put <var>y</var> = 0: (<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> + 9 = 25, so (<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> = 16, <var>x</var> − 4 = 4 or −4, so <var>x</var> = 8 or <var>x</var> = 0. The points are (0, 0) and (8, 0).

Put <var>x</var> = 0: 16 + (<var>y</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> = 25, so (<var>y</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> = 9, <var>y</var> + 3 = 3 or −3, so <var>y</var> = 0 or <var>y</var> = −6. The points are (0, 0) and (0, −6).  (The circle has centre (4, −3) and radius 5, and it passes through the origin, which is why (0, 0) appears in both answers.)

questions.t: The interval <var>AB</var> joins the points <var>A</var>(−2, 3) and <var>B</var>(6, 9).
p: Find the length of <var>AB</var>.
Find the coordinates of the midpoint of <var>AB</var>.
Find the equation of the circle that has <var>AB</var> as a diameter.
ap: Midpoint = (−2 + 62, 3 + 92) = (2, 6).

The centre is the midpoint (2, 6) and the radius is half the diameter, 10 ÷ 2 = 5, so the circle is (<var>x</var> − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − 6)<sup>2</sup> = 25. Check with <var>A</var>: (−2 − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (3 − 6)<sup>2</sup> = 16 + 9 = 25 ✓

questions.t: Find the coordinates of the two points of intersection of the parabola <var>y</var> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3<var>x</var> − 1 and the line <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 7.
questions.a: Equating the two expressions for <var>y</var>: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3<var>x</var> − 1 = <var>x</var> + 7, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 8 = 0, that is (<var>x</var> + 4)(<var>x</var> − 2) = 0, so <var>x</var> = −4 or <var>x</var> = 2. Using <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 7: <var>y</var> = 3 or <var>y</var> = 9. The points are (−4, 3) and (2, 9). Check in the parabola: (−4)<sup>2</sup> + 3(−4) − 1 = 16 − 12 − 1 = 3 ✓ and 2<sup>2</sup> + 6 − 1 = 9 ✓

questions.t: Find the coordinates of the two points where the line <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> − 2 cuts the circle <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 20.
questions.a: Substitute <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> − 2 into the circle: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + (<var>x</var> − 2)<sup>2</sup> = 20, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> + 4 = 20, 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> − 16 = 0, <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>x</var> − 8 = 0, (<var>x</var> − 4)(<var>x</var> + 2) = 0, so <var>x</var> = 4 or <var>x</var> = −2. Then <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> − 2 gives <var>y</var> = 2 or <var>y</var> = −4. The points are (4, 2) and (−2, −4). Check: 4<sup>2</sup> + 2<sup>2</sup> = 20 ✓ and (−2)<sup>2</sup> + (−4)<sup>2</sup> = 20 ✓

questions.t: Find the coordinates of the two points where the line y = x + 1 meets the hyperbola y = 12x.
questions.a: Eliminating y: x + 1 = 12x. Since x ≠ 0 we may multiply both sides by x: x2 + x = 12, so x2 + x − 12 = 0, (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0, so x = −4 or x = 3. Using y = x + 1: y = −3 or y = 4. The points are (−4, −3) and (3, 4). Check on the hyperbola: 12 ÷ (−4) = −3 ✓ and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 ✓

questions.t: Show that the line <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 5 does not meet the circle <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 8.
questions.a: Substituting y = x + 5 into x2 + y2 = 8 gives x2 + (x + 5)2 = 8, that is x2 + x2 + 10x + 25 = 8, so 2x2 + 10x + 17 = 0. For this quadratic, b2 − 4ac = 102 − 4 × 2 × 17 = 100 − 136 = −36, which is negative, so there are no real solutions. Hence no point lies on both graphs and the line does not meet the circle. (Indeed the circle has radius √8 ≈ 2.83, and the closest the line gets to the origin is 5√2 ≈ 3.54.)

questions.t: A region of the plane is defined by the two inequalities <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> ≤ 6 and <var>y</var> ≥ 2<var>x</var>.
p: Find the coordinates of the corner point of this region.
State whether the point (1, 4) lies in the region, justifying your answer.
State whether the point (3, 1) lies in the region, justifying your answer.
ap: The corner point is where the boundary lines <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 6 and <var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var> meet. Substituting <var>y</var> = 2<var>x</var> into <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 6 gives <var>x</var> + 2<var>x</var> = 6, so <var>x</var> = 2 and <var>y</var> = 4. The corner point is (2, 4), and because both inequalities include their boundary lines this point belongs to the region.
Yes. 1 + 4 = 5 ≤ 6, and 4 ≥ 2 × 1 = 2, so both inequalities are satisfied.
No. Although 3 + 1 = 4 ≤ 6, the second inequality requires <var>y</var> ≥ 2<var>x</var>, and 1 ≥ 6 is false, so (3, 1) is not in the region.

questions.t: A circle has centre (5, −2) and touches the <var>y</var>-axis.
p: Explain why the radius must be 5, and write down the equation of the circle.
Find the exact coordinates of the two points where this circle crosses the <var>x</var>-axis.
ap: A circle touches a line when the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line equals the radius. The perpendicular distance from (5, −2) to the <var>y</var>-axis (the line <var>x</var> = 0) is 5, so <var>r</var> = 5 and the circle is (<var>x</var> − 5)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> + 2)<sup>2</sup> = 25.

Put <var>y</var> = 0: (<var>x</var> − 5)<sup>2</sup> + 4 = 25, so (<var>x</var> − 5)<sup>2</sup> = 21, giving <var>x</var> − 5 = √21 or <var>x</var> − 5 = −√21, so <var>x</var> = 5 + √21 or <var>x</var> = 5 − √21. The points are (5 − √21, 0) and (5 + √21, 0). (Since √21 ≈ 4.58, these are about (0.42, 0) and (9.58, 0), both to the right of the <var>y</var>-axis, as expected. The distance from the centre to the <var>x</var>-axis is 2, which is less than 5, so the circle really does cross it twice.)

questions.t: The graph of y = 3 + 4x − 2 is a rectangular hyperbola.
p: Describe how this graph is obtained from the graph of y = 4x by translations.
Write down the equations of both asymptotes.
Find the coordinates of the <var>y</var>-intercept.
Find the coordinates of the <var>x</var>-intercept.
ap: Translate y = 4x two units to the right, which gives y = 4x − 2, and then three units up, which gives y = 3 + 4x − 2.
The vertical asymptote of y = 4x moves from x = 0 to x = 2, and the horizontal asymptote moves from y = 0 to y = 3.
Put x = 0: y = 3 + 4−2 = 3 − 2 = 1, so the y-intercept is (0, 1).
Put y = 0: 3 + 4x − 2 = 0, so 4x − 2 = −3, so 4 = −3(x − 2) = −3x + 6, giving 3x = 2 and x = 23. The x-intercept is (23, 0). Check: 3 + 4 ÷ (23 − 2) = 3 + 4 ÷ (−43) = 3 − 3 = 0 ✓

questions.t: The points <var>O</var>(0, 0), <var>A</var>(8, 0) and <var>B</var>(0, 6) all lie on one circle.
p: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of <var>OA</var>.
Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of <var>OB</var>.
Hence find the centre and the radius of the circle, and write down its equation.
Explain why <var>AB</var> is a diameter of this circle.
ap: <var>OA</var> lies along the <var>x</var>-axis and its midpoint is (4, 0), so its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line <var>x</var> = 4.
<var>OB</var> lies along the <var>y</var>-axis and its midpoint is (0, 3), so its perpendicular bisector is the horizontal line <var>y</var> = 3.

The centre of the circle is equidistant from <var>O</var>, <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>, so it lies on both perpendicular bisectors; hence the centre is (4, 3). The radius is the distance from (4, 3) to <var>O</var>, which is √(4<sup>2</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup>) = √25 = 5. The circle is (<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup> = 25. Check <var>A</var>(8, 0): (8 − 4)<sup>2</sup> + (0 − 3)<sup>2</sup> = 16 + 9 = 25 ✓; check <var>B</var>(0, 6): (0 − 4)<sup>2</sup> + (6 − 3)<sup>2</sup> = 16 + 9 = 25 ✓

The midpoint of AB is (8 + 02, 0 + 62) = (4, 3), which is the centre, and AB = √(82 + 62) = 10 = 2 × 5, twice the radius. So AB is a chord passing through the centre, that is, a diameter. (Equivalently, ∠AOB = 90°, and an angle of 90° at the circumference stands on a diameter.)

questions.t: Two circles have equations <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var> = 0 and <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> + 4<var>y</var> = 0.
p: Show that both circles pass through the origin.
By subtracting one equation from the other, find the coordinates of their second point of intersection.
Find the centre and the radius of each circle.
ap: Substituting <var>x</var> = 0, <var>y</var> = 0 into the first equation gives 0 + 0 − 0 − 0 = 0, which is true; the same substitution in the second gives 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, also true. So (0, 0) lies on both circles.

Subtracting the second equation from the first, the <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> and <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> terms cancel: (−4<var>x</var> − 2<var>y</var>) − (2<var>x</var> + 4<var>y</var>) = 0, so −6<var>x</var> − 6<var>y</var> = 0, that is <var>y</var> = −<var>x</var>. Any common point lies on this line. Substituting <var>y</var> = −<var>x</var> into the first circle: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> − 2(−<var>x</var>) = 0, so 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>x</var> = 0, 2<var>x</var>(<var>x</var> − 1) = 0, giving <var>x</var> = 0 (the origin) or <var>x</var> = 1. When <var>x</var> = 1, <var>y</var> = −1, so the second point of intersection is (1, −1). Check in the second circle: 1 + 1 + 2 − 4 = 0 ✓

First circle: (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> + 4) + (<var>y</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>y</var> + 1) = 4 + 1, so (<var>x</var> − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − 1)<sup>2</sup> = 5; centre (2, 1), radius √5. Second circle: (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> + 1) + (<var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 4<var>y</var> + 4) = 1 + 4, so (<var>x</var> + 1)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> + 2)<sup>2</sup> = 5; centre (−1, −2), radius √5. (Both radii are √5, and each centre is distance √5 from the origin, as it must be.)

questions.t: <var>A</var>(−13, 0) and <var>B</var>(13, 0) are the endpoints of a diameter of the circle <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 169. Let <var>P</var>(<var>x</var>, <var>y</var>) be any point on this circle other than <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>.
p: Explain why <var>y</var> cannot be 0.
Show that <var>AP</var> ⊥ <var>BP</var>.
ap: If <var>y</var> = 0 then <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 169, so <var>x</var> = 13 or <var>x</var> = −13; that is, <var>P</var> would be <var>B</var> or <var>A</var>. Both are excluded, so <var>y</var> ≠ 0.

Since y ≠ 0, we also have x ≠ 13 and x ≠ −13 (either value forces y = 0), so both gradients below exist. Gradient of AP = y − 0x − (−13) = yx + 13. Gradient of BP = y − 0x − 13 = yx − 13. Their product is y2(x + 13)(x − 13) = y2x2 − 169. Because P lies on the circle, x2 + y2 = 169, so y2 = 169 − x2 = −(x2 − 169). Hence the product of the gradients is −(x2 − 169)x2 − 169 = −1. Two lines whose gradients have product −1 are perpendicular, so AP ⊥ BP. ∴ the diameter AB subtends a right angle at every other point of the circle.

questions.t: Consider the line y = px + q and the hyperbola y = 1x, where p ≠ 0.
p: Suppose <var>p</var> > 0. Show that the line always meets the hyperbola at exactly two points, whatever the value of <var>q</var>.
Now let <var>p</var> be any non-zero number. Give the condition on <var>p</var> and <var>q</var> for the line to miss the hyperbola completely, and give one line that does miss it.
ap: At a common point, px + q = 1x. The value x = 0 is not on the hyperbola, so we may multiply both sides by x: px2 + qx = 1, that is px2 + qx − 1 = 0. Since p > 0 this is a genuine quadratic, and its discriminant is q2 − 4 × p × (−1) = q2 + 4p. As q2 ≥ 0 and 4p > 0, the discriminant is positive, so there are two distinct real roots. Neither root is 0, because putting x = 0 in px2 + qx − 1 gives −1, not 0. Each root x gives one point (x, 1x) on both graphs, so the line meets the hyperbola at exactly two points.

The line misses the hyperbola exactly when px2 + qx − 1 = 0 has no real solution, that is when q2 + 4p < 0, i.e. q2 < −4p. This requires p < 0. Any pair satisfying q2 < −4p is acceptable; for example p = −1 and q = 1 gives the line y = −x + 1, for which the discriminant is 12 + 4(−1) = −3 < 0, so y = −x + 1 never meets y = 1x.

questions.t: Calculate the value asked for in each part. Give side lengths correct to two decimal places and angles correct to one decimal place.
p: In △<var>ABC</var>, ∠<var>ABC</var> = 90°, ∠<var>BAC</var> = 34° and <var>AC</var> = 12.5 cm. Find the length of <var>BC</var>.
In △<var>DEF</var>, ∠<var>DEF</var> = 90°, ∠<var>EDF</var> = 57° and <var>DE</var> = 9.4 cm. Find the length of <var>DF</var>.
In △<var>XYZ</var>, ∠<var>XYZ</var> = 90°, <var>XY</var> = 7.2 cm and <var>YZ</var> = 11.5 cm. Find ∠<var>YXZ</var>.
In △<var>LMN</var>, ∠<var>LMN</var> = 90°, <var>LN</var> = 20.4 cm and <var>MN</var> = 13.6 cm. Find ∠<var>MLN</var>.
ap: BC is opposite the 34° angle and AC is the hypotenuse, so BC = 12.5 sin 34° ≈ 6.99 cm.
DE is adjacent to the 57° angle and DF is the hypotenuse, so cos 57° = 9.4/DF, giving DF = 9.4 ÷ cos 57° ≈ 17.26 cm.
MN is opposite ∠MLN and LN is the hypotenuse, so sin ∠MLN = 13.6/20.4 = 2/3, giving ∠MLN ≈ 41.8°.

questions.t: Find the exact value of each expression, rationalising the denominator where appropriate.
p: sin 60° cos 30° − cos 60° sin 30°
tan 30° × tan 60° + cos<sup>2</sup> 45°
sin<sup>2</sup> 120° + cos 135° × cos 45°

questions.t: <var>PQRS</var> is a rhombus, with the vertices in that order, side length 12 cm and ∠<var>PQR</var> = 60°. Its diagonals <var>PR</var> and <var>QS</var> meet at <var>T</var>. (Recall that the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, and each diagonal bisects the two vertex angles it joins.)
p: Find the exact length of the diagonal <var>PR</var>.
Find the exact length of the diagonal <var>QS</var>.
ap: In △PQR, QP = QR = 12 cm and the included angle ∠PQR = 60°, so the base angles are each (180° − 60°) ÷ 2 = 60°. The triangle is equilateral, so PR = 12 cm exactly.
T is the midpoint of QS, ∠QTP = 90° and QT bisects ∠PQR, so ∠PQT = 30°. In right-angled △PQT, QT = 12 cos 30° = 12 × (√3/2) = 6√3, so QS = 2 × 6√3 = 12√3 cm (≈ 20.78 cm).

questions.t: A vertical flagpole <var>BT</var> stands on level ground, with <var>B</var> at its foot and <var>T</var> at its top. <var>A</var> is a point on the ground with <var>AB</var> = 46 m, and the angle of elevation of <var>T</var> from <var>A</var> is 27°.
p: Find the height of the flagpole, correct to two decimal places.

<var>C</var> is a point on the ground on the straight line through <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>, on the opposite side of <var>B</var> from <var>A</var>. The angle of elevation of <var>T</var> from <var>C</var> is 41°. Find the distance <var>AC</var>, correct to two decimal places.
ap: △ABT has a right angle at B, so tan 27° = BT/46 and BT = 46 tan 27° = 23.4381… ≈ 23.44 m.
In right-angled △CBT, tan 41° = BT/BC, so BC = 23.4381…/tan 41° = 26.9625… ≈ 26.96 m. Since B lies between A and C, AC = 46 + 26.9625… ≈ 72.96 m.

questions.t: In △<var>ABC</var>, ∠<var>BAC</var> = 47°, ∠<var>ABC</var> = 68° and <var>AB</var> = 15.2 cm. Find, correct to two decimal places:
p: the length of <var>BC</var>
the length of <var>AC</var>
questions.al: ∠ACB = 180° − 47° − 68° = 65°, and AB = 15.2 cm is the side opposite ∠ACB.

questions.t: In △<var>DEF</var>, <var>DE</var> = 14 cm, <var>EF</var> = 9 cm and ∠<var>DFE</var> = 78°.
p: Find ∠<var>FDE</var>, correct to the nearest degree. (Since <var>EF</var> is shorter than <var>DE</var>, ∠<var>FDE</var> is smaller than 78° and so is acute.)
Hence find the length of <var>DF</var>, correct to two decimal places.
ap: EF = 9 is opposite ∠FDE and DE = 14 is opposite ∠DFE = 78°. By the sine rule, sin ∠FDE/9 = sin 78°/14, so sin ∠FDE = 9 sin 78°/14 = 0.6288…, giving ∠FDE ≈ 38.96°, that is 39° to the nearest degree.
∠DEF = 180° − 78° − 38.96° = 63.04°, and DF is opposite ∠DEF. So DF = 14 sin 63.04°/sin 78° ≈ 12.76 cm. (Using the rounded 63° gives 12.75 cm; accept either.)

questions.t: In △<var>KLM</var>, ∠<var>KLM</var> = 128°, ∠<var>LKM</var> = 21° and <var>KL</var> = 6.5 m. Find, correct to two decimal places:
p: the length of <var>LM</var>
the length of <var>KM</var>
questions.al: ∠KML = 180° − 128° − 21° = 31°, and KL = 6.5 m is opposite ∠KML.
ap: LM is opposite ∠LKM = 21°, so LM = 6.5 sin 21°/sin 31° ≈ 4.52 m.
KM is opposite ∠KLM = 128°, and sin 128° = sin 52°, so KM = 6.5 sin 128°/sin 31° ≈ 9.95 m.

questions.t: Use the formula area = ½ × (product of two sides) × sin (included angle).
p: In △<var>XYZ</var>, <var>XY</var> = 11 cm, <var>YZ</var> = 8.5 cm and ∠<var>XYZ</var> = 38°. Find the area of △<var>XYZ</var>, correct to two decimal places.
In △<var>PQR</var>, <var>PQ</var> = 9 cm, ∠<var>QPR</var> = 115° and the area of the triangle is 40 cm<sup>2</sup>. Find the length of <var>PR</var>, correct to two decimal places.
ap: ∠QPR is the angle included between PQ and PR, so 40 = ½ × 9 × PR × sin 115°. Hence PR = 80/(9 sin 115°) = 80/8.1567… ≈ 9.81 cm.

questions.t: In △<var>ABC</var>, <var>AB</var> = 9.4 cm, <var>BC</var> = 12.7 cm and ∠<var>ABC</var> = 112°.
p: Find the length of <var>AC</var>, correct to two decimal places.
Find the area of △<var>ABC</var>, correct to two decimal places.
ap: ∠ABC is included between AB and BC, so by the cosine rule AC<sup>2</sup> = 9.4<sup>2</sup> + 12.7<sup>2</sup> − 2 × 9.4 × 12.7 × cos 112° = 88.36 + 161.29 − 238.76 × (−0.37461) = 249.65 + 89.44 = 339.09…, so AC ≈ 18.41 cm.

questions.t: A triangular block of land <var>PQR</var> has <var>PQ</var> = 8.5 m, <var>QR</var> = 6.2 m and <var>PR</var> = 11.4 m.
p: Find the size of ∠<var>PQR</var>, correct to one decimal place, and explain why it is the largest angle of the triangle.
Find the area of the block, correct to two decimal places.
ap: By the cosine rule, cos ∠PQR = (8.5<sup>2</sup> + 6.2<sup>2</sup> − 11.4<sup>2</sup>)/(2 × 8.5 × 6.2) = (72.25 + 38.44 − 129.96)/105.4 = −19.27/105.4 = −0.18283, so ∠PQR ≈ 100.5°. It is the largest angle because it is opposite the longest side, PR = 11.4 m (the cosine is negative, so it is the only obtuse angle).

questions.t: A rectangular prism has a horizontal rectangular base <var>ABCD</var> with <var>AB</var> = 24 cm and <var>BC</var> = 10 cm. Its four vertical edges are <var>AE</var>, <var>BF</var>, <var>CG</var> and <var>DH</var>, each of length 15 cm, so <var>E</var> is directly above <var>A</var>, <var>F</var> directly above <var>B</var>, <var>G</var> directly above <var>C</var> and <var>H</var> directly above <var>D</var>.
p: Find the length of the base diagonal <var>AC</var>.
Find the length of <var>AG</var>, correct to two decimal places.
Find the angle that <var>AG</var> makes with the base, that is ∠<var>GAC</var>, correct to one decimal place.
ap: △ABC has a right angle at B, so AC<sup>2</sup> = 24<sup>2</sup> + 10<sup>2</sup> = 576 + 100 = 676 and AC = 26 cm exactly.
CG is vertical and AC lies in the horizontal base, so ∠ACG = 90°. Then AG<sup>2</sup> = AC<sup>2</sup> + CG<sup>2</sup> = 676 + 225 = 901, so AG = √901 ≈ 30.02 cm.
In right-angled △ACG, tan ∠GAC = CG/AC = 15/26 = 0.57692…, so ∠GAC ≈ 30.0°.

questions.t: A vertical tower <var>OT</var> stands on level ground, with <var>O</var> at its foot and <var>T</var> at its top. <var>A</var> is a point on the ground due south of <var>O</var> with <var>OA</var> = 60 m, and <var>B</var> is a point on the ground due east of <var>O</var> with <var>OB</var> = 85 m. The angle of elevation of <var>T</var> from <var>A</var> is 22°.
p: Find the height of the tower, correct to one decimal place.
Find the angle of elevation of <var>T</var> from <var>B</var>, correct to one decimal place.
Find the bearing of <var>A</var> from <var>B</var>, correct to one decimal place.
ap: △AOT has a right angle at O, so OT = 60 tan 22° = 24.2416… ≈ 24.2 m.
△BOT also has a right angle at O, so tan (angle of elevation) = OT/OB = 24.2416/85 = 0.28519…, giving an angle of elevation of ≈ 15.9°.

A is due south of O and B is due east of O, so ∠AOB = 90°. In right-angled △AOB, tan ∠OBA = OA/OB = 60/85 = 0.70588…, so ∠OBA ≈ 35.2°. From B, O lies due west (bearing 270°), and A is a further 35.2° round towards the south, so the bearing of A from B ≈ 270° − 35.2° = 234.8°T.

questions.t: Two ships leave port <var>P</var> at the same time. Ship <var>A</var> sails 240 km on a bearing of 035°T and ship <var>B</var> sails 310 km on a bearing of 128°T.
p: Find the distance between the two ships, correct to the nearest kilometre.
Find the bearing of ship <var>B</var> from ship <var>A</var>, correct to the nearest degree.
ap: The longest side, AB, is opposite ∠APB = 93°, so every other angle is acute. By the sine rule, sin ∠PAB/310 = sin 93°/401.86, so sin ∠PAB = 310 × 0.99863/401.86 = 0.77044 and ∠PAB ≈ 50.4°. From A the bearing of P is 035° + 180° = 215°T, and B lies to the east of the line PA, so the bearing of B from A ≈ 215° − 50.4° = 164.6°, that is 165°T. (Check by components: A is 137.66 km east and 196.60 km north of P, B is 244.28 km east and 190.86 km south of P, so A to B is 106.62 km east and 387.45 km south, giving a bearing of 180° − tan<sup>−1</sup>(106.62/387.45) = 164.6°.)

questions.t: In △<var>ABC</var> the side lengths are labelled in the usual way: <var>a</var> = <var>BC</var>, <var>b</var> = <var>CA</var> and <var>c</var> = <var>AB</var>.
p: Using the formula area = ½ × (product of two sides) × sin (included angle), write down two different expressions for the area of △<var>ABC</var>: one using the angle at <var>A</var> and one using the angle at <var>B</var>.
Hence deduce the sine rule in the form asin A = bsin B.
ap: The two sides containing the angle at A are b and c, so area = ½bc sin A. The two sides containing the angle at B are a and c, so area = ½ac sin B.

These are the same area, so ½bc sin A = ½ac sin B, giving bc sin A = ac sin B. Dividing both sides by c (c ≠ 0) gives b sin A = a sin B. Since 0° < A < 180° and 0° < B < 180°, both sin A and sin B are non-zero, so dividing both sides by sin A sin B gives b/sin B = a/sin A, that is a/sin A = b/sin B.

questions.t: A vertical tower of height <var>h</var> metres stands on level ground with its foot at <var>F</var>. Kai stands at <var>K</var>, and <var>F</var> is due north of <var>K</var>. Mia stands at <var>M</var>, which is 150 m due east of <var>K</var>. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 14° from <var>K</var> and 11° from <var>M</var>.
p: Express <var>KF</var>, the distance from Kai to the foot of the tower, in terms of <var>h</var>.
Express <var>MF</var>, the distance from Mia to the foot of the tower, in terms of <var>h</var>.
Explain why ∠<var>FKM</var> = 90°, then use Pythagoras' theorem in △<var>FKM</var> to find <var>h</var>, correct to one decimal place.
Find the bearing of the tower from Mia, correct to the nearest degree.
ap: The tower is vertical, so tan 14° = h/KF and KF = h/tan 14°.
Similarly tan 11° = h/MF, so MF = h/tan 11°.

F is due north of K and M is due east of K, and north is perpendicular to east, so ∠FKM = 90°. Hence MF<sup>2</sup> = KF<sup>2</sup> + KM<sup>2</sup>: h<sup>2</sup>/tan<sup>2</sup> 11° = h<sup>2</sup>/tan<sup>2</sup> 14° + 150<sup>2</sup>, so h<sup>2</sup>(1/tan<sup>2</sup> 11° − 1/tan<sup>2</sup> 14°) = 22500. Now 1/tan<sup>2</sup> 11° = 26.4664 and 1/tan<sup>2</sup> 14° = 16.0864, so h<sup>2</sup> × 10.3801 = 22500, h<sup>2</sup> = 2167.6 and h ≈ 46.6 m.

KF = 46.5577/tan 14° ≈ 186.73 m and KM = 150 m, so from M the foot of the tower is 150 m west and 186.73 m north. The angle west of north is tan<sup>−1</sup>(150/186.73) ≈ 38.8°, so the bearing is 360° − 38.8° = 321.2°, that is 321°T.

questions.t: △<var>ABC</var> is isosceles with <var>AB</var> = <var>AC</var> = 1 and ∠<var>BAC</var> = 2<var>θ</var>, where 0° < <var>θ</var> < 45°. <var>M</var> is the midpoint of <var>BC</var>.
p: Explain why △<var>ABM</var> ≅ △<var>ACM</var>, and hence why ∠<var>AMB</var> = 90° and ∠<var>BAM</var> = <var>θ</var>.
Show that <var>BC</var> = 2 sin <var>θ</var>.
Use the cosine rule in △<var>ABC</var> to show that <var>BC</var><sup>2</sup> = 2(1 − cos 2<var>θ</var>), and deduce that cos 2<var>θ</var> = 1 − 2 sin<sup>2</sup> <var>θ</var>.
Hence find the exact value of sin<sup>2</sup> 15°.
ap: AB = AC (given), BM = CM (M is the midpoint of BC) and AM is common, so △ABM ≅ △ACM (SSS). Hence ∠AMB = ∠AMC; these two angles are supplementary because B, M, C are collinear, so each is 90°. Also ∠BAM = ∠CAM, and together they make ∠BAC = 2θ, so ∠BAM = θ.
In right-angled △ABM, sin ∠BAM = BM/AB, so BM = 1 × sin θ = sin θ, and BC = 2BM = 2 sin θ.

By the cosine rule, BC<sup>2</sup> = AB<sup>2</sup> + AC<sup>2</sup> − 2 × AB × AC × cos 2θ = 1 + 1 − 2 cos 2θ = 2(1 − cos 2θ). From part b, BC<sup>2</sup> = (2 sin θ)<sup>2</sup> = 4 sin<sup>2</sup> θ, so 4 sin<sup>2</sup> θ = 2 − 2 cos 2θ. Dividing by 2 gives 2 sin<sup>2</sup> θ = 1 − cos 2θ, that is cos 2θ = 1 − 2 sin<sup>2</sup> θ.

questions.t: In △ABC the side lengths are a = BC, b = CA and c = AB, and s = a + b + c2 is half the perimeter.
p: Use the cosine rule to show that 1 + cos A = (b + c)2 − a22bc.
Hence show that 1 + cos A = 2s(s − a)bc.
Show in the same way that 1 − cos A = 2(s − b)(s − c)bc.

Using sin<sup>2</sup> <var>A</var> = (1 − cos <var>A</var>)(1 + cos <var>A</var>) and area = ½<var>bc</var> sin <var>A</var>, deduce Heron's formula, area = √(<var>s</var>(<var>s</var> − <var>a</var>)(<var>s</var> − <var>b</var>)(<var>s</var> − <var>c</var>)).
ap: The cosine rule gives cos A = (b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup> − a<sup>2</sup>)/(2bc). So 1 + cos A = (2bc + b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup> − a<sup>2</sup>)/(2bc) = ((b + c)<sup>2</sup> − a<sup>2</sup>)/(2bc), since b<sup>2</sup> + 2bc + c<sup>2</sup> = (b + c)<sup>2</sup>.

<sup>2</sup> − a<sup>2</sup> = (b + c + a)(b + c − a). Now a + b + c = 2s and b + c − a = (a + b + c) − 2a = 2s − 2a = 2(s − a), so the numerator is 2s × 2(s − a) = 4s(s − a) and 1 + cos A = 4s(s − a)/(2bc) = 2s(s − a)/(bc).  c) 1 − cos A = (2bc − b<sup>2</sup> − c<sup>2</sup> + a<sup>2</sup>)/(2bc) = (a<sup>2</sup> − (b − c)<sup>2</sup>)/(2bc) = (a − b + c)(a + b − c)/(2bc). Here a − b + c = 2s − 2b = 2(s − b) and a + b − c = 2s − 2c = 2(s − c), so 1 − cos A = 4(s − b)(s − c)/(2bc) = 2(s − b)(s − c)/(bc).

sin<sup>2</sup> A = (1 − cos A)(1 + cos A) = [2(s − b)(s − c)/(bc)] × [2s(s − a)/(bc)] = 4s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)/(b<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup>). Then (area)<sup>2</sup> = (½bc sin A)<sup>2</sup> = ¼b<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup> sin<sup>2</sup> A = ¼b<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup> × 4s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)/(b<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup>) = s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c). The area is positive, so area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)).

questions.t: A triangle <var>ABC</var> is to be constructed with <var>AB</var> = 12 cm, ∠<var>ABC</var> = 40° and <var>AC</var> = <var>k</var> cm, where <var>k</var> > 0. Let <var>D</var> be the foot of the perpendicular from <var>A</var> to the ray from <var>B</var> along which <var>C</var> must lie.
p: Find the exact length <var>AD</var>, and its value correct to two decimal places.
State, with reasons, the values of <var>k</var> for which there is (i) no such triangle, (ii) exactly one such triangle, (iii) two non-congruent such triangles.
ap: △ABD has a right angle at D and ∠ABD = 40°, so AD = AB sin 40° = 12 sin 40° = 7.7134… ≈ 7.71 cm.

C must lie on the ray from B making 40° with BA, and also on the circle of centre A and radius k. AD = 12 sin 40° is the shortest distance from A to the line through that ray. (i) If k < 12 sin 40° (about 7.71) the circle never reaches the line, so there is no triangle. (ii) If k = 12 sin 40° ≈ 7.71 the circle touches the line at D only, giving exactly one triangle — right-angled at C. There is also exactly one triangle when k ≥ 12: then k ≥ AB, so the circle meets the required ray just once (when k = 12 the second intersection is B itself, which is degenerate; when k > 12 it lies on the opposite ray). (iii) If 12 sin 40° < k < 12 the circle cuts the ray at two distinct points, giving two non-congruent triangles, one with ∠ACB acute and one with ∠ACB obtuse (the two angles being supplementary, since sin ∠ACB = 12 sin 40°/k in both). Summary: no triangle for 0 < k < 12 sin 40° ≈ 7.71; exactly one for k = 12 sin 40° ≈ 7.71 and for k ≥ 12; two for 7.71 < k < 12.

questions.t: In △<var>ABC</var>, <var>AB</var> = 7 cm, <var>BC</var> = 10 cm and <var>AC</var> = 13 cm. <var>M</var> is the midpoint of <var>BC</var>, so <var>BM</var> = <var>MC</var> = 5 cm, and <var>AM</var> is a median of the triangle.
p: Use the cosine rule to show that cos ∠ABC = −17.
Find the exact length of the median <var>AM</var>, in simplest surd form.
Find the exact area of △<var>ABM</var>, in simplest surd form.
ap: cos ∠ABC = (AB<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup> − AC<sup>2</sup>)/(2 × AB × BC) = (49 + 100 − 169)/(2 × 7 × 10) = −20/140 = −1/7. (So ∠ABC is obtuse, about 98.2°.)
M lies on BC, so ∠ABM = ∠ABC. In △ABM, AM<sup>2</sup> = AB<sup>2</sup> + BM<sup>2</sup> − 2 × AB × BM × cos ∠ABM = 49 + 25 − 2 × 7 × 5 × (−1/7) = 74 + 10 = 84. Hence AM = √84 = 2√21 cm (≈ 9.17 cm).

sin<sup>2</sup> ∠ABC = 1 − (−1/7)<sup>2</sup> = 48/49, and the sine of an angle in a triangle is positive, so sin ∠ABC = √48/7 = 4√3/7. Area of △ABM = ½ × AB × BM × sin ∠ABM = ½ × 7 × 5 × 4√3/7 = 10√3 cm<sup>2</sup> (≈ 17.32 cm<sup>2</sup>). (This is half the area of △ABC, 20√3 cm<sup>2</sup>, as expected since BM = ½BC.)

questions.t: <var>P</var>, <var>Q</var> and <var>R</var> are three points on a circle, and <var>PR</var> is a diameter of the circle. It is given that ∠<var>QPR</var> = 34°.
p: Find ∠<var>PQR</var>, giving a reason.
Find ∠<var>QRP</var>.
ap: ∠PQR = 90° (an angle in a semicircle is a right angle — Thales' theorem — because PR is a diameter).
Angle sum of △PQR: ∠QRP = 180° − 90° − 34° = 56°.

questions.t: <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var> and <var>D</var> lie in that order around a circle with centre <var>O</var>. The arc <var>AC</var> that contains <var>B</var> is a minor arc, and it subtends an angle of 108° at <var>O</var>; that is, the non-reflex angle ∠<var>AOC</var> = 108°.
p: Find ∠<var>ADC</var>, giving a reason.
Find the reflex angle at <var>O</var> subtended by the arc <var>AC</var> that contains <var>D</var>.
Find ∠<var>ABC</var>.
ap: D lies on the other arc, so ∠ADC stands on the arc AC containing B. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc, so ∠ADC = ½ × 108° = 54°.
Angles in a revolution at O: reflex ∠AOC = 360° − 108° = 252°.

B lies on the minor arc, so ∠ABC stands on the arc AC containing D, whose angle at the centre is the reflex 252°. Hence ∠ABC = ½ × 252° = 126°. (Check: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral and 54° + 126° = 180°.)

questions.t: <var>P</var>, <var>Q</var>, <var>R</var> and <var>S</var> lie in that order around a circle. The chords <var>PR</var> and <var>QS</var> meet at the point <var>M</var> inside the circle. It is given that ∠<var>QPR</var> = 28° and ∠<var>PQS</var> = 47°.
p: Find ∠<var>QSR</var>, giving a reason.
Find ∠<var>PRS</var>, giving a reason.
Find ∠<var>PMQ</var>.
ap: ∠QPR and ∠QSR are both angles at the circumference standing on the arc QR that contains neither P nor S, so they are equal: ∠QSR = 28°.
∠PQS and ∠PRS are both angles at the circumference standing on the arc SP that contains neither Q nor R, so ∠PRS = 47°.
M lies on PR between P and R, and on QS between Q and S, so in △PQM we have ∠QPM = 28° and ∠PQM = 47°. Angle sum: ∠PMQ = 180° − 28° − 47° = 105°.

questions.t: <var>ABCD</var> is a cyclic quadrilateral, with its vertices in that order around the circle. It is given that ∠<var>DAB</var> = 104° and ∠<var>ABC</var> = 71°. The side <var>AB</var> is produced beyond <var>B</var> to a point <var>E</var>, so that <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>E</var> lie in that order on a line.
p: Find ∠<var>BCD</var>.
Find ∠<var>CDA</var>.
Find ∠<var>CBE</var>.
ap: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: ∠BCD = 180° − 104° = 76°.
∠ABC and ∠CBE form a straight angle at B, so ∠CBE = 180° − 71° = 109°. (Check: the four interior angles are 104° + 71° + 76° + 109° = 360°, and ∠CBE = ∠ADC as expected.)

questions.t: Two questions about chords and the angles they subtend at the centre.
p: In a circle with centre <var>O</var>, the chords <var>AB</var> and <var>CD</var> have equal length, and ∠<var>AOB</var> = 78°. Find ∠<var>COD</var>, giving a reason.

In a circle with centre <var>O</var> and radius 10 cm, the chord <var>PQ</var> subtends an angle of 120° at <var>O</var>. Let <var>M</var> be the midpoint of <var>PQ</var>. Find <var>OM</var>, and find the exact length of <var>PQ</var> as a surd.
ap: ∠COD = 78°, because chords of equal length subtend equal angles at the centre of a circle.

OM joins the centre to the midpoint of the chord, so OM ⊥ PQ and OM bisects ∠POQ; hence ∠POM = 60° and ∠OMP = 90°. Then OM = 10 cos 60° = 5 cm, and PM = 10 sin 60° = 5√3 cm, so PQ = 2 × 5√3 = 10√3 cm (≈ 17.32 cm).

questions.t: A chord <var>AB</var> of a circle with centre <var>O</var> has length 24 cm, and the radius of the circle is 13 cm. Let <var>M</var> be the midpoint of <var>AB</var>.
p: State why ∠<var>OMA</var> = 90°.
Find <var>OM</var>.
Find ∠<var>AOB</var>, correct to one decimal place.
ap: The interval joining the midpoint of a chord to the centre of a circle is perpendicular to the chord, so ∠OMA = 90°.
AM = ½ × 24 = 12 cm, so by Pythagoras' theorem OM² = 13² − 12² = 169 − 144 = 25, giving OM = 5 cm.
In right-angled △OMA, sin ∠AOM = 12/13, so ∠AOM ≈ 67.380°. OM also bisects ∠AOB, so ∠AOB = 2∠AOM ≈ 134.8°.

questions.t: <var>T</var> is a point on a circle with centre <var>O</var> and radius 9 cm. The line <var>PT</var> is the tangent to the circle at <var>T</var>, and <var>PT</var> = 12 cm. The interval <var>OP</var> crosses the circle at <var>M</var>.
p: State the size of ∠<var>OTP</var>, giving a reason.
Find <var>OP</var>.
Find <var>MP</var>.
ap: ∠OTP = 90°, because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.
Pythagoras' theorem in △OTP: OP² = 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225, so OP = 15 cm.
M lies on OP with OM = 9 cm (a radius), so MP = 15 − 9 = 6 cm.

questions.t: <var>S</var> and <var>T</var> are points on a circle with centre <var>O</var>. The lines <var>PS</var> and <var>PT</var> are the two tangents to the circle from an external point <var>P</var>, touching the circle at <var>S</var> and <var>T</var> respectively. It is given that ∠<var>SPT</var> = 46°.
p: Explain why <var>PS</var> = <var>PT</var>.
Find ∠<var>PST</var>.
Find ∠<var>SOT</var>.
ap: The two tangents to a circle from a point outside the circle have equal length, so PS = PT.
△PST is isosceles with PS = PT, so ∠PST = ∠PTS = (180° − 46°) ÷ 2 = 67° (base angles of an isosceles triangle, angle sum of a triangle).
In quadrilateral OSPT, ∠OSP = ∠OTP = 90° (tangent perpendicular to radius), so ∠SOT = 360° − 90° − 90° − 46° = 134°.

questions.t: In △<var>PQR</var>, ∠<var>PQR</var> = 90°, <var>PQ</var> = 16 cm and <var>QR</var> = 30 cm. Let <var>M</var> be the midpoint of <var>PR</var>.
p: Explain why <var>Q</var> lies on the circle with diameter <var>PR</var>.
Find the radius of the circumcircle of △<var>PQR</var>, and hence find the length <var>MQ</var>.
ap: The interval PR subtends a right angle at Q, so by the converse of Thales' theorem Q lies on the circle with diameter PR.

Pythagoras' theorem: PR² = 16² + 30² = 256 + 900 = 1156, so PR = 34 cm. The circle with diameter PR passes through P, Q and R, so it is the circumcircle of △PQR and its radius is ½ × 34 = 17 cm. M is the midpoint of the diameter, so M is the centre, and MQ is a radius: MQ = 17 cm.

questions.t: <var>A</var>, <var>B</var> and <var>C</var> are points on a circle. The line <var>XAY</var> is the tangent to the circle at <var>A</var>, with <var>A</var> between <var>X</var> and <var>Y</var>. The chord <var>AB</var> has <var>X</var> and <var>C</var> on opposite sides of it, and the chord <var>AC</var> has <var>Y</var> and <var>B</var> on opposite sides of it. It is given that ∠<var>XAB</var> = 58° and ∠<var>ABC</var> = 74°.
p: Find ∠<var>ACB</var>, giving a reason.
Find ∠<var>BAC</var>.
Find ∠<var>YAC</var>, giving a reason.
ap: ∠XAB is the angle between the tangent XAY and the chord AB, and C lies in the alternate segment (on the other side of AB from X). By the alternate segment theorem ∠ACB = ∠XAB = 58°.
Angle sum of △ABC: ∠BAC = 180° − 74° − 58° = 48°.

∠YAC is the angle between the tangent and the chord AC, and B lies in the alternate segment for it (on the other side of AC from Y). By the alternate segment theorem ∠YAC = ∠ABC = 74°. (Check with the straight angle at A: 58° + 48° + 74° = 180°.)

questions.t: Two questions about chords meeting inside a circle.
p: Chords <var>AB</var> and <var>CD</var> of a circle meet at a point <var>M</var> inside the circle. Given <var>AM</var> = 6 cm, <var>MB</var> = 10 cm and <var>CM</var> = 4 cm, find <var>MD</var>.

Chords <var>PQ</var> and <var>RS</var> of a circle meet at a point <var>N</var> inside the circle. Given <var>PN</var> = 4 cm, <var>NQ</var> = 9 cm and <var>RS</var> = 15 cm, with <var>RN</var> < <var>NS</var>, find <var>RN</var> and <var>NS</var>.
ap: Intersecting chords: AM × MB = CM × MD, so 6 × 10 = 4 × MD, giving MD = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 cm.
Intersecting chords: RN × NS = PN × NQ = 4 × 9 = 36. Also RN + NS = RS = 15. So RN and NS are the roots of t² − 15t + 36 = 0, that is (t − 3)(t − 12) = 0. Since RN < NS, RN = 3 cm and NS = 12 cm.

questions.t: Two questions about lines drawn to a circle from a point outside it.
p: From a point <var>M</var> outside a circle, a line meets the circle at <var>B</var> and then at <var>A</var>, so that <var>M</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>A</var> lie in that order, with <var>MB</var> = 5 cm and <var>BA</var> = 11 cm. A second line from <var>M</var> is a tangent to the circle, touching it at <var>T</var>. Find the exact length of <var>MT</var>.

From a point <var>N</var> outside a circle, one line meets the circle at <var>P</var> and then at <var>Q</var>, with <var>N</var>, <var>P</var>, <var>Q</var> in that order, <var>NP</var> = 6 cm and <var>PQ</var> = 10 cm. A second line from <var>N</var> meets the circle at <var>R</var> and then at <var>S</var>, with <var>N</var>, <var>R</var>, <var>S</var> in that order and <var>NR</var> = 4 cm. Find <var>RS</var>.
ap: MA = MB + BA = 5 + 11 = 16 cm. Tangent and secant from an external point: MT² = MB × MA = 5 × 16 = 80, so MT = √80 = 4√5 cm (≈ 8.94 cm).
NQ = NP + PQ = 6 + 10 = 16 cm. Two secants from an external point: NR × NS = NP × NQ = 6 × 16 = 96, so NS = 96 ÷ 4 = 24 cm, and RS = NS − NR = 24 − 4 = 20 cm.

questions.t: <var>ABCD</var> is a cyclic quadrilateral with its vertices in that order around a circle, and <var>AD</var> ∥ <var>BC</var>. Prove that <var>AB</var> = <var>DC</var>.
questions.a: Join the diagonal BD. Since AD ∥ BC with transversal BD, ∠ADB = ∠DBC (alternate angles). Now ∠ADB is an angle at the circumference standing on the arc AB that does not contain D, so the angle subtended at the centre by the chord AB equals 2∠ADB (the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc). In the same way ∠DBC is an angle at the circumference standing on the arc DC that does not contain B, so the angle subtended at the centre by the chord DC equals 2∠DBC. Since ∠ADB = ∠DBC, these two angles at the centre are equal, and chords that subtend equal angles at the centre of a circle have equal length. Therefore AB = DC.

questions.t: <var>ABCD</var> is a cyclic quadrilateral with its vertices in that order around a circle. The diagonals <var>AC</var> and <var>BD</var> meet at <var>P</var>.
p: Prove that △<var>APD</var> is similar to △<var>BPC</var>.
Hence prove that <var>AP</var> × <var>PC</var> = <var>BP</var> × <var>PD</var>.
ap: Because A, B, C, D lie in that order on the circle, the diagonals AC and BD meet at a point P inside the circle, with P on AC between A and C, and on BD between B and D. Now ∠PAD = ∠CAD and ∠PBC = ∠DBC are both angles at the circumference standing on the arc CD that contains neither A nor B, so ∠PAD = ∠PBC. Also ∠APD = ∠BPC (vertically opposite angles). Two pairs of angles are equal, so the third pair is equal too, and therefore △APD ⦀ △BPC (AAA).

Matching sides of similar triangles are in the same ratio, and AP in △APD matches BP in △BPC, while PD matches PC. Hence AP ÷ BP = PD ÷ PC, and cross-multiplying gives AP × PC = BP × PD. (This is the intersecting chords theorem.)

questions.t: △<var>ABC</var> is inscribed in a circle with centre <var>O</var> and radius <var>R</var>, and ∠<var>BAC</var> is acute. Let <var>BP</var> be the diameter of the circle through <var>B</var>, so that <var>B</var>, <var>O</var> and <var>P</var> lie in that order on a line and <var>P</var> is on the circle. Assume that <var>A</var> and <var>P</var> lie on the same one of the two arcs cut off by the chord <var>BC</var>. Write <var>a</var> = <var>BC</var>.
p: Explain why ∠<var>BCP</var> = 90°, and why ∠<var>BPC</var> = ∠<var>BAC</var>.
Hence prove that <var>a</var> = 2<var>R</var> sin ∠<var>BAC</var>; that is, <var>a</var> ÷ sin ∠<var>BAC</var> = 2<var>R</var>.
ap: BP is a diameter and C is a point of the circle other than B or P (it cannot be P, since if BC were a diameter then ∠BAC would be 90°, not acute). So ∠BCP is an angle in a semicircle, and ∠BCP = 90° by Thales' theorem. Next, ∠BPC and ∠BAC are angles at the circumference standing on the same arc — the arc BC that contains neither A nor P, since A and P are on the same arc — so ∠BPC = ∠BAC (angles at the circumference subtended by the same arc are equal).
In △BPC, right-angled at C, the hypotenuse is BP = 2R, so sin ∠BPC = BC ÷ BP = a ÷ (2R). Since ∠BPC = ∠BAC, sin ∠BAC = a ÷ (2R), that is a = 2R sin ∠BAC, or equivalently a ÷ sin ∠BAC = 2R.

questions.t: The intervals <var>AB</var> and <var>CD</var> are not along the same line, and they intersect at a point <var>M</var> that lies strictly between <var>A</var> and <var>B</var> and strictly between <var>C</var> and <var>D</var>. It is given that <var>AM</var> × <var>MB</var> = <var>CM</var> × <var>MD</var>. Draw the circle through <var>A</var>, <var>B</var> and <var>C</var>, and let the line <var>CD</var> meet this circle again at <var>P</var>.
p: Explain why <var>M</var> lies inside this circle, and why <var>M</var> lies between <var>C</var> and <var>P</var>.
Prove that <var>MP</var> = <var>MD</var>, and hence that <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var> and <var>D</var> are concyclic.
questions.al: First note A, B and C are not collinear (C is not on the line AB, because the intervals AB and CD are not along the same line and they meet only at M, which is strictly inside CD), so the circle through A, B and C exists.
ap: A and B are on the circle, so AB is a chord of it, and M lies strictly between A and B, so M is an interior point of the circle. A line through an interior point of a circle meets the circle at exactly two points, one on each side of that point. The line CD meets the circle at C and P, so M lies between C and P.

AB and CP are two chords of the circle meeting at the interior point M, so by the intersecting chords theorem CM × MP = AM × MB. We are given AM × MB = CM × MD, so CM × MP = CM × MD, and since CM ≠ 0 we get MP = MD. Now P lies on the ray from M opposite to the ray MC (part a), and D also lies on that same ray, because M is between C and D. Two points on the same ray from M at the same distance from M must coincide, so P = D. Since P lies on the circle through A, B and C, so does D. Hence A, B, C and D all lie on one circle, that is, they are concyclic.

questions.t: Two circles touch each other externally at <var>P</var>. The line <var>AB</var> is a common tangent, touching the first circle at <var>A</var> and the second circle at <var>B</var>. The common tangent to both circles at <var>P</var> meets the interval <var>AB</var> at <var>C</var>.
p: Prove that <var>CA</var> = <var>CP</var> = <var>CB</var>, and hence that <var>C</var> is the midpoint of <var>AB</var>.
Hence prove that ∠<var>APB</var> = 90°.
ap: C is a point outside the first circle, and CA and CP are both tangents to the first circle from C (CA lies along the common tangent AB, touching at A; CP lies along the tangent at P). The tangents to a circle from an external point have equal length, so CA = CP. In the same way CB and CP are both tangents to the second circle from C, so CB = CP. Hence CA = CP = CB. Since C lies on the interval AB with CA = CB, C is the midpoint of AB.

Since CA = CP, △CAP is isosceles, so ∠CAP = ∠CPA; call this α. Since CB = CP, △CBP is isosceles, so ∠CBP = ∠CPB; call this β. As C lies between A and B, ∠APB = ∠APC + ∠CPB = α + β. Adding the interior angles of △ABP: α + (α + β) + β = 180°, so 2α + 2β = 180° and α + β = 90°. Therefore ∠APB = 90°. (Equivalently: CA = CB = CP means P lies on the circle with centre C and radius ½AB, that is, the circle with diameter AB, so ∠APB = 90° by Thales' theorem.)

questions.t: <var>PQRS</var> is a cyclic quadrilateral with its vertices in that order around a circle. The diagonal <var>PR</var> bisects both ∠<var>SPQ</var> and ∠<var>SRQ</var>. Prove that ∠<var>PQR</var> = 90°.
questions.a: Let ∠SPR = ∠RPQ = α, since PR bisects ∠SPQ, and let ∠SRP = ∠PRQ = β, since PR bisects ∠SRQ. In △PQR the angle sum gives ∠PQR = 180° − ∠RPQ − ∠PRQ = 180° − α − β. In △PSR the angle sum gives ∠PSR = 180° − ∠SPR − ∠SRP = 180° − α − β. Hence ∠PQR = ∠PSR. But ∠PQR and ∠PSR are opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral PQRS, so ∠PQR + ∠PSR = 180°. Substituting, 2∠PQR = 180°, so ∠PQR = 90°.

questions.t: The incircle of △<var>ABC</var> has centre <var>I</var> and radius <var>r</var>. It touches <var>BC</var> at <var>P</var>, touches <var>CA</var> at <var>Q</var> and touches <var>AB</var> at <var>R</var>.
p: By joining <var>IA</var>, <var>IB</var>, <var>IC</var> and the radii <var>IP</var>, <var>IQ</var> and <var>IR</var>, prove that the area of △<var>ABC</var> = ½ × (<var>AB</var> + <var>BC</var> + <var>CA</var>) × <var>r</var>.
△<var>DEF</var> has <var>DE</var> = 6 cm, <var>EF</var> = 8 cm and <var>FD</var> = 10 cm. Find the radius of its incircle.
ap: Each side of the triangle is a tangent to the incircle, and IP, IQ, IR are the radii drawn to the points of contact, so IP ⊥ BC, IQ ⊥ CA and IR ⊥ AB, and IP = IQ = IR = r. The intervals IA, IB and IC cut △ABC into the three triangles IBC, ICA and IAB, which do not overlap and together make up △ABC (I is inside the triangle). Taking BC, CA, AB as the bases, the corresponding heights are IP, IQ, IR, each equal to r. Hence area △ABC = ½ × BC × r + ½ × CA × r + ½ × AB × r = ½ × (AB + BC + CA) × r.

Since 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², the converse of Pythagoras' theorem gives ∠DEF = 90°, so the area of △DEF = ½ × 6 × 8 = 24 cm². The perimeter is 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 cm. By part a, 24 = ½ × 24 × r, so r = 2 cm.

questions.t: <var>A</var> and <var>B</var> are two fixed points with <var>AB</var> = 7 cm, and <var>M</var> is a point on the line <var>AB</var> with <var>B</var> between <var>A</var> and <var>M</var>. A circle is drawn through <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>, and <var>MT</var> is a tangent from <var>M</var> to that circle, touching it at <var>T</var>. It is given that <var>MT</var> = 12 cm.
p: Find <var>MB</var>.

A second, different circle is also drawn through <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>, and <var>MU</var> is a tangent from <var>M</var> to this second circle, touching it at <var>U</var>. Explain why <var>MU</var> = 12 cm as well.
ap: Let <var>MB</var> = x cm. Since B lies between A and M, MA = x + 7. The line MBA is a secant and MT is a tangent, so by the tangent and secant theorem MT² = MB × MA: 144 = x(x + 7), so x² + 7x − 144 = 0, that is (x − 9)(x + 16) = 0. As x > 0, MB = 9 cm. (Check: MA = 16 and 9 × 16 = 144 = 12².)

The line through M, B and A is a secant of the second circle as well, cutting it at B and A, and MU is a tangent to it. So by the same theorem MU² = MB × MA = 9 × 16 = 144, giving MU = 12 cm. (In general, any tangent drawn from M to any circle through A and B has length √(MB × MA), so all such tangents are equal.)

questions.t: Calculate each logarithm.
p: log<sub>2</sub>64
log<sub>5</sub>625
log<sub>10</sub>0.001
log4(116)
ap: 64 = 2<sup>6</sup>, so log<sub>2</sub>64 = 6
625 = 5<sup>4</sup>, so log<sub>5</sub>625 = 4
116 = 4−2, so log4(116) = −2

questions.t: Evaluate each logarithm. Each answer is a fraction.
p: log<sub>2</sub>(16√2)
log<sub>3</sub>(3√3)
log10(1100√10)
log<sub>4</sub>8
ap: 16√2 = 24 × 21/2 = 29/2, so log2(16√2) = 92
3√3 = 31 × 31/2 = 33/2, so log3(3√3) = 32
100√10 = 102 × 101/2 = 105/2, so 1100√10 = 10−5/2 and the logarithm is −52
Let x = log48. Then 4x = 8, so 22x = 23, giving 2x = 3 and x = 32

questions.t: Solve each equation for <var>x</var>.
p: log<sub>3</sub><var>x</var> = 4
log<sub><var>x</var></sub>49 = 2
log<sub>2</sub>(<var>x</var> − 5) = 4
logx(181) = −4
ap: <var>x</var> = 3<sup>4</sup> = 81
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 49, so <var>x</var> = 7 (since <var>x</var> > 0)
<var>x</var> − 5 = 2<sup>4</sup> = 16, so <var>x</var> = 21
x−4 = 181, so x4 = 81 and x = 3 (since x > 0)

questions.t: Simplify each expression, giving your answer as a single number.
p: log<sub>3</sub>45 − log<sub>3</sub>5
log<sub>5</sub>1000 − log<sub>5</sub>8
log<sub>7</sub>2 + log<sub>7</sub>98 − log<sub>7</sub>4
ap: log3(455) = log39 = 2
log5(10008) = log5125 = 3
log7(2 × 984) = log749 = 2

questions.t: Given that log<sub>10</sub>2 = α, log<sub>10</sub>3 = β and log<sub>10</sub>7 = γ, express each logarithm below in terms of α, β and γ. You may also use log<sub>10</sub>10 = 1.
p: log<sub>10</sub>18
log<sub>10</sub>28
log<sub>10</sub>5
log10(356)
ap: 18 = 2 × 3<sup>2</sup>, so log<sub>10</sub>18 = log<sub>10</sub>2 + 2log<sub>10</sub>3 = α + 2β
28 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 7, so log<sub>10</sub>28 = 2α + γ
5 = 102, so log105 = log1010 − log102 = 1 − α
56 = 23 × 7, so log10(356) = log103 − (3log102 + log107) = β − 3α − γ

questions.t: By changing to a suitable base, find the exact value of each logarithm.
p: log<sub>8</sub>32
log<sub>27</sub>81
log125(15)
ap: log832 = log232log28 = 53. Check: 85/3 = (23)5/3 = 25 = 32.
log2781 = log381log327 = 43. Check: 274/3 = 34 = 81.
log125(15) = log5(1/5)log5125 = −13 = −13. Check: 125−1/3 = 15.

questions.t: Use base 10 logarithms for each part, and give each answer correct to four decimal places.
p: Calculate log<sub>6</sub>15.
Solve 5<sup><var>x</var></sup> = 40 for <var>x</var>.
Solve 2<sup>−<var>x</var></sup> = 9 for <var>x</var>.
ap: log615 = log1015log106 = 1.176091…0.778151… ≈ 1.5114
x = log540 = log1040log105 = 1.602060…0.698970… ≈ 2.2920
−x = log29 = log109log102 = 0.954243…0.301030… ≈ 3.1699, so x ≈ −3.1699

questions.t: Consider the function <var>y</var> = log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var> − 4).
p: State the values of <var>x</var> for which the function is defined.
Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote of its graph.
Find the coordinates of the point where the graph cuts the <var>x</var>-axis.
Find the value of <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> = 85.
The graph of <var>y</var> = log<sub>3</sub><var>x</var> is the reflection of the graph of <var>y</var> = 3<sup><var>x</var></sup> in a straight line. State the equation of that line.
ap: <var>x</var> − 4 > 0, so <var>x</var> > 4
<var>x</var> = 4
log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var> − 4) = 0 gives <var>x</var> − 4 = 3<sup>0</sup> = 1, so <var>x</var> = 5; the point is (5, 0)
<var>y</var> = log<sub>3</sub>(85 − 4) = log<sub>3</sub>81 = 4
<var>y</var> = <var>x</var>

questions.t: Use the logarithm laws in each part.
p: Express 4 + log<sub>3</sub>7 as a single logarithm to base 3.
Express 3 − log<sub>2</sub>5 as a single logarithm to base 2.
Given that log<sub>10</sub><var>y</var> = 2 + 3log<sub>10</sub><var>x</var>, find a relation between <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> that does not involve logarithms.
Given that 2log<sub>5</sub><var>x</var> + log<sub>5</sub><var>y</var> = 3, find a relation between <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> that does not involve logarithms.
ap: 4 = log<sub>3</sub>3<sup>4</sup> = log<sub>3</sub>81, so 4 + log<sub>3</sub>7 = log<sub>3</sub>81 + log<sub>3</sub>7 = log<sub>3</sub>(81 × 7) = log<sub>3</sub>567
3 = log28, so 3 − log25 = log28 − log25 = log2(85)
2 + 3log<sub>10</sub><var>x</var> = log<sub>10</sub>100 + log<sub>10</sub><var>x</var><sup>3</sup> = log<sub>10</sub>(100<var>x</var><sup>3</sup>), so <var>y</var> = 100<var>x</var><sup>3</sup>
2log<sub>5</sub><var>x</var> + log<sub>5</sub><var>y</var> = log<sub>5</sub>(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup><var>y</var>) = 3, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup><var>y</var> = 5<sup>3</sup> = 125

questions.t: A bacterial culture initially has a mass of 5 grams and its mass triples every day. Let <var>M</var> grams be the mass of the culture after <var>t</var> days.
p: Write down a formula for <var>M</var> in terms of <var>t</var>.
Find the mass of the culture after 4 days.
Find how long it takes for the mass to reach 1000 grams, correct to three significant figures.
ap: <var>M</var> = 5 × 3<sup><var>t</var></sup>
<var>M</var> = 5 × 3<sup>4</sup> = 5 × 81 = 405 grams
5 × 3t = 1000, so 3t = 200. Taking base 10 logarithms, tlog103 = log10200, so t = 2.301030…0.477121… ≈ 4.8227. The mass reaches 1000 grams after about 4.82 days.

questions.t: The mass <var>M</var> grams of a radioactive substance after <var>t</var> years is given by <var>M</var> = <var>M</var><sub>0</sub> × 10<sup>−<var>kt</var></sup>, where <var>k</var> is a positive constant. The mass is 40 grams when <var>t</var> = 0, and 30 years later the mass is 34 grams.
p: State the value of <var>M</var><sub>0</sub>.
Find <var>k</var>, correct to four significant figures.
Find the half-life of the substance, correct to the nearest year.
ap: <var>M</var><sub>0</sub> = 40 (the mass when <var>t</var> = 0)
When t = 30, 34 = 40 × 10−30k, so 10−30k = 3440 = 0.85. Hence −30k = log100.85 = −0.0705811…, so k = 0.0705811…30 = 0.00235270…, that is k ≈ 0.002353
Half-life: 12 = 10−kt, so −kt = log10(12) = −log102 and t = log102k = 0.301030…0.0023527… ≈ 127.95. The half-life is about 128 years.

questions.t: $40 000 is invested on 1 January at a compound interest rate of 6% per annum. Interest is paid only on 1 January of each year, so the value after <var>n</var> whole years is 40 000(1.06)<sup><var>n</var></sup>.
p: Show that the number of years <var>n</var> for which the investment is worth exactly $70 000 satisfies (1.06)<sup><var>n</var></sup> = 1.75.
At the end of how many whole years will the investment first be worth more than $70 000? State the value of the investment at that time, correct to the nearest cent.
ap: Using An = P(1 + R)n with P = 40 000 and R = 0.06: 40 000(1.06)n = 70 000, so (1.06)n = 70 00040 000 = 1.75.

Taking base 10 logarithms, nlog101.06 = log101.75, so n = 0.243038…0.025306… ≈ 9.604. Checking whole years: after 9 years the value is 40 000 × 1.069 = $67 579.16, which is less than $70 000; after 10 years it is 40 000 × 1.0610 = $71 633.91. So the investment is first worth more than $70 000 at the end of the 10th year, when it is worth $71 633.91.

questions.t: Simplify log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(<var>a</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>a</var><sup>2</sup>) − log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(<var>a</var> + 1), where <var>a</var> > 0 and <var>a</var> ≠ 1.
questions.a: Factorise: <var>a</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>a</var><sup>2</sup> = <var>a</var><sup>2</sup>(<var>a</var> + 1). So the expression equals log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(<var>a</var><sup>2</sup>(<var>a</var> + 1)) − log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(<var>a</var> + 1) = log<sub><var>a</var></sub><var>a</var><sup>2</sup> + log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(<var>a</var> + 1) − log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(<var>a</var> + 1) = log<sub><var>a</var></sub><var>a</var><sup>2</sup> = 2log<sub><var>a</var></sub><var>a</var> = 2.

questions.t: Solve each equation for <var>x</var>, giving exact answers.
p: log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var> + 2) − log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var> − 2) = 2
(log<sub>3</sub><var>x</var>)<sup>2</sup> = log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var><sup>4</sup>) − 3
(log<sub>2</sub><var>x</var>)(log<sub>2</sub>(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>)) − 3log<sub>2</sub><var>x</var> − 2 = 0
ap: log3(x + 2x − 2) = 2, so x + 2x − 2 = 32 = 9. Then x + 2 = 9x − 18, so 8x = 20 and x = 52. This is valid because x > 2; check: 4.50.5 = 9.

Let <var>u</var> = log<sub>3</sub><var>x</var>. Then log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var><sup>4</sup>) = 4<var>u</var>, so <var>u</var><sup>2</sup> = 4<var>u</var> − 3, giving <var>u</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>u</var> + 3 = 0 and (<var>u</var> − 1)(<var>u</var> − 3) = 0. So <var>u</var> = 1 or <var>u</var> = 3, giving <var>x</var> = 3 or <var>x</var> = 27. Check <var>x</var> = 27: (log<sub>3</sub>27)<sup>2</sup> = 9 and log<sub>3</sub>(27<sup>4</sup>) − 3 = 12 − 3 = 9.
Let u = log2x, so log2(x2) = 2u. The equation becomes 2u2 − 3u − 2 = 0, that is (2u + 1)(u − 2) = 0, so u = 2 or u = −12. Hence x = 22 = 4 or x = 2−1/2 = 1√2. Check x = 4: (2)(4) − 3(2) − 2 = 0.

questions.t: Solve each pair of simultaneous equations for <var>x</var> and <var>y</var>.
p: 4<sup><var>x</var></sup> × 8<sup><var>y</var></sup> = 2<sup>13</sup> and 27<sup><var>x</var></sup> = 9<sup><var>y</var></sup>
5<sup><var>x</var> + <var>y</var></sup> = 125 and 25<sup><var>x</var></sup> = 5<sup><var>y</var> + 3</sup>
ap: 4x × 8y = 22x × 23y = 22x + 3y, so 2x + 3y = 13. Also 27x = 33x and 9y = 32y, so 3x = 2y, giving x = 2y3. Substituting: 4y3 + 3y = 13, so 13y3 = 13, y = 3 and x = 2. Check: 42 × 83 = 16 × 512 = 8192 = 213, and 272 = 729 = 93.

5<sup><var>x</var> + <var>y</var></sup> = 5<sup>3</sup> gives <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 3. Also 25<sup><var>x</var></sup> = 5<sup>2<var>x</var></sup>, so 2<var>x</var> = <var>y</var> + 3, that is 2<var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 3. Adding the two equations: 3<var>x</var> = 6, so <var>x</var> = 2 and <var>y</var> = 1. Check: 5<sup>3</sup> = 125, and 25<sup>2</sup> = 625 = 5<sup>4</sup>.

questions.t: Let <var>b</var> = log<sub>3</sub>7.
p: Show that log2749 = 2b3.
Express log<sub>81</sub>7 in terms of <var>b</var>.
ap: Changing to base 3, log2749 = log349log327 = log372log333 = 2log373 = 2b3, as required.
log817 = log37log381 = b4, since log381 = 4.

questions.t: Suppose <var>a</var> is a positive constant with <var>a</var> ≠ 1, and <var>x</var> > 0. Given that 2log<sub><var>a</var></sub><var>x</var> = 1 + log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(9<var>x</var> − 20<var>a</var>), find <var>x</var> in terms of <var>a</var>.
questions.a: The left-hand side is 2log<sub><var>a</var></sub><var>x</var> = log<sub><var>a</var></sub><var>x</var><sup>2</sup>. The right-hand side is 1 + log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(9<var>x</var> − 20<var>a</var>) = log<sub><var>a</var></sub><var>a</var> + log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(9<var>x</var> − 20<var>a</var>) = log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(9<var>a</var><var>x</var> − 20<var>a</var><sup>2</sup>). Equating the arguments: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 9<var>a</var><var>x</var> − 20<var>a</var><sup>2</sup>, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 9<var>a</var><var>x</var> + 20<var>a</var><sup>2</sup> = 0, which factorises as (<var>x</var> − 4<var>a</var>)(<var>x</var> − 5<var>a</var>) = 0. Hence <var>x</var> = 4<var>a</var> or <var>x</var> = 5<var>a</var>. Both are acceptable: each is positive, and 9<var>x</var> − 20<var>a</var> equals 16<var>a</var> > 0 when <var>x</var> = 4<var>a</var> and 25<var>a</var> > 0 when <var>x</var> = 5<var>a</var>. Check <var>x</var> = 5<var>a</var>: left side = log<sub><var>a</var></sub>25<var>a</var><sup>2</sup>, right side = log<sub><var>a</var></sub>(<var>a</var> × 25<var>a</var>) = log<sub><var>a</var></sub>25<var>a</var><sup>2</sup>.

questions.t: Show that log<sub>10</sub>7 cannot be a rational number.
questions.a: Since 1 < 7 < 10, we have 0 < log107 < 1, so log107 is positive and not zero. Suppose, for a contradiction, that log107 is rational. Then log107 = pq for some positive integers p and q. Writing this in exponential form, 10p/q = 7, and raising both sides to the power q gives 10p = 7q. Now 10p = 2p × 5p, so the only prime factors of the left-hand side are 2 and 5, and since p ≥ 1 the number 2 really does occur. The only prime factor of the right-hand side is 7. Every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one prime factorisation, so 10p = 7q is impossible for positive integers p and q. This contradiction shows log107 cannot be rational.

questions.t: A bag contains 15 counters: 4 are red, 6 are blue, 2 are green and 3 are yellow. One counter is taken from the bag at random. Find the probability that the counter is:
p: blue
not green
red or yellow
questions.al: There are 15 equally likely outcomes.
ap: P(blue) = 615 = 25
P(green) = 215, so P(not green) = 1 − 215 = 1315
4 + 3 = 7 counters are red or yellow, so P(red or yellow) = 715

questions.t: A letter is chosen at random from the 11 letters of the word PROBABILITY. Find the probability that the letter chosen is:
p: a B
a vowel
not an I
questions.al: PROBABILITY has 11 letters, with B appearing twice and I appearing twice.
ap: P(B) = 211
The vowels are O, A, I, I — four letters. P(vowel) = 411
P(I) = 211, so P(not an I) = 1 − 211 = 911

questions.t: Two fair six-sided dice are thrown and the sum of the two uppermost numbers is recorded. There are 36 equally likely ordered pairs of face values. Find the probability that the sum is:
p: equal to 9
10 or more
a multiple of 4
ap: The pairs giving 9 are (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), (6, 3) — 4 pairs. P = 436 = 19
Number of pairs: sum 10 gives 3, sum 11 gives 2, sum 12 gives 1, a total of 6. P = 636 = 16
The multiples of 4 available are 4, 8 and 12, given by 3, 5 and 1 pairs respectively, a total of 9. P = 936 = 14

questions.t: An integer is chosen at random from the integers 1 to 60 inclusive. Find the probability that the integer chosen is:
p: divisible by 4
divisible by 6
divisible by both 4 and 6
divisible by 4 or by 6
ap: The multiples of 4 up to 60 are 4, 8, …, 60 — that is 15 numbers. P = 1560 = 14
The multiples of 6 up to 60 are 6, 12, …, 60 — that is 10 numbers. P = 1060 = 16
Divisible by both 4 and 6 means divisible by 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 — that is 5 numbers. P = 560 = 112
Using the addition rule, P = 14 + 16 − 112 = 312 + 212 − 112 = 412 = 13 (20 of the 60 integers)

questions.t: One card is drawn at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. In this question a court card means an Ace, King, Queen or Jack, so there are 16 court cards in the pack. Find the probability that the card drawn is:
p: a Diamond
a court card
a Diamond and a court card
a Diamond or a court card
ap: There are 13 Diamonds, so P = 1352 = 14
There are 16 court cards, so P = 1652 = 413
The Diamond court cards are the Ace, King, Queen and Jack of Diamonds — 4 cards. P = 452 = 113
Addition rule: P = 1352 + 1652 − 452 = 2552

questions.t: A survey of 180 commuters recorded how each person travels to work and where that person lives. Of the 90 commuters who live in the inner city, 20 travel by car, 45 travel by train and 25 travel by bicycle. Of the 90 commuters who live in the suburbs, 50 travel by car, 30 travel by train and 10 travel by bicycle. Every commuter uses exactly one of these three forms of transport. One of the 180 commuters is chosen at random. Find the probability that the person chosen:
p: travels by train
lives in the suburbs and travels by car
lives in the inner city or travels by bicycle
does not travel by bicycle
questions.al: Column totals: car 20 + 50 = 70, train 45 + 30 = 75, bicycle 25 + 10 = 35, and 70 + 75 + 35 = 180.
ap: P(train) = 75180 = 512
P(suburbs and car) = 50180 = 518
Inner city (90) plus the suburban cyclists (10) gives 100 people, so P = 100180 = 59. (Check with the addition rule: 90180 + 35180 − 25180 = 100180.)
180 − 35 = 145 commuters do not cycle, so P = 145180 = 2936

questions.t: In a group of 120 students, 68 play netball, 54 play hockey and 22 play both netball and hockey. One student is chosen at random from the group. Find the probability that the student chosen:
p: plays netball but not hockey
plays neither netball nor hockey
plays exactly one of the two sports
questions.al: Netball only = 68 − 22 = 46; hockey only = 54 − 22 = 32; both = 22; neither = 120 − (46 + 22 + 32) = 20.
ap: P = 46120 = 2360
P(netball or hockey) = 68 + 54 − 22120 = 100120, so P(neither) = 1 − 100120 = 20120 = 16
Exactly one sport: 46 + 32 = 78 students, so P = 78120 = 1320

questions.t: Answer each of the following conditional probability questions.
p: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Find the probability that the number rolled is greater than 3, given that the number rolled is even.
A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Find the probability that the number rolled is a multiple of 3, given that the number rolled is greater than 2.
Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability that both coins show tails, given that at least one coin shows tails.
ap: The condition restricts the sample space to {2, 4, 6}, of which 4 and 6 are greater than 3. P = 23
The condition restricts the sample space to {3, 4, 5, 6}, of which 3 and 6 are multiples of 3. P = 24 = 12
The sample space is {HH, HT, TH, TT}. 'At least one tail' is {HT, TH, TT}, three equally likely outcomes, and only TT has both tails. P = 13

questions.t: At a cinema, 240 people were asked which of two films they had seen and whether they bought popcorn. Of the 100 people who saw film A, 60 bought popcorn and 40 did not. Of the 140 people who saw film B, 56 bought popcorn and 84 did not. Every one of the 240 people saw exactly one of the two films. One of the 240 people is chosen at random.
