Let <var>A</var> be the event 'the person saw film A', let <var>B</var> be the event 'the person saw film B' and let <var>K</var> be the event 'the person bought popcorn'.
p: Find P(<var>K</var>).
Find P(<var>A</var> | <var>K</var>).
Find P(<var>K</var> | <var>B</var>).
Determine whether <var>A</var> and <var>K</var> are independent events, showing the test you use.
questions.al: Popcorn buyers: 60 + 56 = 116, so 240 − 116 = 124 did not buy popcorn.
ap: P(K) = 116240 = 2960
Of the 116 popcorn buyers, 60 saw film A, so P(A | K) = 60116 = 1529
Of the 140 people who saw film B, 56 bought popcorn, so P(K | B) = 56140 = 25

P(A ∩ K) = 60240 = 14. Also P(A) × P(K) = 100240 × 116240 = 512 × 2960 = 29144. Since 14 = 36144 ≠ 29144, P(A ∩ K) ≠ P(A) × P(K), so A and K are not independent. (Equivalently, P(A | K) = 1529 ≠ 512 = P(A).)

questions.t: At a large school, the probability that a randomly chosen student walks to school is 25 and the probability that a randomly chosen student plays a musical instrument is 38. Assume that these two events are independent. One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student:
p: walks to school and plays a musical instrument
neither walks to school nor plays a musical instrument
walks to school or plays a musical instrument
walks to school but does not play a musical instrument
questions.al: Let W be 'walks to school' and M be 'plays a musical instrument', with P(W) = 25 and P(M) = 38.
ap: P(W ∩ M) = 25 × 38 = 640 = 320
Independence carries over to complements: P = 35 × 58 = 1540 = 38
Addition rule: P(W ∪ M) = 25 + 38 − 320 = 1640 + 1540 − 640 = 2540 = 58. (Check: this is 1 − 38, the complement of part b.)
P = 25 × 58 = 1040 = 14

questions.t: A bag contains 8 counters: 5 are white and 3 are black. Answer each part for the sampling method stated in that part.
p: Two counters are taken one after the other with replacement (the first counter is returned to the bag and the bag shaken before the second is taken). Find the probability that both counters are white.
Two counters are taken one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that both counters are white.
Two counters are taken one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that one counter is white and the other is black.
Two counters are taken one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that at least one counter is black.
ap: With replacement the two draws are independent and P(white) = 58 each time, so P = 58 × 58 = 2564
Without replacement, P(second white | first white) = 47, so P = 58 × 47 = 2056 = 514
Two branches: white then black gives 58 × 37 = 1556, and black then white gives 38 × 57 = 1556. Total = 3056 = 1528
'At least one black' is the complement of 'both white', so P = 1 − 514 = 914

questions.t: A fair six-sided die is tossed three times and the uppermost number is recorded each time. Find the probability of obtaining:
p: a 5 on all three tosses
no 5 at all
at least one 5
an even number on each of the first two tosses and an odd number on the third toss
questions.al: The three tosses are independent, and each toss has 6 equally likely results.
ap: P = 16 × 16 × 16 = 1216
P(not a 5 on one toss) = 56, so P = (56)3 = 125216
P(at least one 5) = 1 − 125216 = 91216
P(even) = 36 = 12 and P(odd) = 12, so P = 12 × 12 × 12 = 18

questions.t: Box X contains 8 marbles, of which 3 are red and 5 are yellow. Box Y also contains 8 marbles, of which 6 are red and 2 are yellow. A fair coin is tossed once. If the coin shows heads, one marble is taken at random from box X; if the coin shows tails, one marble is taken at random from box Y. Exactly one marble is taken.
p: Find the probability that the marble taken is red.
Given that the marble taken is red, find the probability that it came from box Y.
questions.al: P(heads) = P(tails) = 12. From box X, P(red) = 38; from box Y, P(red) = 68.
ap: P(red) = 12 × 38 + 12 × 68 = 316 + 616 = 916
P(box Y ∩ red) = 12 × 68 = 616. Hence P(box Y | red) = P(box Y ∩ red)P(red) = 616 ÷ 916 = 69 = 23

questions.t: A debating squad of 5 students is to be chosen from a group of 11 students consisting of 7 girls and 4 boys. All 11 students are distinguishable and the order in which the squad members are chosen does not matter.
p: Find the total number of different squads that can be chosen if there is no restriction.
Find the number of squads that contain exactly 3 girls and exactly 2 boys.
Find the number of squads that contain at least 3 girls.
A squad of 5 is now chosen at random from the 11 students, every possible squad being equally likely. Find the probability that the squad contains at least 3 girls.
ap: Choosing 5 from 11: 11 × 10 × 9 × 8 × 75 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 462 squads.
Choose 3 girls from 7 in 7 × 6 × 53 × 2 × 1 = 35 ways and 2 boys from 4 in 4 × 32 × 1 = 6 ways, giving 35 × 6 = 210 squads.

'At least 3 girls' means 3, 4 or 5 girls.
3 girls, 2 boys: 35 × 6 = 210
4 girls, 1 boy: 35 × 4 = 140 (choosing 4 from 7 gives 35)
5 girls, 0 boys: 21 × 1 = 21 (choosing 5 from 7 gives 21)
Total = 210 + 140 + 21 = 371 squads.
P = 371462. Both 371 = 7 × 53 and 462 = 7 × 66 are divisible by 7, so P = 5366

questions.t: A crate contains 40 oranges. Of these, 24 are large and 16 are small. Of the 24 large oranges, 6 are bruised and 18 are not. Of the 16 small oranges, 2 are bruised and 14 are not. Two oranges are taken from the crate at random, one after the other, without replacement.
p: Find the probability that both oranges are large and at least one of them is bruised.
Find the probability that at least one orange is bruised, given that both oranges are large.
Find the probability that both oranges are large, given that at least one of them is large.
questions.al:
Work with unordered pairs. The number of ways to choose 2 oranges from 40 is 40 × 392 = 780.
Both large: 24 × 232 = 276 pairs. Both large and unbruised: 18 × 172 = 153 pairs.
ap: Both large with at least one bruised = 276 − 153 = 123 pairs, so P = 123780 = 41260
P(at least one bruised | both large) = 123276 = 4192. (Equivalently 41260 ÷ 2365 = 4192, since P(both large) = 276780 = 2365.)
Both small: 16 × 152 = 120 pairs, so 'at least one large' has 780 − 120 = 660 pairs. P(both large | at least one large) = 276660 = 2355

questions.t: Four-digit numbers are formed using only the digits 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8.
p: How many such four-digit numbers can be formed if a digit may be used more than once?
How many such four-digit numbers can be formed if no digit may be used more than once?
One of the numbers counted in part a is chosen at random, all of them being equally likely. Find the probability that it contains at least one 7.
One of the numbers counted in part a is chosen at random, all of them being equally likely. Find the probability that it is even and contains at least one 7.
ap: Each of the 4 places can be filled in 5 ways, so 5<sup>4</sup> = 625 numbers.
Numbers with no 7 use only the 4 digits 2, 3, 5, 8, giving 44 = 256 numbers. So P(at least one 7) = 1 − 256625 = 369625

The number is even exactly when its last digit is 2 or 8, so there are 2 × 53 = 250 even numbers. Even numbers containing no 7 have last digit 2 or 8 and the first three digits from {2, 3, 5, 8}: 2 × 43 = 128. So the count of even numbers containing at least one 7 is 250 − 128 = 122, and P = 122625

questions.t: Three identical closed bags each contain two tokens. Bag 1 contains two green tokens. Bag 2 contains two white tokens. Bag 3 contains one green token and one white token. A bag is chosen at random and one token is taken at random from that bag. The token taken is green. Find the probability that the other token still in that bag is also green. Justify your answer.
questions.a:
23.
Method 1 (equally likely tokens): there are 3 × 2 = 6 equally likely (bag, token) choices. Exactly 3 of them produce a green token: the two green tokens of bag 1 and the green token of bag 3. Of those 3 green outcomes, 2 come from bag 1, where the remaining token is green. Hence the required probability is 23.
Method 2 (conditional probability): P(green) = 13 × 1 + 13 × 0 + 13 × 12 = 12, and P(bag 1 ∩ green) = 13 × 1 = 13. So P(bag 1 | green) = 13 ÷ 12 = 23. The other token is green precisely when the bag is bag 1, so the answer is 23.
Note that the answer is not 12: a green token is twice as likely to have come from bag 1 as from bag 3.

questions.t: In a raffle, n tickets are sold, where n ≥ 5. Three different winning tickets are drawn at random from the n tickets, without replacement, and each winning ticket receives one prize. Ravi holds 2 of the n tickets.
p: Show that the probability that Ravi wins no prize is (n − 3)(n − 4)n(n − 1).
Hence show that the probability that Ravi wins at least one prize is 6(n − 2)n(n − 1).
Find this probability when <var>n</var> = 500, giving your answer as an exact fraction in simplest form and also correct to four decimal places.
ap:
Only which 3 tickets are drawn matters. The number of ways of choosing the 3 winning tickets from n is n(n − 1)(n − 2)6. Ravi wins no prize exactly when all 3 winners come from the other n − 2 tickets, which can happen in (n − 2)(n − 3)(n − 4)6 ways. Hence
P(no prize) = (n − 2)(n − 3)(n − 4)n(n − 1)(n − 2) = (n − 3)(n − 4)n(n − 1), cancelling the factor n − 2.
(Equivalently, drawing one at a time: n − 2n × n − 3n − 1 × n − 4n − 2, which gives the same product.)
P(at least one prize) = 1 − (n − 3)(n − 4)n(n − 1) = n2 − n − (n2 − 7n + 12)n(n − 1) = 6n − 12n(n − 1) = 6(n − 2)n(n − 1)
With n = 500: 6 × 498500 × 499 = 2988249500 = 74762375 ≈ 0.0120 (0.011976 to six decimal places, so 0.0120 to four decimal places).

questions.t: <var>A</var> and <var>B</var> are mutually exclusive events with P(<var>A</var>) + P(<var>B</var>) > 0.
p: Show that P(B | A ∪ B) = P(B)P(A) + P(B).
Hence find P(<var>B</var> | <var>A</var> ∪ <var>B</var>) when P(<var>A</var>) = 0.15 and P(<var>B</var>) = 0.25.
ap:
By the definition of conditional probability,
P(B | A ∪ B) = P(B ∩ (A ∪ B))P(A ∪ B).
Every outcome of B is an outcome of A ∪ B, so B ∩ (A ∪ B) = B and the numerator is P(B).
Since A and B are mutually exclusive, A ∩ B = ∅, so the addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − 0 = P(A) + P(B), which is non-zero by assumption.
∴ P(B | A ∪ B) = P(B)P(A) + P(B)
P(B | A ∪ B) = 0.250.15 + 0.25 = 0.250.40 = 58

questions.t:
Throughout this paper k denotes the constant of proportionality and every variable takes only positive values.
Write each statement in symbols, giving both the ∝ statement and the equation involving k.
p: <var>P</var> is directly proportional to the cube of <var>q</var>.
<var>w</var> is inversely proportional to the square root of <var>z</var>.
ap: <var>P</var> ∝ <var>q</var><sup>3</sup>, that is <var>P</var> = <var>kq</var><sup>3</sup>.
w ∝ 1√z, that is w = k√z.

questions.t: Given that <var>a</var> ∝ <var>b</var>, and that <var>a</var> = 20 when <var>b</var> = 8:
p: find the formula for <var>a</var> in terms of <var>b</var>
find <var>a</var> when <var>b</var> = 14
find <var>b</var> when <var>a</var> = 3
ap: <var>a</var> = <var>kb</var>, so 20 = 8<var>k</var> and <var>k</var> = 2.5. Hence <var>a</var> = 2.5<var>b</var>.
3 = 2.5<var>b</var>, so <var>b</var> = 1.2.

questions.t: <var>y</var> is directly proportional to the square of <var>x</var>, and <var>y</var> = 45 when <var>x</var> = 3.
p: Find the formula for <var>y</var> in terms of <var>x</var>.
Find <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> = 2.
Find <var>x</var> when <var>y</var> = 500.
ap: <var>y</var> = <var>kx</var><sup>2</sup>, so 45 = 9<var>k</var> and <var>k</var> = 5. Hence <var>y</var> = 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>.
<var>y</var> = 5 × 2<sup>2</sup> = 20.
500 = 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 100 and <var>x</var> = 10 (taking the positive value).

questions.t: <var>y</var> is inversely proportional to <var>x</var>, and <var>y</var> = 6 when <var>x</var> = 4.
p: Find the formula for <var>y</var> in terms of <var>x</var>.
Find <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> = 3.
Find <var>x</var> when <var>y</var> = ½.
ap: y = kx, so k = xy = 4 × 6 = 24 and y = 24x.
y = 243 = 8.
½ = 24x, so x = 48.

questions.t: <var>a</var> is inversely proportional to the square of <var>b</var>, and <var>a</var> = 9 when <var>b</var> = 2.
p: Find the formula for <var>a</var> in terms of <var>b</var>.
Find <var>a</var> when <var>b</var> = 6.
Find <var>b</var> when <var>a</var> = 4.
ap: a = kb2, so k = ab2 = 9 × 4 = 36 and a = 36b2.
a = 3636 = 1.
4 = 36b2, so b2 = 9 and b = 3 (positive).

questions.t: On a map, the actual distance <var>D</var> km between two places is directly proportional to the distance <var>x</var> cm between them on the map. A map distance of 1.5 cm represents an actual distance of 24 km.
p: Find the formula for <var>D</var> in terms of <var>x</var>.
Find the actual distance represented by a map distance of 7.5 cm.
Find the map distance that represents an actual distance of 100 km.
ap: <var>D</var> = <var>kx</var>, so 24 = 1.5<var>k</var> and <var>k</var> = 16. Hence <var>D</var> = 16<var>x</var>.
100 = 16<var>x</var>, so <var>x</var> = 6.25 cm.

questions.t: The mass, <var>w</var> grams, of a solid metal sphere is directly proportional to the cube of its radius, <var>r</var> cm. A sphere of radius 2 cm has mass 64 grams.
p: Find the formula for <var>w</var> in terms of <var>r</var>.
Find the mass of a sphere of radius 5 cm.
Find the radius of a sphere of mass 500 grams, correct to two decimal places.
ap: <var>w</var> = <var>kr</var><sup>3</sup>, so 64 = <var>k</var> × 2<sup>3</sup> = 8<var>k</var> and <var>k</var> = 8. Hence <var>w</var> = 8<var>r</var><sup>3</sup>.
<var>w</var> = 8 × 5<sup>3</sup> = 8 × 125 = 1000 grams.

500 = 8<var>r</var><sup>3</sup>, so <var>r</var><sup>3</sup> = 62.5 and <var>r</var> is the cube root of 62.5, giving <var>r</var> ≈ 3.97 cm (3.9685 correct to four decimal places). Check: 3.9685<sup>3</sup> ≈ 62.50.

questions.t: The period, <var>T</var> seconds, of a pendulum is directly proportional to the square root of its length, <var>L</var> cm. A pendulum of length 64 cm has a period of 1.6 seconds.
p: Find the formula for <var>T</var> in terms of <var>L</var>.
Find the period of a pendulum of length 100 cm.
Find the length of a pendulum whose period is 2.4 seconds.
ap: <var>T</var> = <var>k</var>√<var>L</var>, so 1.6 = <var>k</var> × √64 = 8<var>k</var> and <var>k</var> = 0.2. Hence <var>T</var> = 0.2√<var>L</var>.
2.4 = 0.2√<var>L</var>, so √<var>L</var> = 12 and <var>L</var> = 144 cm.

questions.t: <var>y</var> is directly proportional to the cube of <var>x</var>. Find the effect on:
p: <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> is increased by 20%
<var>x</var> when <var>y</var> is multiplied by 8
questions.al: Write <var>y</var> = <var>kx</var><sup>3</sup>.
ap: Take <var>x</var> = 1, so <var>y</var> = <var>k</var>. Increasing <var>x</var> by 20% gives <var>x</var> = 1.2, so the new <var>y</var> = 1.2<sup>3</sup><var>k</var> = 1.728<var>k</var>, which is 172.8% of the old value. So <var>y</var> is increased by 72.8%.
If <var>y</var> is multiplied by 8 then <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> is multiplied by 8, so <var>x</var> is multiplied by 2 (an increase of 100%).

questions.t: <var>m</var> is inversely proportional to the square of <var>n</var>. Find the effect on:
p: <var>m</var> when <var>n</var> is doubled
<var>m</var> when <var>n</var> is decreased by 20%
<var>n</var> when <var>m</var> is multiplied by 25
questions.al: Write m = kn2.
ap: n = 1 gives m = k; n = 2 gives m = k4. So m is divided by 4.
n = 0.8 gives m = k0.64 = 1.5625k, which is 156.25% of the old value, so m is increased by 56.25%.
If m is multiplied by 25 then 1n2 is multiplied by 25, so n2 is divided by 25 and n is divided by 5.

questions.t: <var>y</var> is directly proportional to the square of <var>x</var> and inversely proportional to <var>z</var>. When <var>x</var> = 2 and <var>z</var> = 3, <var>y</var> = 12.
p: Find the formula for <var>y</var> in terms of <var>x</var> and <var>z</var>.
Find <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> = 5 and <var>z</var> = 2.
Find <var>z</var> when <var>y</var> = 9 and <var>x</var> = 6.
ap: y = kx2z. Substituting: 12 = k × 43, so 4k = 36 and k = 9. Hence y = 9x2z.
y = 9 × 252 = 2252 = 112.5.
9 = 9 × 36z, so 9z = 324 and z = 36.

questions.t: The time, <var>T</var> minutes, taken to empty a water tank with a pump is directly proportional to the volume, <var>V</var> litres, of the tank and inversely proportional to the square of the diameter, <var>D</var> cm, of the outlet pipe. A 900-litre tank is emptied in 20 minutes through a pipe of diameter 6 cm.
p: Find the equation connecting <var>T</var>, <var>V</var> and <var>D</var>.
Find the time taken to empty a 1500-litre tank through a pipe of diameter 5 cm.
If both <var>V</var> and <var>D</var> are doubled, what is the effect on <var>T</var>?
If <var>V</var> is increased by 10% and <var>D</var> is decreased by 5%, find the percentage change in <var>T</var>, correct to one decimal place.
ap: T = kVD2. Substituting T = 20, V = 900, D = 6: 20 = 900k36 = 25k, so k = 0.8 and T = 0.8VD2.
T = 0.8 × 150025 = 120025 = 48 minutes.
Take V = 1 and D = 1, giving T = 0.8. With V = 2 and D = 2, T = 0.8 × 24 = 0.4, which is half of 0.8. So T is halved. (In general doubling V multiplies T by 2 and doubling D divides T by 4.)
The new value is 0.8 × 1.1V(0.95D)2 = 1.10.9025 × 0.8VD2 ≈ 1.2188 × T, that is about 121.9% of the old value. So T increases by about 21.9%.

questions.t: It is known that <var>u</var> is directly proportional to <var>x</var>, that <var>v</var> is inversely proportional to the square of <var>x</var>, and that <var>y</var> = <var>u</var> + <var>v</var>. It is found that <var>y</var> = 7 when <var>x</var> = 1, and also that <var>y</var> = 7 when <var>x</var> = 2.
p: Find an expression for <var>y</var> in terms of <var>x</var>.
Find <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> = 4.
ap:
Write u = ax and v = bx2 for positive constants a and b, so y = ax + bx2.
When x = 1: a + b = 7.
When x = 2: 2a + b4 = 7, and multiplying by 4 gives 8a + b = 28.
Subtracting the first equation from the second: 7a = 21, so a = 3 and b = 4.
Hence y = 3x + 4x2. (Check: x = 1 gives 3 + 4 = 7; x = 2 gives 6 + 1 = 7.)
y = 12 + 416 = 12.25.

questions.t: For gemstones of the same quality, the value of a stone is directly proportional to the square of its weight. A stone worth $<var>C</var> is cut into two pieces, with no weight lost in the cutting.
p: If the weights of the two pieces are in the ratio 2 : 3, show that the loss in value is 12C25, and state this loss as a percentage of $C.
Show that if the weights of the two pieces are in the ratio a : b, then the loss in value is 2abC(a + b)2.
questions.al: Let the value of a stone of weight <var>w</var> be <var>kw</var><sup>2</sup>. The whole stone has weight <var>w</var> and value <var>kw</var><sup>2</sup> = <var>C</var>.
ap: The pieces weigh 2w5 and 3w5, so their values are k × 4w225 = 4C25 and k × 9w225 = 9C25. Their total value is 13C25, so the loss is C − 13C25 = 12C25. As a percentage, 1225 = 0.48, so the loss is 48% of $C.

The pieces weigh awa + b and bwa + b, so their total value is k(a2 + b2)w2(a + b)2 = C(a2 + b2)(a + b)2, using kw2 = C. Hence the loss is
C − C(a2 + b2)(a + b)2 = C × (a + b)2 − (a2 + b2)(a + b)2 = 2abC(a + b)2, since (a + b)2 − a2 − b2 = 2ab. (With a = 2 and b = 3 this gives 12C25, agreeing with part a.)

questions.t: Let <var>x</var> and <var>y</var> be positive quantities with <var>x</var> > <var>y</var>, and suppose that <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> is directly proportional to <var>x</var> − <var>y</var>. Prove that <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> is directly proportional to <var>xy</var>. Begin by writing <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = <var>k</var>(<var>x</var> − <var>y</var>) for a constant <var>k</var>, and explain why <var>k</var> > 1.
questions.a:
Since x + y is directly proportional to x − y, there is a constant k with x + y = k(x − y).
Because x > y > 0 we have x − y > 0 and x + y > x − y, so k = x + yx − y > 1. Hence k2 − 1 > 0, so we may divide by it later.
Squaring both sides: (x + y)2 = k2(x − y)2, that is
x2 + 2xy + y2 = k2(x2 − 2xy + y2).
Writing S = x2 + y2, this is S + 2xy = k2S − 2k2xy.
Collecting terms: 2xy + 2k2xy = k2S − S, so 2xy(1 + k2) = (k2 − 1)S.
Therefore S = 2(1 + k2)k2 − 1 xy. The factor 2(1 + k2)k2 − 1 is a positive constant, since k is constant and k > 1.
∴ x2 + y2 is directly proportional to xy, with constant of proportionality 2(1 + k2)k2 − 1.
(Check with an example: if k = 3 then x + y = 3x − 3y, so x = 2y. Then x2 + y2 = 5y2 and xy = 2y2, giving a ratio of 2.5, which equals 2 × 108 = 2.5.)

questions.t: State whether or not each expression is a polynomial in <var>x</var>. If it is not, give the reason.
p: 5<var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 1
3x + 2x
(<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup>
2 − 5x2 + 5x
ap: Polynomial (degree 4).
Not a polynomial: 2x = 2x−1 and −1 is not a whole number.
Polynomial: it expands to <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 8<var>x</var> + 16.
Not a polynomial: it is a quotient of two polynomials and cannot be written as a sum of whole-number powers of <var>x</var>.

questions.t: Rearrange each polynomial in descending order of degree, then state its degree, its leading coefficient and its constant term, and say whether it is monic.
p: P(<var>x</var>) = 5<var>x</var> − 9 + 2<var>x</var><sup>4</sup>
Q(<var>x</var>) = 7 − <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>3</sup>
R(x) = x34 − 6x5
ap: 2<var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 9; degree 4, leading coefficient 2, constant term −9, non-monic.
<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 7; degree 3, leading coefficient 1, constant term 7, monic.
−6x5 + x34; degree 5, leading coefficient −6, constant term 0, non-monic.

questions.t: Let P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 4. Find each of the following, simplifying your answer.
p: P(3<var>a</var>)
ap: P(3<var>a</var>) = (3<var>a</var>)<sup>3</sup> − 2(3<var>a</var>)<sup>2</sup> + 5(3<var>a</var>) − 4 = 27<var>a</var><sup>3</sup> − 18<var>a</var><sup>2</sup> + 15<var>a</var> − 4.

questions.t: Let P(<var>x</var>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 1 and Q(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup>(3<var>x</var> − 4). Expand Q(<var>x</var>) first, then find each of the following in standard form.
p: P(<var>x</var>) + Q(<var>x</var>)
P(<var>x</var>) − Q(<var>x</var>)
questions.al: Q(<var>x</var>) = 3<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>.
ap: P(<var>x</var>) + Q(<var>x</var>) = 5<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 1.

P(<var>x</var>) − Q(<var>x</var>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 3<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 1 = −<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 1.

questions.t: Expand and simplify each polynomial, and then state its degree, its leading coefficient and its constant term.
p: A(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> + 3)(<var>x</var> − 2)(<var>x</var> + 4)
B(<var>x</var>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>(<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 5)(<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 5)
ap: (<var>x</var> + 3)(<var>x</var> − 2) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> − 6, so A(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> − 6)(<var>x</var> + 4) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>x</var> − 24. Degree 3, leading coefficient 1, constant term −24. (Check <var>x</var> = 1: 4 × (−1) × 5 = −20 and 1 + 5 − 2 − 24 = −20.)

(<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 5)(<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 5) = <var>x</var><sup>6</sup> − 25, so B(<var>x</var>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>(<var>x</var><sup>6</sup> − 25) = 2<var>x</var><sup>8</sup> − 50<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>. Degree 8, leading coefficient 2, constant term 0.

questions.t: Multiply out and simplify, writing each answer in standard form.
p: the product P(<var>x</var>)Q(<var>x</var>), where P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> + 4 and Q(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>x</var> + 4
the square (S(<var>x</var>))<sup>2</sup>, where S(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 3<var>x</var>
ap: P(<var>x</var>)Q(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 8<var>x</var> + 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 8<var>x</var> + 16 = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 16. (Neatly: it is (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 4)<sup>2</sup> − (2<var>x</var>)<sup>2</sup>.)
(<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 3<var>x</var>)<sup>2</sup> = <var>x</var><sup>6</sup> − 6<var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + 9<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>.

questions.t: Use the division algorithm to divide P(<var>x</var>) = 3<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 7 by D(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var> − 2, and write the result in the form P(<var>x</var>) = D(<var>x</var>)Q(<var>x</var>) + R(<var>x</var>), where R(<var>x</var>) = 0 or the degree of R(<var>x</var>) is less than the degree of D(<var>x</var>).
questions.a: Long division gives quotient 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> + 4 and remainder 1, so 3<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 7 = (<var>x</var> − 2)(3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> + 4) + 1. Check: (<var>x</var> − 2)(3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> + 4) = 3<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 8, and adding 1 gives P(<var>x</var>). The remainder also agrees with P(2) = 24 − 20 + 4 − 7 = 1.

questions.t: Use the division algorithm to divide P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>x</var> − 5 by D(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3, and write the result in the form P(<var>x</var>) = D(<var>x</var>)Q(<var>x</var>) + R(<var>x</var>), where R(<var>x</var>) = 0 or the degree of R(<var>x</var>) is less than the degree of D(<var>x</var>).
questions.a: The term in <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> is missing, so leave a gap (or write + 0<var>x</var><sup>2</sup>). Long division gives quotient <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>x</var> − 3 and remainder 7<var>x</var> + 4, so <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>x</var> − 5 = (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3)(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>x</var> − 3) + (7<var>x</var> + 4). Check by expanding: (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3)(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 2<var>x</var> − 3) = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 6<var>x</var> − 9, and adding 7<var>x</var> + 4 gives <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>x</var> − 5. The remainder has degree 1, which is less than 2.

questions.t: Let P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> + 6. Use the remainder theorem to find the remainder when P(<var>x</var>) is divided by each of the following, and state in each case whether the divisor is a factor of P(<var>x</var>).
p: <var>x</var> − 1
<var>x</var> + 1
<var>x</var> − 3
<var>x</var> + 2
ap: P(1) = 1 − 4 + 1 + 6 = 4; remainder 4, so <var>x</var> − 1 is not a factor.
P(−1) = −1 − 4 − 1 + 6 = 0; remainder 0, so <var>x</var> + 1 is a factor.
P(3) = 27 − 36 + 3 + 6 = 0; remainder 0, so <var>x</var> − 3 is a factor.
P(−2) = −8 − 16 − 2 + 6 = −20; remainder −20, so <var>x</var> + 2 is not a factor.  (In fact P(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> + 1)(<var>x</var> − 2)(<var>x</var> − 3).)

questions.t: Use the factor theorem or the remainder theorem to find the unknown coefficient in each case.
p: Find <var>k</var>, given that <var>x</var> − 3 is a factor of P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>k</var><var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 15.
Find <var>m</var>, given that P(<var>x</var>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − <var>m</var><var>x</var> + 5 leaves remainder 3 when it is divided by <var>x</var> + 2.
ap: P(3) = 0, so 27 + 9<var>k</var> + 6 − 15 = 0, giving 9<var>k</var> + 18 = 0 and <var>k</var> = −2. Check: 27 − 18 + 6 − 15 = 0.

questions.t: The polynomial P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + <var>a</var><var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>b</var><var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 4<var>x</var> − 12 is divisible by both <var>x</var> − 1 and <var>x</var> + 2. Find <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>, and then write P(<var>x</var>) out in full.
questions.a:
By the factor theorem P(1) = 0 and P(−2) = 0.
P(1) = 1 + a + b + 4 − 12 = 0, so a + b = 7. (1)
P(−2) = 16 − 8a + 4b − 8 − 12 = 0, so −8a + 4b = 4, that is −2a + b = 1. (2)
Subtracting (2) from (1): 3a = 6, so a = 2 and then b = 5.
Thus P(x) = x4 + 2x3 + 5x2 + 4x − 12. Check: P(1) = 1 + 2 + 5 + 4 − 12 = 0 and P(−2) = 16 − 16 + 20 − 8 − 12 = 0.

questions.t: Factorise each polynomial completely into linear factors, showing the factor you test and the division you use.
p: P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 11<var>x</var> − 12
Q(<var>x</var>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 11<var>x</var> + 6
ap: Test the factors of −12. P(−1) = −1 + 2 + 11 − 12 = 0, so <var>x</var> + 1 is a factor. Dividing, P(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> + 1)(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> − 12) = (<var>x</var> + 1)(<var>x</var> + 4)(<var>x</var> − 3). Check at <var>x</var> = 0: 1 × 4 × (−3) = −12.

Test the factors of 6. Q(3) = 54 − 27 − 33 + 6 = 0, so <var>x</var> − 3 is a factor. Dividing, Q(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> − 3)(2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3<var>x</var> − 2) = (<var>x</var> − 3)(2<var>x</var> − 1)(<var>x</var> + 2). Check at <var>x</var> = 0: (−3) × (−1) × 2 = 6.

questions.t: Solve each polynomial equation, giving every solution.
p: <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 10<var>x</var> + 24 = 0
<var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> = 9<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 18<var>x</var>
ap: Testing factors of 24: at <var>x</var> = 2 the value is 8 − 12 − 20 + 24 = 0, so <var>x</var> − 2 is a factor. Dividing gives (<var>x</var> − 2)(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − <var>x</var> − 12) = 0, that is (<var>x</var> − 2)(<var>x</var> − 4)(<var>x</var> + 3) = 0. Solutions <var>x</var> = 2, <var>x</var> = 4, <var>x</var> = −3.

Move everything to the left: <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 9<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 18<var>x</var> = 0. Take out <var>x</var>: <var>x</var>(<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 9<var>x</var> − 18) = 0. Since (−2)<sup>3</sup> + 2(4) + 18 − 18 = 0, <var>x</var> + 2 is a factor, and <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 9<var>x</var> − 18 = (<var>x</var> + 2)(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 9). Hence <var>x</var>(<var>x</var> + 2)(<var>x</var> − 3)(<var>x</var> + 3) = 0, so <var>x</var> = 0, −2, 3 or −3.

questions.t: Consider the curve <var>y</var> = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 3<var>x</var> + 18.
p: Factorise the right-hand side completely.
State the <var>x</var>-intercepts and the <var>y</var>-intercept.
State whether <var>y</var> is positive or negative on each of <var>x</var> < −2, −2 < <var>x</var> < 3 and <var>x</var> > 3.
State, with a reason, whether the curve cuts or touches the <var>x</var>-axis at each intercept.
ap: The value at <var>x</var> = 3 is 27 − 36 − 9 + 18 = 0, so <var>x</var> − 3 is a factor. Dividing gives (<var>x</var> − 3)(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − <var>x</var> − 6) = (<var>x</var> − 3)(<var>x</var> − 3)(<var>x</var> + 2) = (<var>x</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup>(<var>x</var> + 2).
<var>x</var>-intercepts <var>x</var> = −2 and <var>x</var> = 3; <var>y</var>-intercept <var>y</var> = 18 (put <var>x</var> = 0: (−3)<sup>2</sup> × 2 = 18).

(<var>x</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup> is positive except at <var>x</var> = 3, so the sign of <var>y</var> follows the sign of <var>x</var> + 2. For <var>x</var> < −2, <var>y</var> is negative; for −2 < <var>x</var> < 3, <var>y</var> is positive; for <var>x</var> > 3, <var>y</var> is positive. (For example <var>y</var> = −36 at <var>x</var> = −3, <var>y</var> = 18 at <var>x</var> = 0, <var>y</var> = 6 at <var>x</var> = 4.)

At <var>x</var> = −2 the factor <var>x</var> + 2 occurs once (odd multiplicity), the sign changes, so the curve cuts the axis. At <var>x</var> = 3 the factor occurs twice (even multiplicity), the sign does not change, so the curve touches the axis and is flat there.

questions.t: Consider the curve <var>y</var> = (<var>x</var> + 1)<sup>3</sup>(<var>x</var> − 2)<sup>2</sup>.
p: State the zeros and the multiplicity of each, and state the <var>y</var>-intercept.
State all values of <var>x</var> for which <var>y</var> > 0, and all values for which <var>y</var> < 0.
State whether the curve cuts or touches the <var>x</var>-axis at each zero.
Describe what happens to <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> is a large positive number, and when <var>x</var> is a large negative number.
ap: Zeros <var>x</var> = −1 of multiplicity 3 and <var>x</var> = 2 of multiplicity 2. Putting <var>x</var> = 0 gives <var>y</var> = 1<sup>3</sup> × (−2)<sup>2</sup> = 4, so the <var>y</var>-intercept is 4.

(<var>x</var> − 2)<sup>2</sup> is positive except at <var>x</var> = 2, so the sign of <var>y</var> is the sign of (<var>x</var> + 1)<sup>3</sup>, which is the sign of <var>x</var> + 1. So <var>y</var> > 0 for <var>x</var> > −1 with <var>x</var> ≠ 2, and <var>y</var> < 0 for <var>x</var> < −1. (<var>y</var> = 0 at <var>x</var> = −1 and <var>x</var> = 2.)

The sign changes at <var>x</var> = −1 (multiplicity 3 is odd), so the curve cuts the axis there; the sign does not change at <var>x</var> = 2 (multiplicity 2 is even), so the curve touches the axis there. The curve is flat near both zeros because both factors are repeated.

Expanding would give leading term <var>x</var><sup>5</sup>, a degree 5 polynomial with leading coefficient 1. So for large positive <var>x</var>, <var>y</var> is large and positive; for large negative <var>x</var>, <var>y</var> is large and negative.

questions.t: Find the value of <var>a</var>, given that <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2 is a factor of <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + 5<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 5<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>a</var><var>x</var> + 6.
questions.a:
Divide by x2 + 2. The quotient starts x2; subtracting x4 + 2x2 leaves 5x3 + 3x2 + ax + 6. The next quotient term is 5x; subtracting 5x3 + 10x leaves 3x2 + (a − 10)x + 6. The next quotient term is 3; subtracting 3x2 + 6 leaves (a − 10)x.
For x2 + 2 to be a factor the remainder must be zero, so a = 10.
Check: (x2 + 2)(x2 + 5x + 3) = x4 + 5x3 + 3x2 + 2x2 + 10x + 6 = x4 + 5x3 + 5x2 + 10x + 6.

questions.t: Express <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + 64 as the product of two quadratic polynomials with integer coefficients.
questions.a:
Complete the square on the two given terms by adding and subtracting 16x2:
x4 + 64 = (x4 + 16x2 + 64) − 16x2 = (x2 + 8)2 − (4x)2.
This is a difference of two squares, so x4 + 64 = (x2 + 8 − 4x)(x2 + 8 + 4x) = (x2 − 4x + 8)(x2 + 4x + 8).
Check at x = 1: 1 + 64 = 65 and 5 × 13 = 65. Either ordering of the two factors is acceptable.

questions.t: When P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> + <var>a</var><var>x</var> + <var>b</var> is divided by (<var>x</var> + 1)(<var>x</var> − 2), the remainder is 8<var>x</var> + 1. Find <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>.
questions.a:
Write P(x) = (x + 1)(x − 2)Q(x) + 8x + 1, an identity true for all x.
Put x = −1: the first term vanishes, so P(−1) = −8 + 1 = −7. Thus 1 − a + b = −7, giving −a + b = −8. (1)
Put x = 2: P(2) = 16 + 1 = 17. Thus 16 + 2a + b = 17, giving 2a + b = 1. (2)
Subtracting (1) from (2): 3a = 9, so a = 3 and b = −5.
Check: P(x) = x4 + 3x − 5 gives P(−1) = 1 − 3 − 5 = −7 and P(2) = 16 + 6 − 5 = 17, matching 8(−1) + 1 and 8(2) + 1.

questions.t: Let <var>p</var>, <var>q</var> and <var>r</var> be numbers.
p: Given that (<var>x</var> − <var>p</var>)(<var>x</var> − <var>q</var>)(<var>x</var> − <var>r</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>b</var><var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>c</var><var>x</var> + <var>d</var> for all values of <var>x</var>, show that <var>p</var> + <var>q</var> + <var>r</var> = −<var>b</var>, that <var>p</var><var>q</var> + <var>q</var><var>r</var> + <var>r</var><var>p</var> = <var>c</var> and that <var>p</var><var>q</var><var>r</var> = −<var>d</var>.
Hence write down, in expanded form, the monic cubic equation whose solutions are exactly <var>x</var> = −1, <var>x</var> = 2 and <var>x</var> = 5.
ap:
Expand the left-hand side. First (x − p)(x − q) = x2 − (p + q)x + pq. Multiplying by (x − r):
= x3 − (p + q)x2 + pqx − rx2 + r(p + q)x − pqr
= x3 − (p + q + r)x2 + (pq + qr + rp)x − pqr.
Two polynomials are equal for all x exactly when corresponding coefficients are equal, so b = −(p + q + r), c = pq + qr + rp and d = −pqr. Rearranging gives p + q + r = −b, pq + qr + rp = c and pqr = −d.

With <var>p</var> = −1, <var>q</var> = 2, <var>r</var> = 5: sum = 6 so <var>b</var> = −6; <var>p</var><var>q</var> + <var>q</var><var>r</var> + <var>r</var><var>p</var> = −2 + 10 − 5 = 3 so <var>c</var> = 3; product = −10 so <var>d</var> = 10. The equation is <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 6<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 3<var>x</var> + 10 = 0. Check <var>x</var> = 2: 8 − 24 + 6 + 10 = 0, and <var>x</var> = 5: 125 − 150 + 15 + 10 = 0.

questions.t: Without using long division, find the remainder when <var>x</var><sup>51</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>33</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>5</sup> + 2<var>x</var> is divided by <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − <var>x</var>. Explain why your remainder is the only possible one.
questions.a:
Let P(x) = x51 + x33 + x5 + 2x. The divisor x3 − x = x(x − 1)(x + 1) has degree 3, so the remainder has degree at most 2: write
P(x) = (x3 − x)Q(x) + mx2 + nx + k, true for all x.
Put x = 0: P(0) = 0, so k = 0.
Put x = 1: P(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5, so m + n = 5.
Put x = −1: all the powers 51, 33, 5 and 1 are odd, so P(−1) = −1 − 1 − 1 − 2 = −5, giving m − n = −5.
Adding and subtracting: m = 0 and n = 5. The remainder is 5x.
It is the only possible remainder because the three substitutions x = 0, 1, −1 (the zeros of the divisor) determine m, n and k uniquely, and the division algorithm gives exactly one quotient and remainder.

questions.t: Find every ordered pair (<var>x</var>, <var>y</var>) of real numbers satisfying both <var>x</var> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 5 and <var>y</var> + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 5. Give exact values.
questions.a:
Subtract the second equation from the first: (x − y) + (y2 − x2) = 0, so (x − y) − (x − y)(x + y) = 0, that is (x − y)(1 − x − y) = 0. So y = x or x + y = 1.
Case 1: y = x. Then x + x2 = 5, so x2 + x − 5 = 0 and x = −1 + √212 or x = −1 − √212, giving the pairs (−1 + √212, −1 + √212) and (−1 − √212, −1 − √212).
Case 2: y = 1 − x. Then x + (1 − x)2 = 5, so x + 1 − 2x + x2 = 5, that is x2 − x − 4 = 0 and x = 1 + √172 or x = 1 − √172, with y = 1 − x = 1 − √172 or 1 + √172 respectively.
So there are four ordered pairs: (−1 + √212, −1 + √212), (−1 − √212, −1 − √212), (1 + √172, 1 − √172) and (1 − √172, 1 + √172).
Check numerically for the third pair: x ≈ 2.5616, y ≈ −1.5616, so x + y2 ≈ 2.5616 + 2.4384 = 5 and y + x2 ≈ −1.5616 + 6.5616 = 5.

questions.t: Find the range and the interquartile range of each data set.
ap: In order: 4, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15. Range = 15 − 4 = 11. There are 9 values, so the median is the 5th value, 9. Omitting it, the lower group is 4, 4, 6, 7, so Q1 = 4 + 62 = 5; the upper group is 11, 12, 13, 15, so Q3 = 12 + 132 = 12.5. IQR = 12.5 − 5 = 7.5.

In order: 14, 14, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 25, 26, 30. Range = 30 − 14 = 16. There are 10 values, so the median is 19 + 212 = 20. Lower group 14, 14, 17, 18, 19 gives Q1 = 17; upper group 21, 22, 25, 26, 30 gives Q3 = 25. IQR = 25 − 17 = 8.

questions.t:
The stem-and-leaf plot below gives the heights, in centimetres, of the 20 students in a class.
13 | 2 5 8
14 | 0 1 3 3 6 7
15 | 0 2 2 4 5 8
16 | 1 3 4 6
17 | 0
Key: 14 | 3 means 143 cm.
p: What is the range of the heights?
What is the median height?
What is the interquartile range?
ap: With 20 values the median is the average of the 10th and 11th values: 150 + 1522 = 151 cm.

The lower group is the first 10 values, whose median is 141 + 1432 = 142 cm, so Q1 = 142. The upper group is the last 10 values, whose median is 158 + 1612 = 159.5 cm, so Q3 = 159.5. IQR = 159.5 − 142 = 17.5 cm.

questions.t: A survey asked 24 households how many pets they own. Three households own 0 pets, five own 1 pet, four own 2 pets, six own 3 pets, two own 4 pets and four own 5 pets.
p: Calculate the mean number of pets per household, correct to two decimal places.
State the mode.
Find the median number of pets.
ap: Sum of all values = 0×3 + 1×5 + 2×4 + 3×6 + 4×2 + 5×4 = 0 + 5 + 8 + 18 + 8 + 20 = 59. Mean = 5924 ≈ 2.46 pets.
The largest frequency is 6, which belongs to the value 3, so the mode is 3 pets.
With 24 values the median is the average of the 12th and 13th values. The cumulative frequencies are 3, 8, 12, 18, 20, 24, so the 12th value is 2 and the 13th value is 3. Median = 2 + 32 = 2.5 pets.

questions.t: Consider the data set 3, 5, 6, 10, 11.
p: Find the mean and the standard deviation, giving the standard deviation correct to two decimal places.
Each of the five values is now increased by 4. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of the new data set without recalculating from the new values, and state which of the two has changed.
ap: Mean = 3 + 5 + 6 + 10 + 115 = 355 = 7. The deviations are −4, −2, −1, 3, 4, whose squares are 16, 4, 1, 9, 16, with sum 46. So the variance is 465 = 9.2 and the standard deviation is √9.2 ≈ 3.03.

The new values are 7, 9, 10, 14, 15, so the new mean is 7 + 4 = 11. Adding 4 to every value adds 4 to the mean as well, so every deviation (value − mean) is unchanged and the standard deviation is still ≈ 3.03. Only the mean has changed.

questions.t: In a class of 20 students each student sat a spelling test marked out of 6. Three students scored 2, four scored 3, six scored 4, four scored 5 and three scored 6.
p: Calculate the mean mark.
Calculate the standard deviation of the marks, correct to two decimal places.
What percentage of the 20 marks lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
ap: Sum of marks = 2×3 + 3×4 + 4×6 + 5×4 + 6×3 = 6 + 12 + 24 + 20 + 18 = 80. Mean = 8020 = 4.
Using the frequency form, the sum of frequency × (mark − 4)2 is 3×4 + 4×1 + 6×0 + 4×1 + 3×4 = 12 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 12 = 32. Variance = 3220 = 1.6, so the standard deviation is √1.6 ≈ 1.26.

One standard deviation either side of the mean gives the interval from 4 − 1.26 = 2.74 to 4 + 1.26 = 5.26. The marks in this interval are 3, 4 and 5, with frequencies 4 + 6 + 4 = 14. So 1420 = 70% of the marks lie within one standard deviation of the mean.

questions.t: For a particular data set the lower quartile is Q<sub>1</sub> = 46 and the upper quartile is Q<sub>3</sub> = 70. A value is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the nearer end of the box.
p: Find the interquartile range, and find the two boundary values that the 1.5 × IQR test uses.
This data set contains the values 8, 12, 104 and 118. State which of these four values are outliers, and which are not.
ap: IQR = 70 − 46 = 24, so 1.5 × IQR = 36. The boundaries are Q<sub>1</sub> − 36 = 46 − 36 = 10 and Q<sub>3</sub> + 36 = 70 + 36 = 106.
A value is an outlier if it is less than 10 or greater than 106. So 8 is an outlier (8 < 10) and 118 is an outlier (118 > 106). The values 12 and 104 are not outliers, since 10 < 12 and 104 < 106.

p: Write down the five-number summary (minimum, Q<sub>1</sub>, median, Q<sub>3</sub>, maximum).
Find the interquartile range and 1.5 × IQR, and name any outliers.
State the two values at which the whiskers of the boxplot would end.
ap: Minimum = 210. With 20 values the median is 246 + 2502 = 248. The lower group is the first 10 values, whose median is 230 + 2352 = 232.5, so Q1 = 232.5. The upper group is the last 10 values, whose median is 266 + 2722 = 269, so Q3 = 269. Maximum = 355. Five-number summary: 210, 232.5, 248, 269, 355.

IQR = 269 − 232.5 = 36.5 and 1.5 × IQR = 54.75. The boundaries are 232.5 − 54.75 = 177.75 and 269 + 54.75 = 323.75. The only value outside these is 355, so 355 ms is the one outlier (210 is above 177.75, so the minimum is not an outlier).
The whiskers end at the extreme values that are not outliers: the left whisker ends at 210 ms and the right whisker ends at 296 ms, the largest value below 323.75.

questions.t: Nadia scored 68 in a physics test for which the class mean was 59 and the standard deviation was 6. In the same week she scored 74 in a chemistry test for which the class mean was 68 and the standard deviation was 10. In which test did Nadia perform better relative to her class? Support your answer with a calculation for each test.
questions.a:
Physics: 68 − 596 = 96 = 1.5, so Nadia was 1.5 standard deviations above the class mean.
Chemistry: 74 − 6810 = 0.6, so she was 0.6 of a standard deviation above the class mean.
Since 1.5 > 0.6, Nadia performed better relative to her class in the physics test, even though her raw chemistry mark was higher.

questions.t: A machine fills bags of flour. The masses of the filled bags have a mean of 502 g and a standard deviation of 3.5 g.
p: Find the range of masses that lie within one standard deviation of the mean.
Find the range of masses that lie within two standard deviations of the mean.

Chebyshev’s inequality states that, for any data set and any k > 1, at most 1k2 of the data can lie outside the interval from mean − k × (standard deviation) to mean + k × (standard deviation). Taking k = 2, what is the least possible percentage of bags whose mass lies in the interval found in part b?
ap: 502 − 2 × 3.5 = 495 g and 502 + 2 × 3.5 = 509 g, so the masses from 495 g to 509 g.
With k = 2, at most 122 = 14 = 25% of the bags can lie outside the interval. So at least 100% − 25% = 75% of the bags must have a mass between 495 g and 509 g.

questions.t:
A ski-hire business recorded its quarterly revenue, in thousands of dollars, for three years.
2023: Jan–Mar 48, Apr–Jun 62, Jul–Sep 95, Oct–Dec 37
2024: Jan–Mar 52, Apr–Jun 68, Jul–Sep 104, Oct–Dec 41
2025: Jan–Mar 57, Apr–Jun 75, Jul–Sep 118, Oct–Dec 45
p: In which quarter of each year is the revenue highest, and in which quarter of each year is it lowest?
By comparing the same quarter across the three years, decide whether the business is growing. Quote figures.
Explain why comparing the Jul–Sep 2025 figure with the Oct–Dec 2025 figure would give a misleading impression of the trend.
ap: The revenue is highest in Jul–Sep in every year (95, 104, 118) and lowest in Oct–Dec in every year (37, 41, 45).

Comparing like quarters: Jan–Mar goes 48, 52, 57; Apr–Jun goes 62, 68, 75; Jul–Sep goes 95, 104, 118; Oct–Dec goes 37, 41, 45. Every one of the four quarters increases in each successive year, so the business is growing. (The annual totals 242, 265 and 295 thousand dollars confirm this.)

The time series has a strong seasonal pattern: Jul–Sep is always the peak of the ski season and Oct–Dec is always the trough. The fall from 118 to 45 is caused by the season, not by a decline in the business. To judge the trend you must compare the same quarter in different years, as in part b.

questions.t: A line of best fit was drawn on a scatter plot relating the mass of a watermelon, <var>x</var> kg, to the number of seeds it contains, <var>y</var>. The line passes through the points (2, 260) and (8, 500). The masses actually recorded ranged from 1.5 kg to 9 kg.
p: Find the equation of the line of best fit in the form <var>y</var> = <var>mx</var> + <var>c</var>.
Use the equation to estimate the number of seeds in a watermelon of mass 5.5 kg.
Use the equation to estimate the mass of a watermelon containing 620 seeds.
State which of your answers to parts b and c is interpolation and which is extrapolation, and explain how you decided.
ap: Gradient m = 500 − 2608 − 2 = 2406 = 40. Using the point–gradient form, y − 260 = 40(x − 2), so y = 40x − 80 + 260, giving y = 40x + 180. (Check: x = 8 gives 40 × 8 + 180 = 500, as required.)
620 = 40<var>x</var> + 180, so 40<var>x</var> = 440 and <var>x</var> = 11 kg.

The recorded masses ran from 1.5 kg to 9 kg. Part b uses <var>x</var> = 5.5 kg, which lies inside that range, so it is interpolation. Part c gives <var>x</var> = 11 kg, which lies outside that range, so it is extrapolation and should be treated with caution — there is no guarantee the linear relationship continues beyond 9 kg.

questions.t: A data set of 12 numbers has mean 30, standard deviation 4, median 28 and interquartile range 9.
p: Every value in the data set is increased by 6. Write down the new mean, standard deviation, median and interquartile range.
Instead, every value of the original data set is multiplied by 3. Write down the new mean, standard deviation, median and interquartile range.
Explain why adding 6 to every value leaves both the standard deviation and the interquartile range unchanged.
ap: Mean 36, standard deviation 4, median 34, interquartile range 9.
Mean 90, standard deviation 12, median 84, interquartile range 27.

If 6 is added to every value then the mean also increases by 6, so each deviation (value − mean) becomes (value + 6) − (mean + 6), which is exactly the old deviation. The squared deviations, their sum, the variance and hence the standard deviation are therefore all unchanged. Similarly, adding 6 to every value moves each value 6 places up the scale without changing the order, so both quartiles increase by 6; their difference Q<sub>3</sub> − Q<sub>1</sub> is unchanged, so the interquartile range stays 9. Multiplying by 3, on the other hand, multiplies every deviation and every gap by 3, which is why the standard deviation and the interquartile range are both tripled in part b.

questions.t: The deviation of a data value from the mean is (value − mean).
p: Show that for any three numbers <var>a</var>, <var>b</var> and <var>c</var> the sum of the deviations from their mean is zero.
Prove that for any data set <var>x</var><sub>1</sub>, <var>x</var><sub>2</sub>, …, <var>x</var><sub>n</sub> the sum of the deviations from the mean is zero.
Hence explain why the average of the deviations could never be used as a measure of spread, and say what is done instead.
ap: The mean of the three numbers is m = a + b + c3, so 3m = a + b + c. The sum of the deviations is (a − m) + (b − m) + (c − m) = (a + b + c) − 3m = 3m − 3m = 0.

Let the mean be m, so that m = x1 + x2 + … + xnn and therefore x1 + x2 + … + xn = nm. Summing the n deviations gives (x1 − m) + (x2 − m) + … + (xn − m) = (x1 + x2 + … + xn) − nm, because m is subtracted exactly n times. This equals nm − nm = 0. ∴ the sum of the deviations is always zero.

Since the sum of the deviations is 0 for every data set, the average of the deviations is 0n = 0 for every data set, no matter how tightly or widely spread the values are. A quantity that takes the same value for all data sets carries no information about spread. Instead the deviations are squared first, so that negative and positive deviations can no longer cancel; the squares are averaged and the square root taken, giving the standard deviation.

questions.t: A data set consists of nine whole numbers. Its minimum is 6, its lower quartile is 10, its median is 15, its upper quartile is 22 and its maximum is 45.
p: Show, using the 1.5 × IQR test, that the maximum value 45 is an outlier while the minimum value 6 is not.
Write down one set of nine whole numbers with exactly this five-number summary.
State the conditions a marker should check in order to accept a different, equally valid set of nine whole numbers.
ap: IQR = 22 − 10 = 12, so 1.5 × IQR = 18. The upper boundary is Q<sub>3</sub> + 18 = 22 + 18 = 40 and the lower boundary is Q<sub>1</sub> − 18 = 10 − 18 = −8. Since 45 > 40, the maximum 45 is an outlier. Since 6 > −8, the minimum 6 is not an outlier.

One valid set is 6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 20, 21, 23, 45. Check: with nine values the median is the 5th value, which is 15, as required. Omitting the median, the lower group is 6, 9, 11, 13, whose median is 9 + 112 = 10, so Q1 = 10, as required. The upper group is 20, 21, 23, 45, whose median is 21 + 232 = 22, so Q3 = 22, as required. The minimum is 6 and the maximum is 45, as required.

Accept any nine whole numbers which, written in non-decreasing order as <var>v</var><sub>1</sub> ≤ <var>v</var><sub>2</sub> ≤ … ≤ <var>v</var><sub>9</sub>, satisfy all of: <var>v</var><sub>1</sub> = 6; <var>v</var><sub>5</sub> = 15; <var>v</var><sub>9</sub> = 45; <var>v</var><sub>2</sub> + <var>v</var><sub>3</sub> = 20 with 6 ≤ <var>v</var><sub>2</sub> ≤ <var>v</var><sub>3</sub> ≤ <var>v</var><sub>4</sub> ≤ 15; and <var>v</var><sub>7</sub> + <var>v</var><sub>8</sub> = 44 with 15 ≤ <var>v</var><sub>6</sub> ≤ <var>v</var><sub>7</sub> ≤ <var>v</var><sub>8</sub> ≤ 45. For example 6, 10, 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 22, 45 also works.

questions.t: Ten numbers are to be written down. Each number must be either 2 or 14. (No trial-and-error arithmetic on all the cases is required — think about where the mean sits.)
p: Choose the ten numbers so that the standard deviation is as large as possible, and find that standard deviation exactly.
Now choose the ten numbers so that the standard deviation is as small as possible, given that the ten numbers must not all be the same. Find that standard deviation exactly.
Explain why your choice in part a gives the largest possible standard deviation.
ap: Take five 2s and five 14s. Mean = 5 × 2 + 5 × 1410 = 10 + 7010 = 8. Every deviation is −6 or 6, so every squared deviation is 36 and their sum is 10 × 36 = 360. Variance = 36010 = 36, so the standard deviation is exactly 6. Accept the five 2s and five 14s in any order.

Take one 2 and nine 14s (or, equally, nine 2s and one 14). Mean = 2 + 9 × 1410 = 12810 = 12.8. The deviations are 2 − 12.8 = −10.8 once and 14 − 12.8 = 1.2 nine times, giving squares 116.64 and 9 × 1.44 = 12.96, with sum 129.6. Variance = 129.610 = 12.96, so the standard deviation is exactly 3.6. Accept either the one–nine or the nine–one split, in any order.

In general, if <var>k</var> of the numbers are 2 then the mean is 14 − 1.2<var>k</var>, the deviation of a 2 is 1.2(<var>k</var> − 10) and the deviation of a 14 is 1.2<var>k</var>, and the variance simplifies to 1.44<var>k</var>(10 − <var>k</var>). The product <var>k</var>(10 − <var>k</var>) is largest when <var>k</var> = 5, giving variance 1.44 × 25 = 36. In words: only two distances from the mean are available, and the mean is pulled towards whichever value is more common. Splitting the ten numbers evenly puts the mean midway between 2 and 14, at 8, so that every one of the ten values is the full 6 away from the mean — the largest distance any value can be from the mean. Any uneven split drags the mean close to the majority value, so most values sit near the mean and the spread is smaller. (The same formula shows <var>k</var> = 1 or <var>k</var> = 9 gives the smallest non-zero variance, 1.44 × 9 = 12.96, confirming part b.)

questions.t: A data set of 20 measurements has mean 46 and range 79. When the single largest measurement is removed, the remaining 19 measurements have mean 43 and range 39.
p: Find the measurement that was removed.
The 19 remaining measurements have Q<sub>1</sub> = 38 and Q<sub>3</sub> = 50. Show that the removed measurement is an outlier for that set of 19.
Using the figures in this question, explain why the interquartile range is a more useful measure of spread here than the range.
ap: Sum of the 20 measurements = 20 × 46 = 920. Sum of the remaining 19 = 19 × 43 = 817. The removed measurement = 920 − 817 = 103.
For the 19 measurements, IQR = 50 − 38 = 12, so 1.5 × IQR = 18 and the upper boundary is 50 + 18 = 68. Since 103 > 68, the value 103 is an outlier.

The two ranges show that this one value contributed 79 − 39 = 40 to the range — more than half of the whole range of the original data was created by a single measurement, and removing it also moved the mean by 3 (from 46 to 43). Both the range and the mean are therefore controlled by one freak value rather than by the bulk of the data. The quartiles, by contrast, are found from the positions of the values in the middle of the ordered list, so replacing 103 by any other value larger than 63 leaves the first 19 places of the ordered list of 20 untouched and therefore does not change the quartiles of the full set of 20 at all. The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data and is unaffected by the outlier, so it describes the typical spread far better than the range does.

questions.t:
A shop recorded the number of heaters it sold in each quarter for three years.
2023: Q1 210, Q2 480, Q3 620, Q4 190
2024: Q1 240, Q2 540, Q3 700, Q4 220
2025: Q1 270, Q2 600, Q3 780, Q4 250
p: Find the mean number of heaters sold per quarter in each of the three years.
Let <var>x</var> be the year number, with 2023 as year 1, and let <var>y</var> be that year’s mean quarterly sales. Show that the three points lie exactly on a straight line and find its equation.
Use the line to forecast the mean quarterly sales for 2026, and hence the total number of heaters sold in 2026.
The owner also uses the line to forecast 2035. Give one reason why the 2035 forecast deserves much more caution than the 2026 forecast.
ap: 2023 total = 210 + 480 + 620 + 190 = 1500, so the mean is 15004 = 375. 2024 total = 240 + 540 + 700 + 220 = 1700, so the mean is 17004 = 425. 2025 total = 270 + 600 + 780 + 250 = 1900, so the mean is 19004 = 475.

The points are (1, 375), (2, 425) and (3, 475). From (1, 375) to (2, 425) the rise is 50 for a run of 1, and from (2, 425) to (3, 475) the rise is again 50 for a run of 1, so the gradient is the same, 50, and the three points are collinear. Using the point–gradient form, <var>y</var> − 375 = 50(<var>x</var> − 1), so <var>y</var> = 50<var>x</var> + 325. (Check: <var>x</var> = 3 gives 50 × 3 + 325 = 475, as required.)
2026 is year 4, so <var>y</var> = 50 × 4 + 325 = 525 heaters per quarter. The forecast total for 2026 is 4 × 525 = 2100 heaters.

Both forecasts are extrapolation, since years 4 and 13 lie outside the observed range of years 1 to 3. But 2026 is only one year beyond the data, whereas 2035 is year 13 — ten years beyond it. The further outside the observed range you go, the less reason there is to believe the straight-line pattern continues: over ten years the market can saturate, competitors can arrive, climate or technology can change, or the shop can reach the limit of what it can stock. The 2035 forecast of 50 × 13 + 325 = 975 heaters per quarter is nearly double the current level and rests on nothing but the assumption that the trend never changes.
