ap: third
second
fourth
second

questions.t: Write down the related angle (the acute angle made with the <var>x</var>-axis) for each angle.
ap: −80° + 360° = 280°, which is in the fourth quadrant, so the related angle is 360° − 280° = 80°

questions.t: Without evaluating, express each number as the trigonometric function of an acute angle, with the correct sign.
p: sin 168°
cos 216°
tan 305°
sin 260°
ap: 168° is in the second quadrant where sine is positive, related angle 12°, so sin 168° = sin 12°.
216° is in the third quadrant where cosine is negative, related angle 36°, so cos 216° = −cos 36°.
305° is in the fourth quadrant where tangent is negative, related angle 55°, so tan 305° = −tan 55°.
260° is in the third quadrant where sine is negative, related angle 80°, so sin 260° = −sin 80°.

questions.t: Find the exact value of each of the following. Leave surds in your answers; do not use a calculator.
p: cos 150°
sin 225°
tan 240°
cos 315°
ap: Second quadrant, related angle 30°, cosine negative: cos 150° = −cos 30° = −√32.
Third quadrant, related angle 45°, sine negative: sin 225° = −sin 45° = −1√2.
Third quadrant, related angle 60°, tangent positive: tan 240° = tan 60° = √3.
Fourth quadrant, related angle 45°, cosine positive: cos 315° = cos 45° = 1√2.

questions.t: Each angle below lies outside the range 0° to 360°. Add or subtract a multiple of 360° first, then find the exact value.
p: sin 495°
cos 660°
ap: sin 495° = sin (495° − 360°) = sin 135° = sin 45° = 1√2.
cos 660° = cos (660° − 360°) = cos 300° = cos 60° = 12.
sin (−240°) = sin (−240° + 360°) = sin 120° = sin 60° = √32.

questions.t: In which quadrant does <var>θ</var> lie in each case? Give one quadrant for each part.
p: sin <var>θ</var> < 0 and cos <var>θ</var> > 0
tan <var>θ</var> > 0 and cos <var>θ</var> < 0
sin <var>θ</var> > 0 and tan <var>θ</var> < 0
ap: Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants; cosine is positive in the first and fourth. Both hold only in the fourth quadrant.
Tangent is positive in the first and third; cosine is negative in the second and third. Both hold only in the third quadrant.
Sine is positive in the first and second; tangent is negative in the second and fourth. Both hold only in the second quadrant.

questions.t: Find all angles <var>θ</var> with 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360° that satisfy each equation. Work from the related angle; do not use a calculator.
p: cos θ = −1√2
tan <var>θ</var> = −√3
sin θ = √32
ap: The related angle is 45°. Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, so <var>θ</var> = 180° − 45° = 135° or <var>θ</var> = 180° + 45° = 225°.
The related angle is 60°. Tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, so <var>θ</var> = 120° or <var>θ</var> = 300°.
The related angle is 60°. Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so <var>θ</var> = 60° or <var>θ</var> = 120°.

questions.t: Use a calculator to find all angles θ with 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360° that satisfy each equation, correct to the nearest degree.
p: sin <var>θ</var> = 0.2419
cos <var>θ</var> = −0.7314
tan <var>θ</var> = −1.4826
ap: sin<sup>−1</sup> 0.2419 ≈ 14°, and sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so <var>θ</var> ≈ 14° or <var>θ</var> ≈ 180° − 14° = 166°.
Work with the related angle: cos<sup>−1</sup> 0.7314 ≈ 43°. Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, so <var>θ</var> ≈ 180° − 43° = 137° or <var>θ</var> ≈ 180° + 43° = 223°.
Work with the related angle: tan<sup>−1</sup> 1.4826 ≈ 56°. Tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, so <var>θ</var> ≈ 180° − 56° = 124° or <var>θ</var> ≈ 360° − 56° = 304°.

questions.t: The function <var>y</var> = 4 sin 2<var>θ</var> is graphed for 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360°.
p: State the amplitude and the period of the function.
Find the exact value of <var>y</var> when <var>θ</var> = 15°.
How many values of <var>θ</var> in 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360° give <var>y</var> = 0? List them.
State the maximum value of <var>y</var> and every value of <var>θ</var> in 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360° at which it occurs.
ap: Amplitude 4; period 360°2 = 180°.
y = 4 sin 30° = 4 × 12 = 2.
4 sin 2θ = 0 needs sin 2θ = 0, so 2θ = 0°, 180°, 360°, 540° or 720° (as 0° ≤ 2θ ≤ 720°). Hence θ = 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°, which is 5 values.
Maximum <var>y</var> = 4, needing sin 2<var>θ</var> = 1, so 2<var>θ</var> = 90° or 450°, giving <var>θ</var> = 45° and <var>θ</var> = 225°.

questions.t: Consider the function <var>y</var> = 3 cos <var>θ</var> − 1 for 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360°.
p: State the greatest and least values of <var>y</var>, and the value of <var>θ</var> at which each occurs.
Find the exact value of <var>y</var> when <var>θ</var> = 120°.
How many values of <var>θ</var> in 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360° satisfy <var>y</var> = 0? You do not need to find them.
Find every value of <var>θ</var> in 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360° for which <var>y</var> = −1.
ap: Since −1 ≤ cos <var>θ</var> ≤ 1, the greatest value is 3(1) − 1 = 2, at <var>θ</var> = 0° and <var>θ</var> = 360°; the least value is 3(−1) − 1 = −4, at <var>θ</var> = 180°.
cos 120° = −12, so y = 3 × (−12) − 1 = −32 − 1 = −52.
y = 0 gives cos θ = 13, which is positive, so θ is in the first or the fourth quadrant: 2 values (they are about 70.5° and 289.5°).
3 cos <var>θ</var> − 1 = −1 gives cos <var>θ</var> = 0, so <var>θ</var> = 90° or <var>θ</var> = 270°.

questions.t: Solve each equation for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°, giving exact answers.
p: 2 cos <var>θ</var> + √3 = 0
√3 tan <var>θ</var> − 1 = 0
2 sin <var>θ</var> + 1 = 0
ap: cos θ = −√32; related angle 30°, cosine negative, so θ = 150° or 210°.
tan θ = 1√3; related angle 30°, tangent positive, so θ = 30° or 210°.
sin θ = −12; related angle 30°, sine negative, so θ = 210° or 330°.

questions.t: Solve each equation for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°, giving exact answers. Remember that a square has two square roots.
p: sin2 θ = 34
3 tan<sup>2</sup> <var>θ</var> = 1
ap: sin θ = √32 or sin θ = −√32. The related angle is 60°, and sine takes both signs, so θ can be in any quadrant: θ = 60°, 120°, 240° or 300°.
tan2 θ = 13, so tan θ = 1√3 or tan θ = −1√3. The related angle is 30°, so θ = 30°, 150°, 210° or 330°.

questions.t: Use the identity sin2 θ + cos2 θ = 1 (or a right-angled triangle) together with the sign rules. Give exact answers as fractions.
p: Given that sin θ = 35 and θ lies in the second quadrant, find cos θ and tan θ.
Given that tan θ = −512 and 270° < θ < 360°, find sin θ and cos θ.
ap: cos2 θ = 1 − (35)2 = 1 − 925 = 1625, so cos θ = ±45. In the second quadrant cosine is negative, so cos θ = −45. Then tan θ = sin θcos θ = 35 ÷ (−45) = −34.

The related angle has tangent 512, so it sits in a right-angled triangle with opposite 5, adjacent 12 and hypotenuse √(25 + 144) = 13. As 270° < θ < 360°, θ is in the fourth quadrant, where sine is negative and cosine positive: sin θ = −513 and cos θ = 1213. Check: sin θcos θ = −512, as given.

questions.t:
Recall that sec θ = 1cos θ, cosec θ = 1sin θ and cot θ = 1tan θ. Find the exact value of
cos2 150° sec 180° + sin2 240° cosec 270° − tan2 135° cot 225°.
questions.a:
cos 150° = −√32, so cos2 150° = 34; cos 180° = −1, so sec 180° = −1. First term = 34 × (−1) = −34.
sin 240° = −√32, so sin2 240° = 34; sin 270° = −1, so cosec 270° = −1. Second term = 34 × (−1) = −34.
tan 135° = −tan 45° = −1, so tan2 135° = 1; tan 225° = tan 45° = 1, so cot 225° = 1. Third term = 1 × 1 = 1.
Total = −34 − 34 − 1 = −32 − 1 = −52.

questions.t: Show that cos 750° sin 405° − sin 750° cos 405° = √3 − 12√2. Show every exact value you use.
questions.a:
Reduce each angle by a multiple of 360°:
cos 750° = cos (750° − 720°) = cos 30° = √32; sin 750° = sin 30° = 12;
sin 405° = sin (405° − 360°) = sin 45° = 1√2; cos 405° = cos 45° = 1√2.
So the left-hand side = √32 × 1√2 − 12 × 1√2 = √32√2 − 12√2 = √3 − 12√2, as required. (Numerically both sides are ≈ 0.2588.)

questions.t: Consider the function <var>y</var> = sin 3<var>θ</var> for 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360°.
p: State the amplitude and the period.
Find every value of <var>θ</var> with 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360° for which <var>y</var> = 0, and say how many there are.
Find every value of <var>θ</var> with 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360° for which <var>y</var> = 1.
Find the exact value of <var>y</var> when <var>θ</var> = 10°.
questions.al: As <var>θ</var> runs from 0° to 360°, 3<var>θ</var> runs from 0° to 1080°.
ap: Amplitude 1; period 360°3 = 120°.
sin 3<var>θ</var> = 1 needs 3<var>θ</var> = 90°, 450° or 810° (the next, 1170°, is beyond 1080°), so <var>θ</var> = 30°, 150° or 270°.
y = sin 30° = 12.

questions.t: Solve cos2 θ cosec θ = 2 cot θ for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°, where θ ≠ 0°, 180°, 360°. (Here cosec θ = 1sin θ and cot θ = cos θsin θ.)
questions.a:
Write both sides over sin θ: cos2 θsin θ = 2 cos θsin θ. The excluded values guarantee sin θ ≠ 0, so we may multiply by sin θ:
cos2 θ = 2 cos θ
cos2 θ − 2 cos θ = 0
cos θ (cos θ − 2) = 0
so cos θ = 0 or cos θ = 2. Since −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1, cos θ = 2 is impossible. Hence cos θ = 0, giving θ = 90° or θ = 270°. Both are allowed (sin 90° = 1 and sin 270° = −1 are non-zero), and both check: each side is 0.

questions.t: Each equation below is a quadratic in a trigonometric function. Solve for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°, giving exact answers, and reject any impossible value.
p: 2 cos<sup>2</sup> <var>θ</var> − 5 cos <var>θ</var> + 2 = 0
2 sin<sup>2</sup> <var>θ</var> − sin <var>θ</var> − 1 = 0
ap: Factorising, (2 cos θ − 1)(cos θ − 2) = 0, so cos θ = 12 or cos θ = 2. The value 2 is impossible since −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1. With cos θ = 12 the related angle is 60° and cosine is positive, so θ = 60° or 300°.
Factorising, (2 sin θ + 1)(sin θ − 1) = 0, so sin θ = −12 or sin θ = 1. From sin θ = −12 (related angle 30°, sine negative) θ = 210° or 330°; from sin θ = 1, θ = 90°. Hence θ = 90°, 210° or 330°.

questions.t: The Challenge exercise of this chapter proves, by comparing areas, that sin 2<var>θ</var> = 2 sin <var>θ</var> cos <var>θ</var> for every angle <var>θ</var>. Use that result in both parts.
p: Find the exact value of sin 15° cos 15°.
Solve sin 2<var>θ</var> = sin <var>θ</var> for 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> ≤ 360°, giving exact answers.
ap: Putting θ = 15° in the identity gives sin 30° = 2 sin 15° cos 15°, so sin 15° cos 15° = 12 sin 30° = 12 × 12 = 14.

Replace sin 2θ:
2 sin θ cos θ = sin θ
2 sin θ cos θ − sin θ = 0
sin θ (2 cos θ − 1) = 0
So sin θ = 0, giving θ = 0°, 180° or 360°; or cos θ = 12, giving θ = 60° or 300°.
Hence θ = 0°, 60°, 180°, 300° or 360°. (Check θ = 300°: sin 600° = sin 240° = −√32 and sin 300° = −√32, which agree. Note that dividing by sin θ instead of factorising would lose the solutions 0°, 180° and 360°.)

questions.t: State the natural domain of each function.
p: y = 6<var>x</var> − 11
y = 4x + 6
y = √(<var>x</var> − 9)
y = 5x2 − 16
ap: All real numbers.
<var>x</var> ≠ −6, since the denominator <var>x</var> + 6 must not be 0.
<var>x</var> ≥ 9, since √ is only defined for a non-negative number, so we need <var>x</var> − 9 ≥ 0.
All real numbers except <var>x</var> = 4 and <var>x</var> = −4, because <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 16 = 0 exactly when <var>x</var> = 4 or <var>x</var> = −4.

questions.t: Let f(<var>x</var>) = 4 − 3<var>x</var> and g(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 5. Find and simplify:
p: g(2<var>t</var>)
f(<var>a</var>) + g(<var>a</var>)
ap: g(2<var>t</var>) = (2<var>t</var>)<sup>2</sup> − 5 = 4<var>t</var><sup>2</sup> − 5.
f(<var>a</var>) + g(<var>a</var>) = (4 − 3<var>a</var>) + (<var>a</var><sup>2</sup> − 5) = <var>a</var><sup>2</sup> − 3<var>a</var> − 1.

questions.t: For each relation below, state whether <var>y</var> is a function of <var>x</var>. Justify each answer using the vertical line test: either say that each value of <var>x</var> gives exactly one value of <var>y</var>, or give one value of <var>x</var> that gives two different values of <var>y</var>.
p: y = 7 − 2<var>x</var>
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 36
<var>x</var> = <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 1
ap: Yes, <var>y</var> is a function of <var>x</var>. Each value of <var>x</var> gives exactly one value of 7 − 2<var>x</var>, so every vertical line <var>x</var> = c meets the line at exactly one point.

No. Putting <var>x</var> = 0 gives <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 36, so <var>y</var> = 6 or <var>y</var> = −6. The vertical line <var>x</var> = 0 meets the circle at (0, 6) and (0, −6), so the vertical line test fails.

No. Putting <var>x</var> = 5 gives <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 4, so <var>y</var> = 2 or <var>y</var> = −2. The vertical line <var>x</var> = 5 meets the graph at (5, 2) and (5, −2), so the vertical line test fails.

questions.t: State the domain and the range of each function.
p: f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 7
f(<var>x</var>) = 9 − <var>x</var><sup>2</sup>
f(x) = 3x − 4
ap: Domain: all real numbers. Range: <var>y</var> ≥ 7. (The graph is the parabola y = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> translated 7 units up, with minimum point (0, 7).)
Domain: all real numbers. Range: <var>y</var> ≤ 9. (The graph is y = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> reflected in the <var>x</var>-axis and translated 9 units up, with maximum point (0, 9).)
Domain: x ≠ 4. Range: y ≠ 0, because 3x − 4 is never 0, while every non-zero value y is obtained by taking x = 4 + 3y.

questions.t: Let f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup>. For each graph below, describe fully the transformation of the graph of y = f(<var>x</var>) that produces it, and write the equation of the new graph in terms of <var>x</var>.
p: y = f(<var>x</var>) − 6
y = −f(<var>x</var>)
y = f(<var>x</var> − 4)
y = 3f(<var>x</var>)
ap: Translation of 6 units down; y = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 6.
Reflection in the <var>x</var>-axis; y = −<var>x</var><sup>3</sup>.
Translation of 4 units to the right (in the positive <var>x</var>-direction); y = (<var>x</var> − 4)<sup>3</sup>.
Stretch from the <var>x</var>-axis by a factor of 3, so each y-value is trebled; y = 3<var>x</var><sup>3</sup>.

questions.t: Find the inverse function f−1(x) of each function, by writing y = f(x), interchanging x and y, and making y the subject. (Recall that f−1 means the inverse function, not the reciprocal 1f(x).)
p: f(<var>x</var>) = 5<var>x</var> − 3
f(<var>x</var>) = 4 − 3<var>x</var>
f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 8
ap: y = 5x − 3, so x = 5y − 3, giving 5y = x + 3 and f−1(x) = x + 35.
y = 4 − 3x, so x = 4 − 3y, giving 3y = 4 − x and f−1(x) = 4 − x3.

y = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 8, so <var>x</var> = y<sup>3</sup> + 8, giving y<sup>3</sup> = <var>x</var> − 8 and f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> − 8)<sup>⅓</sup>, the cube root of <var>x</var> − 8. Check: f(f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>)) = (<var>x</var> − 8) + 8 = <var>x</var>.

questions.t: Let f(<var>x</var>) = 3<var>x</var> − 1 and g(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2. Find, simplifying where possible:
p: g(f(<var>x</var>))
f(g(<var>x</var>))
ap: g(f(<var>x</var>)) = (3<var>x</var> − 1)<sup>2</sup> + 2 = 9<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> + 1 + 2 = 9<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> + 3.

f(g(<var>x</var>)) = 3(<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2) − 1 = 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6 − 1 = 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5. Check by substituting <var>x</var> = 2: c gives 36 − 12 + 3 = 27 and d gives 12 + 5 = 17, agreeing with a and b. Notice f(g(<var>x</var>)) ≠ g(f(<var>x</var>)).

questions.t: Let f(x) = 1x − 5 and g(x) = x + 2.
p: State the domain of f(<var>x</var>).
Find f(g(<var>x</var>)) in simplest form and state its domain.
Explain why f(g(3)) is not defined.
ap: The domain of f is <var>x</var> ≠ 5, since the denominator <var>x</var> − 5 must not be 0.
f(g(x)) = 1(x + 2) − 5 = 1x − 3, whose domain is x ≠ 3.
g(3) = 3 + 2 = 5, and 5 is not in the domain of f, so f(g(3)) would be 15 − 5 = 10, which is not defined. This agrees with part b: x = 3 is excluded from the domain of f(g(x)).

questions.t: Each function below has domain all real numbers. Use the horizontal line test to decide whether it has an inverse function. Give a reason; where the answer is no, give two different values of <var>x</var> that have the same value of f(<var>x</var>).
p: f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6
f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 4
f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup>
ap: No inverse function. f(2) = 4 + 6 = 10 and f(−2) = 4 + 6 = 10, so the horizontal line y = 10 meets the graph at the two points (2, 10) and (−2, 10). The horizontal line test fails. (An inverse would have to send 10 to both 2 and −2, which no function can do.)

It does have an inverse function. For any number c, the equation <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> − 4 = c has the single solution <var>x</var> = (c + 4)<sup>⅓</sup>, so each horizontal line y = c meets the graph exactly once. The inverse is f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> + 4)<sup>⅓</sup>.
No inverse function. f(1) = 1 and f(−1) = 1, so the horizontal line y = 1 meets the graph at (1, 1) and (−1, 1). The horizontal line test fails.

questions.t: Let f(x) = 1x + 4.
p: State the domain and the range of f(<var>x</var>).
Find the inverse function f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>), and state its domain and its range.
Verify your answer by showing that f<sup>−1</sup>(f(<var>x</var>)) = <var>x</var> for every <var>x</var> ≠ −4.
ap: Domain: x ≠ −4. Range: y ≠ 0, because 1x + 4 is never 0; every non-zero y occurs, since x = 1y − 4 gives f(x) = y.

Write y = 1x + 4 and interchange x and y: x = 1y + 4. Then y + 4 = 1x, so y = 1x − 4. Hence f−1(x) = 1x − 4. Its domain is x ≠ 0 (which is the range of f) and its range is y ≠ −4 (which is the domain of f).
Since f(x) = 1x + 4, the reciprocal of f(x) is x + 4. Therefore f−1(f(x)) = (x + 4) − 4 = x, as required.

questions.t: Let f(<var>x</var>) = 3<sup><var>x</var></sup> − 2.
p: State the domain and the range of f(<var>x</var>).
Find f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>).
State the domain and the range of f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>).
ap: Domain: all real numbers. The graph of y = 3<sup><var>x</var></sup> is translated 2 units down, so the horizontal asymptote is y = −2. Since 3<sup><var>x</var></sup> > 0 for every <var>x</var>, the range is <var>y</var> > −2.

Write y = 3<sup><var>x</var></sup> − 2 and interchange <var>x</var> and y: <var>x</var> = 3<sup>y</sup> − 2, so 3<sup>y</sup> = <var>x</var> + 2 and y = log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var> + 2). Hence f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) = log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var> + 2).

The domain of f<sup>−1</sup> is <var>x</var> + 2 > 0, that is <var>x</var> > −2 (the range of f), and the range of f<sup>−1</sup> is all real numbers (the domain of f). Check: f<sup>−1</sup>(f(1)) = log<sub>3</sub>(3 − 2 + 2) = log<sub>3</sub>3 = 1.

questions.t: Let f(x) = 3x + 5x − 3.
p: State the domain of f(<var>x</var>).
Show that f(f(<var>x</var>)) = <var>x</var> for every <var>x</var> in the domain, and hence explain why f is its own inverse function, that is, f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) = f(<var>x</var>).
ap: The domain is <var>x</var> ≠ 3, since the denominator <var>x</var> − 3 must not be 0.

First note f(x) is itself always in the domain of f: f(x) = 3 would need 3x + 5 = 3(x − 3) = 3x − 9, that is 5 = −9, which is impossible. Now f(f(x)) = 3f(x) + 5f(x) − 3. Multiply numerator and denominator by x − 3 (which is non-zero) to clear the inner fractions: f(f(x)) = 3(3x + 5) + 5(x − 3)(3x + 5) − 3(x − 3) = 9x + 15 + 5x − 153x + 5 − 3x + 9 = 14x14 = x. So f(f(x)) = x for all x ≠ 3. Two functions are inverses of each other when each undoes the other; here f composed with f returns every input, so f is the inverse of itself and f−1(x) = 3x + 5x − 3. (Sample check: f(4) = 171 = 17 and f(17) = 5614 = 4.)

questions.t: A function has the form f(<var>x</var>) = <var>a</var><var>x</var> + <var>b</var>, where <var>a</var> and <var>b</var> are constants. It is known that f(2) = 1 and f(5) = 13.
p: Find the values of <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>.
Hence find f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>).
ap: f(2) = 2<var>a</var> + <var>b</var> = 1 and f(5) = 5<var>a</var> + <var>b</var> = 13. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives 3<var>a</var> = 12, so <var>a</var> = 4, and then <var>b</var> = 1 − 2 × 4 = −7. So f(<var>x</var>) = 4<var>x</var> − 7. Check: f(2) = 8 − 7 = 1 and f(5) = 20 − 7 = 13.
Write y = 4x − 7 and interchange: x = 4y − 7, so 4y = x + 7 and f−1(x) = x + 74. Check: f−1(1) = 84 = 2 and f−1(13) = 204 = 5.

questions.t: Let f(<var>x</var>) = 5<var>x</var>.
p: Show that f(<var>a</var> + <var>b</var>) = f(<var>a</var>) + f(<var>b</var>) for all real numbers <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>.
Show that f(k<var>a</var>) = kf(<var>a</var>) for all real numbers k and <var>a</var>.
Now let g(<var>x</var>) = 5<var>x</var> + 3. Show that there are no real numbers <var>a</var> and <var>b</var> whatsoever for which g(<var>a</var> + <var>b</var>) = g(<var>a</var>) + g(<var>b</var>).
ap: f(<var>a</var> + <var>b</var>) = 5(<var>a</var> + <var>b</var>) = 5<var>a</var> + 5<var>b</var> = f(<var>a</var>) + f(<var>b</var>). This holds for all real <var>a</var>, <var>b</var>.
f(k<var>a</var>) = 5(k<var>a</var>) = k(5<var>a</var>) = kf(<var>a</var>), using the associative and commutative laws for multiplication.

g(<var>a</var> + <var>b</var>) = 5(<var>a</var> + <var>b</var>) + 3 = 5<var>a</var> + 5<var>b</var> + 3, while g(<var>a</var>) + g(<var>b</var>) = (5<var>a</var> + 3) + (5<var>b</var> + 3) = 5<var>a</var> + 5<var>b</var> + 6. If these were equal, then subtracting 5<var>a</var> + 5<var>b</var> from both sides would give 3 = 6, which is false. Hence no real numbers <var>a</var>, <var>b</var> satisfy the equation — the two expressions always differ by exactly 3.

questions.t: Let f(<var>x</var>) = 3<sup><var>x</var></sup>.
p: Show that f(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = f(<var>x</var>)f(<var>y</var>) for all real numbers <var>x</var> and <var>y</var>.
Show that f(x − y) = f(x)f(y) for all real numbers x and y.
Find every real number <var>x</var> for which f(2<var>x</var>) = f(<var>x</var> + 3).
ap: f(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = 3<sup><var>x</var> + <var>y</var></sup> = 3<sup><var>x</var></sup> × 3<sup><var>y</var></sup> = f(<var>x</var>)f(<var>y</var>), by the index law a<sup>m</sup> × a<sup>n</sup> = a<sup>m + n</sup>.
f(x − y) = 3x − y = 3x3y = f(x)f(y), by the index law aman = am − n. The division is always allowed because 3y > 0, so it is never 0.

f(2<var>x</var>) = f(<var>x</var> + 3) means 3<sup>2<var>x</var></sup> = 3<sup><var>x</var> + 3</sup>. The function y = 3<sup><var>x</var></sup> is increasing and so passes the horizontal line test: different exponents give different values. Hence the exponents must be equal: 2<var>x</var> = <var>x</var> + 3, so <var>x</var> = 3, and this is the only solution. Check: f(2 × 3) = 3<sup>6</sup> = 729 and f(3 + 3) = 3<sup>6</sup> = 729.

questions.t: In each part, describe every pair of integers that works, not just some examples.
p: Let f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var> + 1. Find all pairs of integers <var>x</var>, <var>y</var> for which f(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = f(<var>x</var>)f(<var>y</var>).
Let h(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var>. Find all pairs of integers <var>x</var>, <var>y</var> for which h(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = h(<var>x</var>)h(<var>y</var>).
ap: f(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> + 1, and f(<var>x</var>)f(<var>y</var>) = (<var>x</var> + 1)(<var>y</var> + 1) = <var>x</var><var>y</var> + <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> + 1. Setting these equal and cancelling <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> + 1 from both sides gives <var>x</var><var>y</var> = 0, so <var>x</var> = 0 or <var>y</var> = 0. Criterion for marking: the pairs are exactly those integer pairs in which at least one of <var>x</var>, <var>y</var> is 0 — for instance (0, 7), (−4, 0) and (0, 0). Any answer stating this criterion is correct.

h(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>) = h(<var>x</var>)h(<var>y</var>) means <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = <var>x</var><var>y</var>. Rearranging, <var>x</var><var>y</var> − <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> = 0, so <var>x</var><var>y</var> − <var>x</var> − <var>y</var> + 1 = 1, that is (<var>x</var> − 1)(<var>y</var> − 1) = 1. Now <var>x</var> − 1 and <var>y</var> − 1 are integers whose product is 1, so either both equal 1, giving <var>x</var> = <var>y</var> = 2, or both equal −1, giving <var>x</var> = <var>y</var> = 0. Hence the only pairs are (2, 2) and (0, 0). Check: 2 + 2 = 4 = 2 × 2 and 0 + 0 = 0 = 0 × 0.

questions.t: A function f(x) whose domain is all real numbers is called even if f(−x) = f(x) for all x, and odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for all x. Assume throughout this question that every function mentioned has domain all real numbers.
p: State whether f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> is even, odd or neither, showing your working.
Prove that if p(<var>x</var>) and q(<var>x</var>) are both odd functions, then the product r(<var>x</var>) = p(<var>x</var>)q(<var>x</var>) is an even function.
Prove that if p(<var>x</var>) and q(<var>x</var>) are both odd functions, then the composite s(<var>x</var>) = p(q(<var>x</var>)) is an odd function.
ap: f(−<var>x</var>) = (−<var>x</var>)<sup>4</sup> − 3(−<var>x</var>)<sup>2</sup> = <var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = f(<var>x</var>), since an even power of −<var>x</var> equals the same power of <var>x</var>. So f is even.

Let <var>x</var> be any real number. Because p is odd, p(−<var>x</var>) = −p(<var>x</var>); because q is odd, q(−<var>x</var>) = −q(<var>x</var>). Then r(−<var>x</var>) = p(−<var>x</var>)q(−<var>x</var>) = (−p(<var>x</var>)) × (−q(<var>x</var>)) = p(<var>x</var>)q(<var>x</var>) = r(<var>x</var>). Since this holds for every <var>x</var>, r is even.

Let <var>x</var> be any real number. Since q is odd, q(−<var>x</var>) = −q(<var>x</var>). Since p is odd, p(−t) = −p(t) for every real number t; apply this with t = q(<var>x</var>). Then s(−<var>x</var>) = p(q(−<var>x</var>)) = p(−q(<var>x</var>)) = −p(q(<var>x</var>)) = −s(<var>x</var>). Since this holds for every <var>x</var>, s is odd.

questions.t: Assume every function mentioned here has domain all real numbers, and use the definitions of even and odd from the previous question.
p: Explain why a function f(<var>x</var>) that is even can never have an inverse function.
Suppose f(<var>x</var>) is odd and does have an inverse function f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>). Prove that f<sup>−1</sup> is also an odd function.
ap: Let f be even. Then f(−1) = f(1), and −1 ≠ 1, so the horizontal line y = f(1) passes through the two different points (1, f(1)) and (−1, f(1)) of the graph. The horizontal line test therefore fails, so f has no inverse function. Put another way, an inverse function would have to send the single number f(1) to both 1 and −1, and no function can take two values at one input.

Let c be any number in the domain of f<sup>−1</sup>, and put <var>a</var> = f<sup>−1</sup>(c), so that f(<var>a</var>) = c. Since f is odd, f(−<var>a</var>) = −f(<var>a</var>) = −c. So −c is also a value of f, hence lies in the domain of f<sup>−1</sup>, and applying f<sup>−1</sup> to f(−<var>a</var>) = −c gives f<sup>−1</sup>(−c) = −<var>a</var> = −f<sup>−1</sup>(c). As c was arbitrary, f<sup>−1</sup>(−<var>x</var>) = −f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) for all <var>x</var> in the domain of f<sup>−1</sup>, so f<sup>−1</sup> is odd. (Example: f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> is odd and f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>⅓</sup> is odd.)

questions.t: Let f(x) = 4x − 1x + 2.
p: State the domain of f(x). Then verify that f(x) = 4 − 9x + 2, and use this form to find the range of f(x).
Find f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) and state its domain and its range.

Solve the equation f(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var>, and explain what your answer tells you about where the graphs of y = f(<var>x</var>) and y = f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>) meet the line y = <var>x</var>.
ap: Domain: x ≠ −2. Verification: 4 − 9x + 2 = 4(x + 2) − 9x + 2 = 4x + 8 − 9x + 2 = 4x − 1x + 2 = f(x). Since x + 2 ≠ 0, the term 9x + 2 is never 0, so f(x) ≠ 4; and every value y ≠ 4 is reached, because 9x + 2 = 4 − y can be solved for x whenever 4 − y ≠ 0. Range: y ≠ 4.

Write y = 4x − 1x + 2 and interchange x and y: x = 4y − 1y + 2. Then x(y + 2) = 4y − 1, so xy + 2x = 4y − 1, giving xy − 4y = −1 − 2x, so y(x − 4) = −(2x + 1) and y = 2x + 14 − x. Hence f−1(x) = 2x + 14 − x, with domain x ≠ 4 (the range of f) and range y ≠ −2 (the domain of f). Check: f(0) = −12 = −½ and f−1(−½) = −1 + 14 + ½ = 0.

f(x) = x gives 4x − 1x + 2 = x, so 4x − 1 = x(x + 2) = x2 + 2x, that is x2 − 2x + 1 = 0, so (x − 1)2 = 0 and x = 1 is the only solution. (It is allowed, since 1 ≠ −2.) So the graph of y = f(x) meets the line y = x at exactly one point, (1, 1). Because the graph of y = f−1(x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and (1, 1) lies on that line, (1, 1) is also the only point where y = f−1(x) meets y = x. Direct check: f−1(1) = 33 = 1.

questions.t: Find the exact value of each of the following.
p: cos 150°
sin 225°
tan 300°
ap: 150° is in the second quadrant with related angle 30°, and cosine is negative there, so cos 150° = −√32.
225° is in the third quadrant with related angle 45°, and sine is negative there, so sin 225° = −1√2 = −√22.
300° is in the fourth quadrant with related angle 60°, and tangent is negative there, so tan 300° = −√3.

questions.t: Circles in the coordinate plane.
p: Write <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> + 10<var>y</var> + 25 = 0 in the form (<var>x</var> − <var>h</var>)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − <var>k</var>)<sup>2</sup> = <var>r</var><sup>2</sup>, and state the centre and the radius of the circle.
Write down the equation of the circle with centre (−2, 4) and radius √7.
ap: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 6<var>x</var> = (<var>x</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup> − 9 and <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> + 10<var>y</var> = (<var>y</var> + 5)<sup>2</sup> − 25, so the equation becomes (<var>x</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup> − 9 + (<var>y</var> + 5)<sup>2</sup> − 25 + 25 = 0, that is (<var>x</var> − 3)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> + 5)<sup>2</sup> = 9. Centre (3, −5), radius 3.
(<var>x</var> + 2)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> − 4)<sup>2</sup> = 7.

questions.t: <var>y</var> is inversely proportional to the square of <var>x</var>, and <var>y</var> = 12 when <var>x</var> = 3.
p: Find the constant of proportionality and write the formula for <var>y</var> in terms of <var>x</var>.
Find <var>y</var> when <var>x</var> = 6.
Find the positive value of <var>x</var> for which <var>y</var> = 27.
ap: y = kx2, so 12 = k9 and k = 108. Hence y = 108x2.
y = 10836 = 3.
27 = 108x2 gives x2 = 4, so the positive value is x = 2.

questions.t: Solve each equation for <var>x</var>.
p: log<sub>2</sub>(3<var>x</var> − 1) = 5
log<sub>5</sub><var>x</var> + log<sub>5</sub>3 = 2
log<sub><var>x</var></sub>81 = 4
log<sub>3</sub>(<var>x</var> + 4) − log<sub>3</sub>2 = 2
ap: 3<var>x</var> − 1 = 2<sup>5</sup> = 32, so 3<var>x</var> = 33 and <var>x</var> = 11.
log5(3x) = 2, so 3x = 52 = 25 and x = 253.
<var>x</var><sup>4</sup> = 81 with <var>x</var> > 0, so <var>x</var> = 3.
log3(x + 42) = 2, so x + 42 = 32 = 9, giving x + 4 = 18 and x = 14.

questions.t: f(<var>x</var>) = 3<var>x</var> − 5 and g(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup>.
p: Find f(g(2)).
Find g(f(2)).
Find f(g(<var>x</var>)) in simplest form.
Find f<sup>−1</sup>(<var>x</var>).
ap: f(g(<var>x</var>)) = 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 5.
Put y = 3x − 5 and swap: x = 3y − 5, so y = x + 53. Hence f−1(x) = x + 53.

questions.t: Solve each equation for 0° ≤ <var>θ</var> < 360°.
p: 2 sin <var>θ</var> + 1 = 0
√3 tan <var>θ</var> + 1 = 0
2 cos <var>θ</var> − √2 = 0
ap: sin <var>θ</var> = −½, related angle 30°, sine negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so <var>θ</var> = 210° or 330°.
tan θ = −1√3, related angle 30°, tangent negative in the second and fourth quadrants, so θ = 150° or 330°.
cos θ = √22 = 1√2, related angle 45°, cosine positive in the first and fourth quadrants, so θ = 45° or 315°.

questions.t: P(<var>x</var>) = 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 13<var>x</var> + <var>a</var>.
p: Find <var>a</var>, given that P(2) = 0.
Using this value of <var>a</var>, factorise P(<var>x</var>) completely.
Hence solve P(<var>x</var>) = 0.
ap: P(2) = 2 × 8 + 4 − 26 + <var>a</var> = <var>a</var> − 6, and this is 0, so <var>a</var> = 6.

Since P(2) = 0, <var>x</var> − 2 is a factor. Dividing 2<var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 13<var>x</var> + 6 by <var>x</var> − 2 gives the quotient 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 3, and 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 5<var>x</var> − 3 = (2<var>x</var> − 1)(<var>x</var> + 3). So P(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> − 2)(2<var>x</var> − 1)(<var>x</var> + 3).
<var>x</var> = 2, <var>x</var> = ½ or <var>x</var> = −3.

questions.t: A hiker leaves camp <var>P</var>, walks 8 km due east to point <var>Q</var>, then walks 6 km due south to point <var>R</var>.
p: Find the distance <var>PR</var>.
Find the bearing of <var>R</var> from <var>P</var>, to the nearest degree.
Find the bearing of <var>P</var> from <var>R</var>, to the nearest degree.
ap: ∠<var>PQR</var> = 90°, so <var>PR</var> = √(8<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup>) = √100 = 10 km.
From P, the point R is 8 km east and 6 km south. If α is the angle between due south and PR, then tan α = 86, so α = 53.13°. The bearing is 180° − 53.13° = 126.87°, that is 127°T.
The bearing of <var>P</var> from <var>R</var> is the back bearing, 126.87° + 180° = 306.87°, that is 307°T.

questions.t: In a group of 80 Year 10 students, 50 study Music, 32 study Drama and 18 study both subjects. One of the 80 students is chosen at random.
p: Find the probability that the student studies Music or Drama or both.
Find the probability that the student studies neither subject.
Given that the student studies Drama, find the probability that they also study Music.
Are the events 'studies Music' and 'studies Drama' independent? Support your answer with a calculation.
ap: The number studying at least one subject is 50 + 32 − 18 = 64, so the probability is 6480 = 45.
80 − 64 = 16 study neither, so the probability is 1680 = 15.
P(Music | Drama) = 1832 = 916.

Not independent. P(Music) = 5080 = 58 = 0.625 and P(Drama) = 3280 = 0.4, so P(Music) × P(Drama) = 0.25, while P(Music and Drama) = 1880 = 0.225. Since 0.225 ≠ 0.25 the events are not independent. (Equivalently, P(Music | Drama) = 916 ≠ 1016 = P(Music).)

questions.t: Ten students each completed a puzzle. Their times, in minutes, were 9, 11, 12, 15, 15, 15, 18, 21, 24, 30.
p: Find the mean.
Find the median.
Find the interquartile range.
Find the standard deviation, correct to two decimal places. Divide the sum of the squared deviations by 10, the number of scores.
ap: The total is 170, so the mean is 17010 = 17 minutes.
With 10 scores the median is the average of the 5th and 6th scores: 15 + 152 = 15 minutes.
The lower half is 9, 11, 12, 15, 15 so Q<sub>1</sub> = 12; the upper half is 15, 18, 21, 24, 30 so Q<sub>3</sub> = 21. IQR = 21 − 12 = 9 minutes.
The squared deviations from 17 are 64, 36, 25, 4, 4, 4, 1, 16, 49 and 169, with total 372. The variance is 37210 = 37.2, so the standard deviation is √37.2 ≈ 6.10 minutes.

questions.t: Find the coordinates of the points of intersection of each pair of graphs.
p: <var>y</var> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 5 and <var>y</var> = 3<var>x</var> + 1
<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = 25 and <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 1
y = 6x and y = x + 1
ap: <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 5 = 3<var>x</var> + 1 gives <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − <var>x</var> − 6 = 0, so (<var>x</var> − 3)(<var>x</var> + 2) = 0 and <var>x</var> = 3 or <var>x</var> = −2. The points are (3, 10) and (−2, −5).

<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + (<var>x</var> + 1)<sup>2</sup> = 25 gives 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 24 = 0, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> − 12 = 0 and (<var>x</var> + 4)(<var>x</var> − 3) = 0. The points are (3, 4) and (−4, −3).
6x = x + 1 gives x2 + x − 6 = 0 (x ≠ 0), so (x + 3)(x − 2) = 0. The points are (2, 3) and (−3, −2).

questions.t: <var>ABCDEFGH</var> is a rectangular prism. <var>ABCD</var> is the horizontal base, with <var>AB</var> = 12 cm and <var>BC</var> = 5 cm. The four vertical edges <var>AE</var>, <var>BF</var>, <var>CG</var> and <var>DH</var> are each 6 cm long, with <var>E</var> directly above <var>A</var>, <var>F</var> directly above <var>B</var>, <var>G</var> directly above <var>C</var> and <var>H</var> directly above <var>D</var>.
p: Find the exact length of the diagonal <var>AG</var>.
Find the angle that <var>AG</var> makes with the base <var>ABCD</var>, correct to one decimal place.
ap: <var>ABCD</var> is a rectangle with ∠<var>ABC</var> = 90°, so <var>AC</var><sup>2</sup> = 12<sup>2</sup> + 5<sup>2</sup> = 169 and <var>AC</var> = 13 cm. <var>CG</var> ⊥ base, so ∠<var>ACG</var> = 90° and <var>AG</var><sup>2</sup> = 13<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup> = 205, giving <var>AG</var> = √205 cm (≈ 14.32 cm).
The required angle is ∠GAC, since AC is the projection of AG onto the base. tan ∠GAC = 613 = 0.46154, so ∠GAC ≈ 24.8°.

questions.t: Circle geometry.
p: Two chords <var>AC</var> and <var>BD</var> of a circle meet at a point <var>E</var> inside the circle. Given that <var>AE</var> = 8 cm, <var>EC</var> = 3 cm and <var>BE</var> = 6 cm, find <var>ED</var>.

<var>PT</var> is a tangent to a circle, touching it at <var>T</var>. A second line through <var>P</var> cuts the circle at <var>X</var> and then again at <var>Y</var>, with <var>X</var> between <var>P</var> and <var>Y</var>. Given that <var>PX</var> = 4 cm and <var>XY</var> = 12 cm, find <var>PT</var>.

<var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var> and <var>D</var> lie in this order around a circle with centre <var>O</var>, so that <var>B</var> lies on the major arc <var>AC</var> and <var>D</var> lies on the minor arc <var>AC</var>. The angle ∠<var>AOC</var> standing on the minor arc <var>AC</var> is 130°. Find ∠<var>ABC</var> and ∠<var>ADC</var>.
ap: Intersecting chords: <var>AE</var> × <var>EC</var> = <var>BE</var> × <var>ED</var>, so 8 × 3 = 6 × <var>ED</var>, giving <var>ED</var> = 4 cm.
<var>PY</var> = <var>PX</var> + <var>XY</var> = 4 + 12 = 16 cm. The tangent-secant result gives <var>PT</var><sup>2</sup> = <var>PX</var> × <var>PY</var> = 4 × 16 = 64, so <var>PT</var> = 8 cm.

B is on the major arc, so ∠ABC is the angle at the circumference standing on the same (minor) arc AC as ∠AOC. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so ∠ABC = 130°2 = 65°. ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, so its opposite angles ∠ABC and ∠ADC are supplementary: ∠ADC = 180° − 65° = 115°.

questions.t: A yacht leaves marina <var>M</var> and sails 12 km on a bearing of 040°T to buoy <var>B</var>. It then sails 9 km on a bearing of 160°T to buoy <var>C</var>.
p: Show that ∠<var>MBC</var> = 60°.
Find the distance <var>MC</var>, correct to one decimal place.
Find the bearing of <var>M</var> from <var>C</var>, to the nearest degree.
ap: The bearing of <var>M</var> from <var>B</var> is the back bearing of 040°T, namely 040° + 180° = 220°T. The bearing of <var>C</var> from <var>B</var> is 160°T. Hence ∠<var>MBC</var> = 220° − 160° = 60°.
By the cosine rule in △<var>MBC</var>: <var>MC</var><sup>2</sup> = 12<sup>2</sup> + 9<sup>2</sup> − 2 × 12 × 9 × cos 60° = 144 + 81 − 108 = 117, so <var>MC</var> = √117 ≈ 10.8 km.

By the cosine rule, cos ∠BCM = 92 + 117 − 1222 × 9 × √117 = 54194.70 = 0.27736, so ∠BCM ≈ 73.9°. The bearing of B from C is the back bearing of 160°T, namely 340°T, and M lies 73.9° anticlockwise from that direction, so the bearing of M from C is 340° − 73.9° = 266.1°, that is 266°T.

questions.t: <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, <var>C</var> and <var>D</var> lie in this order around a circle. The chords <var>AC</var> and <var>BD</var> meet at right angles at the point <var>E</var> inside the circle. <var>AC</var> = 12 cm, <var>BD</var> = 12 cm, <var>AE</var> = <var>x</var> cm and <var>BE</var> = <var>y</var> cm.
p: Write down <var>CE</var> in terms of <var>x</var>, and <var>DE</var> in terms of <var>y</var>.
Use the intersecting-chords result to show that either <var>x</var> = <var>y</var> or <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 12.
The area of △<var>ABE</var> is 8 cm<sup>2</sup>. Show that <var>xy</var> = 16.
Given also that <var>x</var> > <var>y</var>, find the exact values of <var>x</var> and <var>y</var>.
ap: <var>CE</var> = (12 − <var>x</var>) cm and <var>DE</var> = (12 − <var>y</var>) cm.

Intersecting chords give <var>AE</var> × <var>EC</var> = <var>BE</var> × <var>ED</var>, so <var>x</var>(12 − <var>x</var>) = <var>y</var>(12 − <var>y</var>). Then 12<var>x</var> − <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 12<var>y</var> − <var>y</var><sup>2</sup>, so 12(<var>x</var> − <var>y</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − <var>y</var><sup>2</sup> = (<var>x</var> − <var>y</var>)(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var>), giving (<var>x</var> − <var>y</var>)(<var>x</var> + <var>y</var> − 12) = 0. Hence <var>x</var> = <var>y</var> or <var>x</var> + <var>y</var> = 12.
∠<var>AEB</var> = 90°, so <var>AE</var> and <var>BE</var> are the base and height of △<var>ABE</var>: area = ½ × <var>x</var> × <var>y</var> = 8, so <var>xy</var> = 16.

If x = y then x2 = 16 and x = y = 4, which contradicts x > y. So x + y = 12 and xy = 16, meaning x and y are the roots of t2 − 12t + 16 = 0. Then t = 12 ± √(144 − 64)2 = 12 ± 4√52 = 6 ± 2√5. Since x > y, x = 6 + 2√5 (≈ 10.47) and y = 6 − 2√5 (≈ 1.53).

questions.t: A circular garden bed has centre (2, −1) and radius 5, where 1 unit represents 1 m. A straight path runs along the line <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 2.
p: Write down the equation of the circle forming the edge of the garden bed.
Find the coordinates of the two points where the path crosses the edge of the bed.
Find the exact length of the part of the path that lies inside the bed.
Find the exact shortest distance from the centre of the bed to the path.
ap: (<var>x</var> − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>y</var> + 1)<sup>2</sup> = 25.

Substituting <var>y</var> = <var>x</var> + 2: (<var>x</var> − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (<var>x</var> + 3)<sup>2</sup> = 25, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> + 4 + <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 6<var>x</var> + 9 = 25, giving 2<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + 2<var>x</var> − 12 = 0, so <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> − 6 = 0 and (<var>x</var> − 2)(<var>x</var> + 3) = 0. The crossing points are (2, 4) and (−3, −1).

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so half the chord is 5√22. The distance d satisfies d2 = 52 − (5√22)2 = 25 − 12.5 = 12.5, so d = √12.5 = 5√22 m ≈ 3.54 m. (Check: the midpoint of the chord is (−½, 1½), and its distance from (2, −1) is √(2.52 + 2.52) = √12.5.)

questions.t: The number of bacteria in a culture <var>t</var> hours after it is set up is <var>N</var> = 200 × 2<sup><var>t</var>/3</sup>.
p: How many bacteria are there 9 hours after the culture is set up?
Find the exact value of <var>t</var> for which <var>N</var> = 5000, giving it in the form <var>t</var> = 3 log<sub>2</sub><var>k</var>, and hence give <var>t</var> correct to one decimal place.
Rearrange the formula to express <var>t</var> in terms of <var>N</var>.
ap: <var>t</var> = 9 gives <var>N</var> = 200 × 2<sup>3</sup> = 200 × 8 = 1600 bacteria.
200 × 2t/3 = 5000, so 2t/3 = 25, hence t3 = log225 and t = 3 log225 (so k = 25). Numerically log225 = log1025log102 = 1.397940.30103 = 4.6439, so t = 3 × 4.6439 ≈ 13.9 hours.
2t/3 = N200, so t3 = log2(N200) and t = 3 log2(N200).

questions.t: P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + <var>ax</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>bx</var> − 12, and both <var>x</var> − 2 and <var>x</var> + 3 are factors of P(<var>x</var>).
p: Find <var>a</var> and <var>b</var>.
Factorise P(<var>x</var>) completely.
Solve P(<var>x</var>) = 0.
Hence solve <var>x</var><sup>6</sup> + 3<var>x</var><sup>4</sup> − 4<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 12 = 0.
ap: P(2) = 8 + 4<var>a</var> + 2<var>b</var> − 12 = 0 gives 2<var>a</var> + <var>b</var> = 2. P(−3) = −27 + 9<var>a</var> − 3<var>b</var> − 12 = 0 gives 3<var>a</var> − <var>b</var> = 13. Adding, 5<var>a</var> = 15, so <var>a</var> = 3 and <var>b</var> = 2 − 6 = −4. Hence P(<var>x</var>) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> − 12.

Dividing by (<var>x</var> − 2)(<var>x</var> + 3) = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> + <var>x</var> − 6 gives the linear factor <var>x</var> + 2, so P(<var>x</var>) = (<var>x</var> − 2)(<var>x</var> + 2)(<var>x</var> + 3). (Check by expanding: (<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4)(<var>x</var> + 3) = <var>x</var><sup>3</sup> + 3<var>x</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>x</var> − 12.)
<var>x</var> = 2, <var>x</var> = −2 or <var>x</var> = −3.

Put <var>u</var> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup>. The equation becomes <var>u</var><sup>3</sup> + 3<var>u</var><sup>2</sup> − 4<var>u</var> − 12 = 0, which is P(<var>u</var>) = 0, so <var>u</var> = 2, −2 or −3. Since <var>u</var> = <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> ≥ 0, only <var>u</var> = 2 is possible, giving <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> = 2 and <var>x</var> = √2 or <var>x</var> = −√2.

questions.t: A bag contains 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green marbles, identical apart from colour. Three marbles are drawn one at a time, without replacement.
p: Find the probability that all three marbles are red.
Find the probability that one marble of each colour is drawn.
Find the probability that at least one green marble is drawn.
Given that no red marble is drawn, find the probability that all three marbles are blue.
questions.al: There are 12 marbles altogether.
ap: 512 × 411 × 310 = 601320 = 122.

One particular order, say red then blue then green, has probability 512 × 411 × 310 = 122, and every one of the 3! = 6 orders of the three colours has the same probability, so the answer is 6 × 122 = 311.
P(no green) = 912 × 811 × 710 = 5041320 = 2155, so P(at least one green) = 1 − 2155 = 3455.
If no red is drawn, the three marbles come from the 4 blue and 3 green, so the required probability is 47 × 36 × 25 = 24210 = 435.

chapters.focus: Fraction-decimal conversion, multiplying and dividing by a decimal, recurring decimals and rounding.
Unit conversions, the unitary method, perimeter and composite areas, volume of prisms, elapsed time and average speed.
A full review of Chapters 1–9, then number bases, binary arithmetic and written problem-solving arguments.
Angle sum and exterior angle theorem, isosceles and equilateral triangles, circle vocabulary, ruler-and-compasses constructions, and the angle sum of a quadrilateral.
Ordering negative fractions, the four operations with negative fractions and decimals, order of operations, and substituting negative values into expressions.
Converting between percentages, fractions and decimals; one quantity as a percentage of another; percentage of a quantity; simplifying and dividing in a ratio; unit prices and best buys.
Sample spaces, favourable outcomes, complementary ('not') events, and probabilities read from grouped counts.
Translations, rotations and reflections in the Cartesian plane, combinations of transformations, and rotational and reflection symmetry.
Reading and constructing tables, pictograms, column graphs, divided bar charts, pie charts, line graphs, conversion graphs and travel graphs.
Frequency tables, dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots; mode, median, mean and range, including working backwards from a given mean.
Faces, edges and vertices; Euler's formula; prisms, pyramids and the Platonic solids; front, side and plan views.
Integers on the number line, adding and subtracting negatives, products and quotients, order of operations with indices, the Cartesian plane and negative fractions.
Angles at a point, transversals and parallel lines, angle sums of triangles and quadrilaterals, isosceles and equilateral triangles — always with reasons.
Substitution with negatives and powers, expanding brackets, collecting like terms, solving multi-step equations and simplifying algebraic fractions.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage of a quantity; sums, differences and products of percentages; increase, decrease, discount, profit and loss; the unitary method and GST.
Hypotenuse and shorter sides, the converse test, irrational answers to 2 decimal places, and multi-step problems in composite and 3-D figures.
Mixed revision of the year's topics, then modular arithmetic: congruences, powers modulo n and divisibility tests.
Unitary method, rates and unit conversion, speed, simplifying ratios, dividing a quantity in a given ratio, and scale drawings.
Expanding with negatives, adding algebraic fractions, solving equations that contain fractions, and building equations for number, money and speed problems.
The four congruence tests (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS), writing proofs with full reasons, and the isosceles and equilateral triangle theorems.
Angle and length chases in parallelograms, rhombuses, rectangles and squares, and congruence proofs of their diagonal properties and tests.
Circumference and area of circles, sectors and semicircles, annuluses, and composite figures — exact answers in terms of π and approximations using π ≈ 22/7 or 3.14.
Areas of parallelograms, trapeziums, rhombuses and kites; volumes of prisms and cylinders; surface area; converting area and volume units; elapsed time.
Sample spaces and complements, ‘or’ and ‘and’ with the addition rule, two-way tables and Venn diagrams.
Substituting into formulas and solving for any pronumeral, taking out the highest common factor, expanding binomial products and factorising monic quadratics.
Tables of values, y = mx + c, gradient and y-intercept, points on a line, constant-rate graphs and non-linear graphs.
Mean versus median, stem-and-leaf plots, sampling, and the variability of sample means and proportions.
Ratios and rates, algebraic fractions and equations, congruence and quadrilaterals, circles and solids, probability, factorising and straight lines.
Substitution, like terms, algebraic fractions, expanding brackets, binomial products, perfect squares and the difference of two squares.
Exact surd arithmetic, rationalising binomial denominators, Pythagoras in three dimensions, and recurring decimals as fractions.
Percentages of quantities, commission, profit and loss, income tax, simple interest, GST, reversing a percentage change, repeated increases and decreases, compound interest and depreciation.
Common factors, the difference of two squares, simple quadratics and perfect squares — and choosing the right method when more than one is needed.
Equations with brackets, fractions and decimals; literal equations; word problems involving money, perimeter and rates; solving linear inequalities.
Substituting into formulas, changing the subject, and constructing a formula from a description.
Angle chasing with reasons, the four congruence tests, and proofs about parallelograms, rhombuses, rectangles and squares.
Zero, negative and fractional indices, scientific notation, significant figures, and indices with a pronumeral in the exponent.
Enlargements and scale, similarity ratios, the AAA, SAS, SSS and RHS similarity tests, and similarity proofs that produce lengths, parallel lines and midpoint results.
Whole-year revision — algebraic fractions, surds and Pythagoras, indices and standard form, percentages and interest, equations, formulas, similarity — then multi-step problem-solving.
Distance and midpoint of an interval, gradient, equations of straight lines, parallel and perpendicular lines, and circles with centre the origin.
Sample spaces and events, the complement, union and intersection, two-way tables, relative frequency, arrays and tree diagrams, and two-step experiments with and without replacement.
Naming sides, the three basic ratios, finding unknown sides and angles, exact values, angles of elevation and depression, true bearings and multi-step problems.
Substitution and elimination (including multiplying both equations), worded problems needing two pronumerals, concurrency, areas of triangles cut off by lines, and families of lines.
Grouping in pairs, factorising the general quadratic ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c, algebraic fractions, and completing the square.
Composite areas and sectors, surface area and volume of prisms and cylinders, reversing a formula, converting area and volume units, and very small or very large units.
Solving quadratics by factorising (including when the coefficient of <var>x</var><sup>2</sup> is not 1), quadratics in disguise, applications, completing the square and turning points of parabolas.
Converting rates, average speed, straight-line rate formulas, finding constants of proportionality, and the effect of scaling or percentage changes.
Stem-and-leaf and back-to-back plots, grouped data and histograms, mean, median, mode and range, and weighted averages.
Reversing a percentage change, repeated increases and decreases, and the compound interest and depreciation formulas.
Simplifying and combining surds, expanding binomial products, and rationalising single-term and binomial denominators.
Expanding and factorising (including surds and non-monic quadratics), linear inequalities, rearranging formulas, and algebraic fractions.
Distance, midpoint and gradient; every form of the equation of a line; perpendicular bisectors; simultaneous equations and the problems they solve.
Factorising non-monic quadratics, completing the square, the quadratic formula and the discriminant, and word problems that lead to quadratic equations.
Prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres; reversing the formulas, composite solids, frustums, and the area and volume factors under enlargement.
Completing the square, the vertex and axis of symmetry, the discriminant, quadratic inequalities and maximum-minimum applications.
Angle chasing, the four congruence and similarity tests, similar-triangle calculations, and geometric proofs.
Index laws with negative and rational indices, scientific notation and significant figures, exponential graphs and equations, growth and decay models, and logarithms.

Cumulative review: percentage change and compound interest, surds, algebraic fractions, lines, quadratics and the parabola, measurement, similarity, indices and logarithms — then multi-step problem-solving.
Standard form and completing the square for circles, features of rectangular hyperbolas, intersections of lines with circles, parabolas and hyperbolas, and regions of the plane.
Exact values, three-dimensional problems with elevations and bearings, the sine and cosine rules, obtuse angles and the area formula.
